citations.quote:
Throughout, $R$ is a commutative ring, $n\ge0$, and $\lambda\vdash n$ with
Young diagram $[\lambda]$. Tabloids, the left action
$\sigma\cdot\{t\}:=\{\sigma\cdot t\}$ of $S_n$ on the finite set
$\Omega_\lambda$ of $\lambda$-tabloids, and the complex tabloid module
$M^\lambda=\mathbb C^{(\Omega_\lambda)}$ are as in
[[def-young-subgroup-tabloid-and-permutation-module]]: rows are labelled and
the order of entries inside a row is forgotten.

**The tabloid module over $R$.** Put
$$M^\lambda_R:=R^{(\Omega_\lambda)},$$
the free left $R$-module with the tabloids as $R$-basis, and let $S_n$ act on
$M^\lambda_R$ by $R$-linear extension of
$\sigma\cdot\{t\}:=\{\sigma\cdot t\}$ on basis elements. The row-set
computation of [[def-young-subgroup-tabloid-and-permutation-module]] shows
that this rule is well defined on tabloids, and because the action on tableaux
is a left action, $\mathrm{id}\cdot\{t\}=\{t\}$ and
$\sigma\cdot(\tau\cdot\{t\})=(\sigma\tau)\cdot\{t\}$; hence $M^\lambda_R$ is a
left module over $S_n$ and over the group ring $R[S_n]$.

**Antisymmetrizers, polytabloids, and Specht modules.** Let $t$ be a
$\lambda$-tableau with column stabilizer $C_t$
([[def-row-and-column-stabilizers-of-a-tableau]]), and let
$\operatorname{sgn}:S_n\to\{+1,-1\}$ be the sign homomorphism
([[thm-sign-is-a-homomorphism]]); its values are read in $R$ through the
unique unital ring homomorphism $\mathbb Z\to R$. Define
$$\kappa_t:=\sum_{\gamma\in C_t}\operatorname{sgn}(\gamma)\,\gamma\ \in R[S_n],\qquad e_t:=\kappa_t\cdot\{t\}=\sum_{\gamma\in C_t}\operatorname{sgn}(\gamma)\,\{\gamma\cdot t\}\ \in M^\lambda_R,$$
and let
$$S^\lambda_R:=\operatorname{span}_R\{\,e_t:\ t\text{ is a }\lambda\text{-tableau}\,\}\ \subseteq M^\lambda_R.$$
All sums here are finite sums over the finite group $C_t$, so $\kappa_t$,
$e_t$ and $S^\lambda_R$ are well defined for every commutative ring $R$. For
the empty partition the empty tableau is the unique one and has
$C_t=\{1\}$, so $\kappa_t=1$, $e_t=\{\varnothing\}$ and
$S^\varnothing_R=R$. For every tableau $t$ one has $C_t\cap R_t=\{1\}$: a
permutation preserving every row set and every column set must fix the entry
in each row-column intersection, since each intersection contains a single
box. Hence the tabloids $\gamma\cdot\{t\}$, $\gamma\in C_t$, are distinct and
the coefficient of $\{t\}$ in $e_t$ is $1$. Thus $e_t\ne0$ whenever $R$ is
nonzero; if $R$ is the zero ring, then $M^\lambda_R=S^\lambda_R=0$ and
$e_t=0$.

**Covariance of the construction over $R$.** For every $\lambda$-tableau $t$
and every $\sigma\in S_n$,
$$\kappa_{\sigma\cdot t}=\sigma\kappa_t\sigma^{-1}\qquad\text{and}\qquad e_{\sigma\cdot t}=\sigma\cdot e_t,$$
and for every $\gamma\in C_t$ one has $\gamma\cdot e_t=\operatorname{sgn}(\gamma)e_t$.
Consequently $S^\lambda_R$ is an $R[S_n]$-submodule of $M^\lambda_R$, and for
any single $\lambda$-tableau $t$ the orbit of $e_t$ spans $S^\lambda_R$. These
identities are the ones published for $R=\mathbb C$ in
[[lem-polytabloid-covariance-and-column-sign]]; because the argument there
consists only of reindexing the finite sums over $C_t$ and over $C_{\sigma\cdot t}$,
it is valid verbatim over an arbitrary commutative ring. The two reindexings
are written out in the remarks below.

**Agreement with the complex Specht module.** For $R=\mathbb C$ the module
$M^\lambda_{\mathbb C}$, the element $\kappa_t$, the polytabloid $e_t$ and the
space $S^\lambda_{\mathbb C}$ coincide with $M^\lambda$, $\kappa_t$, $e_t$ and
$S^\lambda$ of [[def-column-antisymmetrizer-polytabloid-and-specht-module]]:
the tabloid set and the left action are the same, the permutation sign used
there is the sign of [[thm-sign-is-a-homomorphism]] transported along the
order-preserving relabelling described in that item, and the defining formulas
are identical. In particular every published statement about
$\kappa_t,e_t,S^\lambda$ applies to $S^\lambda_{\mathbb C}$.

Let $n\ge0$ and let $\lambda\vdash n$. Write $M^\lambda_R$ for the free
$R$-module on the $\lambda$-tabloids and $S^\lambda_R$ for the $R$-span of the
polytabloids over a commutative ring $R$
([[def-polytabloid-specht-module-over-an-arbitrary-field]]). Then:

1. **(Integral Garnir relation.)** Let $t$ be a $\lambda$-tableau, let
   $j,j+1$ be adjacent columns, let $X$ be a set of entries of column $j$ and
   $Y$ a set of entries of column $j+1$, with
   $|X|+|Y|>\lambda'_j$. Let $G_{X,Y}:=\sum_{g\in T}\operatorname{sgn}(g)g$,
   where $T$ is any set of representatives containing $1$ for the left cosets
   of $H:=S_X\times S_Y$ in $S_{X\cup Y}$ (the transpositions in $S_X$ and
   $S_Y$ act on the corresponding labels and fix all other labels). Then
   $$G_{X,Y}\,e_t=0\qquad\text{in }M^\lambda_{\mathbb Z};$$
   the same identity holds after base change in $M^\lambda_F$ for every field
   $F$, for the same transversal $T$.
2. **(Straightening over $\mathbb Z$.)** For every $\lambda$-tableau $t$, the
   polytabloid $e_t$ is a finite $\mathbb Z$-linear combination of standard
   $\lambda$-polytabloids.
3. **(Integral and field-uniform basis.)** The standard polytabloids
   $\{e_t:t\text{ standard}\}$ are a $\mathbb Z$-basis of $S^\lambda_{\mathbb Z}$;
   for every field $F$, their images under coefficient reduction are an
   $F$-basis of $S^\lambda_F$. In particular
   $\dim_F S^\lambda_F=f^\lambda$ for every field $F$, including $F$ of
   characteristic $2$.

For every $n\ge0$ and $\lambda\vdash n$, the nonzero complex
$S_n$-representation $S^\lambda$ is irreducible.

For every $n\ge0$, the modules $\{S^\lambda:\lambda\vdash n\}$ form a
complete irredundant list, up to isomorphism, of finite-dimensional irreducible
complex $S_n$-representations.

If $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$ and $S^\lambda\cong S^\mu$ as complex
$S_n$-representations, then $\lambda=\mu$.

Let $G$ be a finite group, let $k$ be a field with
$\operatorname{char} k \nmid |G|$, let $\rho:G \to \operatorname{GL}(V)$ be a
finite-dimensional representation of $G$ over $k$, and let $W \le V$ be a
subrepresentation. Then there is a subrepresentation $U \le V$ such that

$$V=W\oplus U.$$

Let $R$ be a commutative ring ([[def-commutative-ring]]) and let $G$ be a group
([[def-group]]). The **group ring** $R[G]$ is the free left $R$-module on the
set $G$ ([[def-free-module-on-a-set-and-standard-basis]]).

For each $g \in G$, write $[g] \in R[G]$ for the standard basis vector indexed
by $g$. Thus every element of $R[G]$ has a unique expression
$$\sum_{g \in F} r_g [g]$$
with $F \subseteq G$ finite and $r_g \in R$.

The notation is deliberately that of **formal** finite sums: at this stage
$R[G]$ is only the underlying free $R$-module with its distinguished basis. The
multiplication satisfying
$$[g][h]=[gh]$$
and the resulting $R$-algebra structure are constructed in
[[thm-group-ring-is-a-unital-algebra-with-basis-g]].

Let $R$ be a commutative ring and let $G$ be a group. Write $[g] \in R[G]$ for
the basis vector of [[def-group-ring]] indexed by $g \in G$.

There is a unique $R$-bilinear multiplication on $R[G]$ satisfying
$$[g][h]=[gh]\qquad(g,h\in G).$$
With this product, $R[G]$ is a unital $R$-algebra whose underlying
$R$-module has basis $\{[g]:g\in G\}$. Its identity is $[e]$, where $e$ is the
identity of $G$, and every basis element $[g]$ is a unit with inverse
$[g^{-1}]$.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $G$ be a group, and let $M$ be a left
$R$-module. Then:

1. every $R$-linear action of $G$ on $M$ extends uniquely to a left
   $R[G]$-module structure on $M$ satisfying
   $$(r[e]) \cdot m=rm\qquad(r \in R,\ m \in M);$$
2. every left $R[G]$-module structure on $M$ satisfying
   $$(r[e]) \cdot m=rm\qquad(r \in R,\ m \in M)$$
   restricts to an $R$-linear action of $G$ on $M$;
3. these two constructions are inverse to each other.

Moreover, if $M$ and $N$ carry the corresponding structures, then an
$R$-linear map $f:M \to N$ is $G$-equivariant if and only if it is an
$R[G]$-module homomorphism.

Let $V$ and $W$ be irreducible representations of a group $G$ over a field $k$.
Then every nonzero intertwiner $f:V \to W$ is an isomorphism. Consequently
$\operatorname{End}_G(V)$ is a division ring.

Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field, let $G$ be a group, and let $V$ be an
irreducible representation of $G$ over $k$. Then every $T \in \operatorname{End}_G(V)$
is of the form $T=\lambda \operatorname{id}_V$ for some $\lambda \in k$.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring. If $M$ is free with basis $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ and $N$ is free with basis $(f_j)_{j\in J}$, then $M\otimes_RN$ is free with basis

$$\bigl(e_i\otimes f_j\bigr)_{(i,j)\in I\times J}.$$

Equivalently, the canonical map $R^{(I\times J)}\to M\otimes_RN$ sending the standard basis vector at $(i,j)$ to $e_i\otimes f_j$ is an isomorphism. This includes an empty basis in either factor.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $(M_i)_{i\in I}$ be any family of $R$-modules, and let $N$ be an $R$-module. The homomorphism induced by the coordinate inclusions is a natural $R$-module isomorphism

$$\Phi:\bigoplus_{i\in I}(M_i\otimes_RN)\longrightarrow\left(\bigoplus_{i\in I}M_i\right)\otimes_RN,$$

$$\Phi\bigl(\jmath_i(m\otimes n)\bigr)=\jmath_i(m)\otimes n.$$

The same holds with the direct sum in the second variable: there is a natural $R$-module isomorphism

$$\Phi':\bigoplus_{i\in I}(N\otimes_RM_i)\longrightarrow N\otimes_R\left(\bigoplus_{i\in I}M_i\right),\qquad \Phi'\bigl(\jmath_i(n\otimes m)\bigr)=n\otimes\jmath_i(m).$$

The assertion includes $I=\varnothing$, when both sides are zero.

Let $f:R\to S$ be a unital homomorphism of commutative rings ([[def-ring-homomorphism]]).

For an $S$-module $N$, its **restriction of scalars** along $f$, denoted $\operatorname{Res}^S_RN$, is the same abelian group with $R$-action

$$r\cdot n:=f(r)n.$$

For an $R$-module $M$, its **extension of scalars** along $f$ is

$$S\otimes_RM.$$

Here $S$ is an $(S,R)$-bimodule with left action by multiplication and right action $s\cdot r:=s f(r)$ ([[def-bimodule]]). The induced outer action

$$s'(s\otimes m):=(s's)\otimes m$$

makes $S\otimes_RM$ an $S$-module ([[thm-bimodule-actions-induced-on-tensor-products]]).

Restriction acts on a homomorphism by leaving its underlying function unchanged. Extension sends $u:M\to M'$ to $1_S\otimes u:S\otimes_RM\to S\otimes_RM'$.

Let $R$ be a unital ring, $M$ a right $R$-module, and $N$ a left $R$-module. Let

$$F:=\mathbb Z^{(M\times N)}$$

be the free $\mathbb Z$-module on the set $M\times N$ ([[def-free-module-on-a-set-and-standard-basis]], [[thm-universal-property-of-free-modules]]), and write $e_{(m,n)}$ for its standard basis elements. The additive group of $F$ is abelian. Let $H$ be the subgroup generated ([[def-generated-subgroup]]) by all elements

$$e_{(m+m',n)}-e_{(m,n)}-e_{(m',n)},$$

$$e_{(m,n+n')}-e_{(m,n)}-e_{(m,n')},$$

and

$$e_{(mr,n)}-e_{(m,rn)}$$

as $m,m'$ range over $M$, $n,n'$ over $N$, and $r$ over $R$. Since every subgroup of an abelian group is normal, the quotient group $F/H$ is defined ([[def-quotient-group]]). The **tensor product of $M$ and $N$ over $R$** is

$$M\otimes_RN:=F/H.$$

The coset of $e_{(m,n)}$ is the **elementary tensor** $m\otimes n$. Every tensor is a finite sum of elementary tensors, because every element of $F$ is a finite $\mathbb Z$-linear combination of basis elements and integer coefficients may be absorbed into either additive variable. The defining relations give

$$(m+m')\otimes n=m\otimes n+m'\otimes n,\qquad m\otimes(n+n')=m\otimes n+m\otimes n',$$

and

$$(mr)\otimes n=m\otimes(rn).$$

In particular $0\otimes n=0=m\otimes0$. No $R$-module structure on $M\otimes_RN$ is part of this arbitrary-ring definition; at this stage it is an abelian group.

derivations.claim: Fix $\lambda\vdash n$. For every field $E$ the standard polytabloids are an $E$-basis of $S^\lambda_E$, so $\dim_ES^\lambda_E=f^\lambda\ge1$ and $S^\lambda_E\ne0$. If $K/E$ is a field extension, the coefficient inclusion $S^\lambda_E\to S^\lambda_K$ is $E$-linear and sends $e_t$ to $e_t$, so it induces a $K$-linear map $K\otimes_ES^\lambda_E\to S^\lambda_K$ with $1\otimes e_t\mapsto e_t$; this map carries the $K$-basis $(1\otimes e_t)_{t\text{ standard}}$ of $K\otimes_ES^\lambda_E$ to the $K$-basis $(e_t)_{t\text{ standard}}$ of $S^\lambda_K$ and is compatible with the actions because both actions are given by the same formulas on tabloids. Hence $K\otimes_ES^\lambda_E\cong S^\lambda_K$; in particular $S^\lambda_{\mathbb C}\cong\mathbb C\otimes_{\mathbb Q}S^\lambda_{\mathbb Q}$ and $F\otimes_{\mathbb Q}S^\lambda_{\mathbb Q}\cong S^\lambda_F$.

Let $V,W$ be finite-dimensional $ES_n$-modules and $K/E$ a field extension. Choose $E$-bases and identify $\operatorname{Hom}_E(V,W)$ with the space of $k\times m$ matrices, $m=\dim_EV$, $k=\dim_EW$; an element is $ES_n$-linear if and only if $\rho_W(\sigma)A=A\rho_V(\sigma)$ for all $\sigma\in S_n$, a finite system of linear equations with coefficients in $E$. Its solution space is the kernel of a matrix with entries in $E$, and Gaussian elimination over $E$ shows that the rank of such a matrix, hence the dimension of the solution space, is the same over $E$ and over $K$; the $K$-solutions are exactly the $K$-span of the $E$-solutions. In the chosen coordinates this says that the natural map $K\otimes_E\operatorname{Hom}_{ES_n}(V,W)\to\operatorname{Hom}_{KS_n}(K\otimes_EV,K\otimes_EW)$ is an isomorphism.

Taking $E=\mathbb Q$, $K=\mathbb C$ in $1.2$ with $V=W=S^\lambda_{\mathbb Q}$ and using $S^\lambda_{\mathbb C}\cong\mathbb C\otimes_{\mathbb Q}S^\lambda_{\mathbb Q}$ gives $\dim_{\mathbb Q}\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb QS_n}(S^\lambda_{\mathbb Q})=\dim_{\mathbb C}\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb CS_n}(S^\lambda_{\mathbb C})=1$ by [F3, F6]; as the scalars lie in $\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb QS_n}(S^\lambda_{\mathbb Q})$, that endomorphism ring is $\mathbb Q$. For $\lambda\ne\mu$, $1.2$ gives $\mathbb C\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb QS_n}(S^\lambda_{\mathbb Q},S^\mu_{\mathbb Q})\cong\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb CS_n}(S^\lambda_{\mathbb C},S^\mu_{\mathbb C})=0$, so $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb QS_n}(S^\lambda_{\mathbb Q},S^\mu_{\mathbb Q})=0$.

Suppose $0\ne U\subseteq S^\lambda_{\mathbb Q}$ is a proper $\mathbb QS_n$-submodule. By [F4, F5] there is a $\mathbb QS_n$-submodule $V\ne0$ with $S^\lambda_{\mathbb Q}=U\oplus V$, and the projection $\pi$ onto $U$ along $V$ is a $\mathbb QS_n$-endomorphism that is not a scalar: $\pi$ acts as $1$ on $U$ and as $0$ on $V$. This contradicts step 2.1, so $S^\lambda_{\mathbb Q}$ is irreducible.

Applying step 1.2 with $E=\mathbb Q$, $K=F$ and step 2.1 gives $\operatorname{End}_{FS_n}(S^\lambda_F)\cong F\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb QS_n}(S^\lambda_{\mathbb Q})=F$ and $\operatorname{Hom}_{FS_n}(S^\lambda_F,S^\mu_F)=0$ for $\lambda\ne\mu$.

Then $W_{\mathbb C}:=\mathbb C\otimes_{\mathbb Q}W$ is a nonzero finite-dimensional complex $S_n$-module, so by [F3] it has an irreducible submodule isomorphic to $S^\lambda_{\mathbb C}$ for some $\lambda\vdash n$; hence $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb CS_n}(S^\lambda_{\mathbb C},W_{\mathbb C})

Suppose $0

e0$, $S^\lambda_F=U\oplus V$, and the projection $\pi$ onto $U$ along $V$ lies in $\operatorname{End}_{FS_n}(S^\lambda_F)$ and is not a scalar, since it acts as $1$ on $U

e0$. This contradicts step 3.2, so $S^\lambda_F$ is irreducible.

By [F4, F5] the finite-dimensional $\mathbb QS_n$-module $\mathbb QS_n$ is a finite direct sum of simple modules, and by step 4.1 each is isomorphic to some $S^\lambda_{\mathbb Q}$; collecting isomorphic summands and using the pairwise non-isomorphism from step 2.1 gives $\mathbb QS_n\cong\bigoplus_{\lambda\vdash n}(S^\lambda_{\mathbb Q})^{m_\lambda}$ for multiplicities $m_\lambda\ge0$. Each $m_\lambda\ge1$: by step 3.1 and step 4.1 the module $S^\lambda_{\mathbb Q}$ is simple, and for $0\ne v\in S^\lambda_{\mathbb Q}$ the surjection $\mathbb QS_n\to S^\lambda_{\mathbb Q}$, $x\mapsto xv$, splits by [F4], exhibiting $S^\lambda_{\mathbb Q}$ as a direct summand of $\mathbb QS_n$.

The canonical map $F\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb QS_n\to FS_n$, $c\otimes[\sigma]\mapsto c[\sigma]$, sends the $F$-basis $(1\otimes[\sigma])_{\sigma\in S_n}$ of $F\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb QS_n$ to the basis $([\sigma])_{\sigma\in S_n}$ of $FS_n$ and is compatible with multiplication by [F5]; hence it is an isomorphism of $FS_n$-modules. Applying $F\otimes_{\mathbb Q}-$ to step 5.1 and using [F7] together with step 1.1 gives $FS_n\cong F\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb QS_n\cong\bigoplus_{\lambda\vdash n}(F\otimes_{\mathbb Q}S^\lambda_{\mathbb Q})^{m_\lambda}\cong\bigoplus_{\lambda\vdash n}(S^\lambda_F)^{m_\lambda}$ with all $m_\lambda\ge1$.

Let $W$ be a simple $FS_n$-module, so $W\ne0$. For $0\ne w\in W$ the map $FS_n\to W$, $x\mapsto xw$, is a nonzero $FS_n$-linear map onto $W$; hence $\dim_FW<\infty$ and $W$ is a quotient of $FS_n$. By step 6.1, $FS_n\cong\bigoplus_{\lambda\vdash n}(S^\lambda_F)^{m_\lambda}$ with $m_\lambda\ge1$, so some component $(S^\lambda_F)^{m_\lambda}\to W$ of the quotient map is nonzero, and then some single copy $S^\lambda_F\to W$ is nonzero. The module $S^\lambda_F$ is irreducible (step 4.2), so this nonzero map is an isomorphism [F6]; hence $W\cong S^\lambda_F$.

Steps 1.1, 3.1 and 4.2 show that every $S^\lambda_F$ is nonzero and irreducible over $F$ (and over $\mathbb Q$, with the complex case being [F3]); steps 2.1 and 3.2 show that distinct partitions give modules with no nonzero homomorphism between them, and steps 4.1 and 7.1 show over $\mathbb Q$ and over $F$ that every irreducible module is isomorphic to one of them. Finally, a finite-dimensional $FS_n$-module decomposes into simple submodules by [F4, F5] applied repeatedly (each proper submodule splits off a nonzero complement, and the dimension strictly decreases), and each simple summand is isomorphic to some $S^\lambda_F$ by step 7.1. Thus the $S^\lambda_F$ are a complete irredundant list of irreducible $FS_n$-modules, and over $F=\mathbb C$ this is the published complex classification [F3].

boundaries.evidence: step 1.1: for n = 0 the empty partition gives S^emptyset_E = E, nonzero and irreducible, so the classification begins at the empty partition.

boundaries.reason: The base field is a field, so the zero ring never arises; rank n = 0 is handled inside the empty-partition case rather than as a zero-parameter degeneration.

boundaries.evidence: step 1.1: the one-box partition (1) gives S^{(1)}_E = E, the trivial module, the smallest nonempty label.

step 1.2: the comparison of endomorphism algebras under a field extension is carried out for arbitrary finite-dimensional modules; the algebraic-closure detour of step 2.1 is used only where Q -> C is available.
step 3.1: the proper-submodule hypothesis is contradicted for every lambda, so both endpoint possibilities U = 0 and U = S^lambda are covered and only the interior is excluded.
step 1.2 selects E-bases of finite-dimensional modules for a trace comparison; these are finitely many algebraic choices available without a choice principle, as the item states.
step 8.1: the forward listing, that each S^lambda_F is nonzero and irreducible, is recorded there as part of the classification.
step 8.1: the reverse listing, that every simple FS_n-module is isomorphic to exactly one S^lambda_F, is recorded there as the completeness half.

Let $n\ge0$ and let $\lambda\vdash n$. Write $M^\lambda_R$ for the free
$R$-module on the $\lambda$-tabloids and $S^\lambda_R$ for the $R$-span of the
polytabloids over a commutative ring $R$
([[def-polytabloid-specht-module-over-an-arbitrary-field]]). Then:

1. **(Integral Garnir relation.)** Let $t$ be a $\lambda$-tableau, let
   $j,j+1$ be adjacent columns, let $X$ be a set of entries of column $j$ and
   $Y$ a set of entries of column $j+1$, with
   $|X|+|Y|>\lambda'_j$. Let $G_{X,Y}:=\sum_{g\in T}\operatorname{sgn}(g)g$,
   where $T$ is any set of representatives containing $1$ for the left cosets
   of $H:=S_X\times S_Y$ in $S_{X\cup Y}$ (the transpositions in $S_X$ and
   $S_Y$ act on the corresponding labels and fix all other labels). Then
   $$G_{X,Y}\,e_t=0\qquad\text{in }M^\lambda_{\mathbb Z};$$
   the same identity holds after base change in $M^\lambda_F$ for every field
   $F$, for the same transversal $T$.
2. **(Straightening over $\mathbb Z$.)** For every $\lambda$-tableau $t$, the
   polytabloid $e_t$ is a finite $\mathbb Z$-linear combination of standard
   $\lambda$-polytabloids.
3. **(Integral and field-uniform basis.)** The standard polytabloids
   $\{e_t:t\text{ standard}\}$ are a $\mathbb Z$-basis of $S^\lambda_{\mathbb Z}$;
   for every field $F$, their images under coefficient reduction are an
   $F$-basis of $S^\lambda_F$. In particular
   $\dim_F S^\lambda_F=f^\lambda$ for every field $F$, including $F$ of
   characteristic $2$.

Let $F$ be a field of characteristic $0$ and let $n\ge0$. For every partition
$\lambda\vdash n$ the field-valued Specht module $S^\lambda_F$ of
[[def-polytabloid-specht-module-over-an-arbitrary-field]] is nonzero and
irreducible, distinct partitions give non-isomorphic modules, and every
irreducible $FS_n$-module is isomorphic to exactly one of them. Consequently,
by Maschke's theorem, every finite-dimensional $FS_n$-module is a direct sum of
copies of the $S^\lambda_F$; thus the irreducible $FS_n$-modules are indexed by
the partitions of $n$ and the modules $\{S^\lambda_F:\lambda\vdash n\}$ form a
complete irredundant list.

This is the constituent convention used throughout the pair: over
$F=\mathbb C$ it specialises to the published complex classification, and over
a general characteristic-zero field $F$ it is proved by extending the rational
Specht models along $\mathbb Q\to F$, never by a scalar extension from
$\mathbb C$ to $F$.

Let $G$ be a finite group, let $k$ be a field with
$\operatorname{char} k \nmid |G|$, let $\rho:G \to \operatorname{GL}(V)$ be a
finite-dimensional representation of $G$ over $k$, and let $W \le V$ be a
subrepresentation. Then there is a subrepresentation $U \le V$ such that

$$V=W\oplus U.$$

Let $V$ and $W$ be irreducible representations of a group $G$ over a field $k$.
Then every nonzero intertwiner $f:V \to W$ is an isomorphism. Consequently
$\operatorname{End}_G(V)$ is a division ring.

Let $\mu\vdash m$ and let $r\ge1$. Then, as complex $S_{m+r}$-modules,

$$\operatorname{Ind}_{S_m\times S_r}^{S_{m+r}}\bigl(S^\mu\boxtimes S^{(r)}\bigr)\cong\bigoplus_{\substack{\lambda\vdash m+r\\ \lambda\supseteq\mu\\ \lambda/\mu\ \text{horizontal }r\text{-strip}}}S^\lambda,$$

where a horizontal strip has at most one added node in each column, and

$$\operatorname{Ind}_{S_m\times S_r}^{S_{m+r}}\bigl(S^\mu\boxtimes S^{(1^r)}\bigr)\cong\bigoplus_{\substack{\lambda\vdash m+r\\ \lambda\supseteq\mu\\ \lambda/\mu\ \text{vertical }r\text{-strip}}}S^\lambda,$$

where a vertical strip means that at most one added node lies in each row. Every listed summand has multiplicity one, and no other Specht module occurs. Here $S^{(r)}$ is the trivial representation of $S_r$ and $S^{(1^r)}$ is its sign representation, as verified from the Specht-module definition below. For $r=0$, both factors are $S^\varnothing$, and each induced module is $S^\mu$, corresponding to the unique empty strip. No choice principle is used.

The present page defines induction by $H$-covariant functions because that model
is self-contained in the library's existing module language. When $R$ is
commutative and $[G:H]$ is finite, this is the same object as the tensor-product
model.

Indeed, the subgroup inclusion makes $R[G]$ an $(R[G],R[H])$-bimodule
([[def-bimodule]]), so $R[G]\otimes_{R[H]}W$ is defined by the universal
property of the tensor product
([[thm-universal-property-of-module-tensor-products]]). The elementary formula

$$ [g]\otimes w\longmapsto f_{g,w}, \qquad f_{g,w}(gh):=h^{-1}\cdot w, $$

with $f_{g,w}$ zero off the left coset $gH$, is balanced in the $R[H]$-variable
and therefore descends uniquely
([[prop-elementary-tensor-formulas-descend-exactly-when-balanced]]).
Comparing both sides on a finite left transversal shows that this descended map
is a $G$-equivariant isomorphism

$$ R[G]\otimes_{R[H]}W\cong \operatorname{Ind}_H^G W. $$

Thus, in the finite-index setting used for finite-group character theory, the
function model and the tensor-product model are two descriptions of the same
induced module. For infinite index, the displayed function model is instead
larger: the tensor product corresponds to the finitely supported covariant
functions.
For $H\le G$, induction is left adjoint and coinduction is right adjoint to restriction.

Let $G$ be a finite group, let $H\le G$, let $\chi$ be a complex character of
$H$, and let $\psi$ be a complex character of $G$. Then

$$\langle \operatorname{Ind}_H^G\chi,\psi\rangle_G = \langle \chi,\operatorname{Res}_H^G\psi\rangle_H.$$

Let $R\to S$ be a homomorphism of commutative rings, let $N$ be a right $S$-module, and let $M$ be a left $R$-module. There is a natural group isomorphism

$$N\otimes_RM\cong N\otimes_S(S\otimes_RM)$$

given by

$$n\otimes m\longmapsto n\otimes(1_S\otimes m),$$

with inverse $n\otimes(s\otimes m)\mapsto ns\otimes m$.

Let $M$ be a right $R$-module, let ${}_RN_S$ be an $(R,S)$-bimodule, and let $P$ be a left $S$-module. There is a canonical group isomorphism

$$\alpha_{M,N,P}:(M\otimes_RN)\otimes_SP\longrightarrow M\otimes_R(N\otimes_SP)$$

determined by

$$\alpha_{M,N,P}((m\otimes n)\otimes p)=m\otimes(n\otimes p).$$

It respects any compatible outer module actions and is natural in $M,N,P$.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $(M_i)_{i\in I}$ be any family of $R$-modules, and let $N$ be an $R$-module. The homomorphism induced by the coordinate inclusions is a natural $R$-module isomorphism

$$\Phi:\bigoplus_{i\in I}(M_i\otimes_RN)\longrightarrow\left(\bigoplus_{i\in I}M_i\right)\otimes_RN,$$

$$\Phi\bigl(\jmath_i(m\otimes n)\bigr)=\jmath_i(m)\otimes n.$$

The same holds with the direct sum in the second variable: there is a natural $R$-module isomorphism

$$\Phi':\bigoplus_{i\in I}(N\otimes_RM_i)\longrightarrow N\otimes_R\left(\bigoplus_{i\in I}M_i\right),\qquad \Phi'\bigl(\jmath_i(n\otimes m)\bigr)=n\otimes\jmath_i(m).$$

The assertion includes $I=\varnothing$, when both sides are zero.

Let $f:R\to S$ be a unital homomorphism of commutative rings ([[def-ring-homomorphism]]).

For an $S$-module $N$, its **restriction of scalars** along $f$, denoted $\operatorname{Res}^S_RN$, is the same abelian group with $R$-action

$$r\cdot n:=f(r)n.$$

For an $R$-module $M$, its **extension of scalars** along $f$ is

$$S\otimes_RM.$$

Here $S$ is an $(S,R)$-bimodule with left action by multiplication and right action $s\cdot r:=s f(r)$ ([[def-bimodule]]). The induced outer action

$$s'(s\otimes m):=(s's)\otimes m$$

makes $S\otimes_RM$ an $S$-module ([[thm-bimodule-actions-induced-on-tensor-products]]).

Restriction acts on a homomorphism by leaving its underlying function unchanged. Extension sends $u:M\to M'$ to $1_S\otimes u:S\otimes_RM\to S\otimes_RM'$.

Let $R$ be a unital ring, $M$ a right $R$-module, and $N$ a left $R$-module. Let

$$F:=\mathbb Z^{(M\times N)}$$

be the free $\mathbb Z$-module on the set $M\times N$ ([[def-free-module-on-a-set-and-standard-basis]], [[thm-universal-property-of-free-modules]]), and write $e_{(m,n)}$ for its standard basis elements. The additive group of $F$ is abelian. Let $H$ be the subgroup generated ([[def-generated-subgroup]]) by all elements

$$e_{(m+m',n)}-e_{(m,n)}-e_{(m',n)},$$

$$e_{(m,n+n')}-e_{(m,n)}-e_{(m,n')},$$

and

$$e_{(mr,n)}-e_{(m,rn)}$$

as $m,m'$ range over $M$, $n,n'$ over $N$, and $r$ over $R$. Since every subgroup of an abelian group is normal, the quotient group $F/H$ is defined ([[def-quotient-group]]). The **tensor product of $M$ and $N$ over $R$** is

$$M\otimes_RN:=F/H.$$

The coset of $e_{(m,n)}$ is the **elementary tensor** $m\otimes n$. Every tensor is a finite sum of elementary tensors, because every element of $F$ is a finite $\mathbb Z$-linear combination of basis elements and integer coefficients may be absorbed into either additive variable. The defining relations give

$$(m+m')\otimes n=m\otimes n+m'\otimes n,\qquad m\otimes(n+n')=m\otimes n+m\otimes n',$$

and

$$(mr)\otimes n=m\otimes(rn).$$

In particular $0\otimes n=0=m\otimes0$. No $R$-module structure on $M\otimes_RN$ is part of this arbitrary-ring definition; at this stage it is an abelian group.

For a left $G$-module $M$, its coinvariants are
$M_G=M/\langle gm-m:g\in G,m\in M\rangle$. If
$f:M\to N$ is $G$-linear, define $f_G:M_G\to N_G$ by
$f_G([m])=[f(m)]$. Equivariance makes this well defined, and identities and
composites are preserved, so $M\mapsto M_G$ is a functor. The map
$1\otimes m\mapsto[m]$ naturally identifies
$\mathbb Z\otimes_{\mathbb Z[G]}M$ (with right trivial $\mathbb Z$) with
$M_G$.

Let $G$ be a finite group, let $k$ be a field with
$\operatorname{char} k \nmid |G|$, let $\rho:G \to \operatorname{GL}(V)$ be a
finite-dimensional representation of $G$ over $k$, and let $W \le V$ be a
subrepresentation. Then there is a subrepresentation $U \le V$ such that

$$V=W\oplus U.$$

citations.quote:
For all $\lambda,\rho\vdash n$,

$$\chi^\lambda(\rho)=\langle s_\lambda,p_\rho\rangle_H,$$

the coefficient of $p_\rho/z_\rho$ in the power-sum expansion of $s_\lambda$.
Equivalently,

$$s_\lambda=\sum_{\rho\vdash n}\chi^\lambda(\rho)\,\frac{p_\rho}{z_\rho}.$$

For integers $N,d\ge0$, let $A_N^d$ be the degree-$d$ homogeneous part of
$\mathbb Z[x_1,\ldots,x_N]^{S_N}$, using
[[def-symmetric-polynomial]] and the convention $A_0^0=\mathbb Z$ and
$A_0^d=0$ for $d>0$. For $M\ge N$, the transition
$\pi_{M,N}:A_M^d\to A_N^d$ sets $x_{N+1},\ldots,x_M$ equal to zero.
These maps compose, so define
$$\Lambda^d:=\varprojlim_{N\ge0}A_N^d,\qquad \Lambda:=\bigoplus_{d\ge0}\Lambda^d.$$

An element of $\Lambda^d$ is a compatible sequence of homogeneous
degree-$d$ symmetric polynomials, one in each rank. Multiplication of a
degree-$a$ sequence and a degree-$b$ sequence is coordinatewise polynomial
multiplication and lies in $\Lambda^{a+b}$; compatibility follows because
each $\pi_{M,N}$ is a ring homomorphism. Extend this product distributively
to $\Lambda$. The unit is the compatible constant sequence $1$, and each
element of $\Lambda$ has only finitely many nonzero homogeneous components.

This direct sum is not the ungraded inverse limit of the rings
$\mathbb Z[x_1,\ldots,x_N]^{S_N}$. For example, the compatible sequence
$\prod_{i=1}^N(1+x_i)$ belongs to that ungraded inverse limit and has nonzero
homogeneous components in every degree, so it is not an element of the direct
sum $\Lambda$. The partition notation and empty partition follow
[[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]].

For a partition $\lambda$ and an integer $N\ge\ell(\lambda)$, pad $\lambda$
with zero parts to length $N$ and set
$\delta_N=(N-1,N-2,\ldots,0)$. Define the alternating polynomial
$$a_{\lambda+\delta_N}(x_1,\ldots,x_N):=\det\bigl(x_i^{\lambda_j+N-j}\bigr)_{1\le i,j\le N},$$
and define $a_{\delta_N}$ by the same formula with $\lambda=\varnothing$.
The finite-rank Schur polynomial is
$$s_\lambda(x_1,\ldots,x_N):=\frac{a_{\lambda+\delta_N}(x_1,\ldots,x_N)}{a_{\delta_N}(x_1,\ldots,x_N)}.$$
For $0\le N<\ell(\lambda)$, define $s_\lambda(x_1,\ldots,x_N):=0$.
Thus a component is specified at every rank, including rank zero; empty
determinants have value $1$.

**Well-definedness and stability.** The exponents $\lambda_j+N-j$ are
strictly decreasing, so the numerator is alternating. Setting $x_i=x_j$
makes it zero; the factor theorem therefore gives divisibility by each
$x_i-x_j$ in $\mathbb Z[x_1,\ldots,x_N]$. These pairwise nonassociate prime
factors therefore have product $a_{\delta_N}$ dividing the numerator, so the quotient is an
integral polynomial. Since numerator and denominator both change by the sign
of a variable permutation, their quotient is symmetric. Its degree is
$|\lambda|$.

If $N+1>\ell(\lambda)$, setting $x_{N+1}=0$ in the rank-$(N+1)$ numerator
and denominator expands each determinant along its last row; both resulting
minors have the common factor $x_1\cdots x_N$, and after cancelling it the
quotient is exactly the rank-$N$ quotient. At the remaining boundary
$N+1=\ell(\lambda)>0$, every exponent in the rank-$(N+1)$ numerator
is positive, so its last row becomes zero when $x_{N+1}=0$.
The denominator specializes to
$(x_1\cdots x_N)a_{\delta_N}$, a nonzero polynomial (equal to $1$ when
$N=0$). Specializing the polynomial identity
$a_{\lambda+\delta_{N+1}}=a_{\delta_{N+1}}s_\lambda$
and cancelling this nonzero polynomial shows that the specialized Schur
polynomial is zero, as required by the rank-$N$ definition. Below this
boundary both components are zero. Hence these polynomials form a
compatible sequence in the inverse limit
[[def-stable-graded-ring-of-symmetric-functions]], defining
$s_\lambda\in\Lambda^{|\lambda|}$. With the empty determinant equal to $1$,
$s_{\varnothing}=1$. The partition length and padding convention is that of
[[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]].

At the minimal rank $N=1$, the one-box partition gives
$s_{(1)}(x_1)=x_1$ directly from the quotient; its stable sequence is
nonzero.

The **Hall inner product** is the graded $\mathbb Z$-bilinear form on the
stable ring $\Lambda$ ([[def-stable-graded-ring-of-symmetric-functions]])
characterized by
$$\langle h_\lambda,m_\mu\rangle_H=\delta_{\lambda\mu}$$
for all partitions $\lambda,\mu$ ([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]],
[[thm-elementary-and-complete-families-freely-generate-the-stable-ring]],
[[thm-monomial-symmetric-functions-form-the-integral-stable-basis]]), where
$\delta_{\lambda\mu}=1$ if $\lambda=\mu$ and $0$ otherwise. In particular,
homogeneous components of unequal degrees are orthogonal.
For the empty partition, $h_\varnothing=m_\varnothing=1$, so
$\langle1,1\rangle_H=1$.

For each $d\ge0$, the proven integral bases give unique finite expansions
$$f_d=\sum_{\lambda\vdash d}a_\lambda h_\lambda,\qquad g_d=\sum_{\mu\vdash d}b_\mu m_\mu$$
for $f_d,g_d\in\Lambda^d$. Define their degree-$d$ pairing by
$$\langle f_d,g_d\rangle_H:=\sum_{\lambda,\mu\vdash d}a_\lambda b_\mu\delta_{\lambda\mu}.$$
For $f=\sum_d f_d$ and $g=\sum_d g_d$ in the algebraic direct sum $\Lambda$,
set $$\langle f,g\rangle_H:=\sum_d\langle f_d,g_d\rangle_H.$$
Only finitely many $d$ contribute because $f$ and $g$ have finite degree
support. The unique expansions in the two integral bases make this a
well-defined $\mathbb Z$-bilinear form; the displayed basis rule determines it
uniquely on all of $\Lambda$.

For $k\ge1$, the **$k$-th power-sum symmetric polynomial** is

$$p_k:=x_1^k+\cdots+x_n^k.$$

For $k\ge0$, the **$k$-th complete homogeneous symmetric polynomial** is

$$h_k:=\sum_{a_1+\cdots+a_n=k}x_1^{a_1}\cdots x_n^{a_n}.$$

Thus $h_0=1$, while for $n=0$ one has $h_k=0$ when $k>0$. Both families are fixed by every permutation of the variables.

For integers $N,d\ge0$, let $A_N^d$ be the degree-$d$ homogeneous part of
$\mathbb Z[x_1,\ldots,x_N]^{S_N}$, using
[[def-symmetric-polynomial]] and the convention $A_0^0=\mathbb Z$ and
$A_0^d=0$ for $d>0$. For $M\ge N$, the transition
$\pi_{M,N}:A_M^d\to A_N^d$ sets $x_{N+1},\ldots,x_M$ equal to zero.
These maps compose, so define
$$\Lambda^d:=\varprojlim_{N\ge0}A_N^d,\qquad \Lambda:=\bigoplus_{d\ge0}\Lambda^d.$$

An element of $\Lambda^d$ is a compatible sequence of homogeneous
degree-$d$ symmetric polynomials, one in each rank. Multiplication of a
degree-$a$ sequence and a degree-$b$ sequence is coordinatewise polynomial
multiplication and lies in $\Lambda^{a+b}$; compatibility follows because
each $\pi_{M,N}$ is a ring homomorphism. Extend this product distributively
to $\Lambda$. The unit is the compatible constant sequence $1$, and each
element of $\Lambda$ has only finitely many nonzero homogeneous components.

This direct sum is not the ungraded inverse limit of the rings
$\mathbb Z[x_1,\ldots,x_N]^{S_N}$. For example, the compatible sequence
$\prod_{i=1}^N(1+x_i)$ belongs to that ungraded inverse limit and has nonzero
homogeneous components in every degree, so it is not an element of the direct
sum $\Lambda$. The partition notation and empty partition follow
[[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]].

For $i\ge1$ and $n\ge0$ let $X_i\colon S_n\to\mathbb N$ be the function
sending a permutation $\sigma\in S_n$ to the number
$X_i(\sigma):=c_i(\sigma)$ of $i$-element orbits in its cycle type
([[def-permutation-support-disjoint-cycles-and-cycle-type]],
[[def-finite-symmetric-group-and-permutation-notation]],
[[def-natural-numbers]]); thus $X_1(\sigma)$ is the number of fixed points of
$\sigma$, and $X_i(\sigma)=0$ whenever $i>n$. Each $X_i$ is a **class
function** on $S_n$ ([[def-class-function-and-the-space-of-complex-class-functions]]):
if $\tau\sigma\tau^{-1}$ is a conjugate of $\sigma$, then $O\mapsto\tau(O)$ is
a bijection from the orbits of $\sigma$ onto the orbits of
$\tau\sigma\tau^{-1}$ that preserves cardinalities, so
$c_i(\tau\sigma\tau^{-1})=c_i(\sigma)$.

Let $\mathbb Q[X_1,X_2,\dots]$ be the polynomial ring on the family of
indeterminates indexed by $i\ge1$
([[def-polynomial-ring-on-a-family-of-indeterminates]]); its elements are
finitely supported coefficient families on the monomials of
[[def-monomials-on-an-index-set]], so every element involves only finitely many
of the indeterminates. A **character polynomial** is an element
$P\in\mathbb Q[X_1,X_2,\dots]$. Setting $\deg X_i:=i$ gives the monomial
$X^a=\prod_iX_i^{a_i}$ the **weighted degree** $\sum_ii\,a_i$ (a finite sum); a
character polynomial has **weighted degree $\le d$** when every monomial
occurring in it has weighted degree at most $d$, and the **weighted degree** of
$P\ne0$ is the largest weighted degree of a monomial of $P$. Products and
rational linear combinations of class functions on $S_n$ are again class
functions, so every character polynomial defines for each $n\ge0$ a class
function

$$P\colon S_n\longrightarrow\mathbb Q,\qquad \sigma\longmapsto P(X_1(\sigma),X_2(\sigma),\dots),$$

the defining sum being finite because $P$ has finite support and
$X_i(\sigma)=0$ for $i>n$; equivalently, the substitution $X_i\mapsto
X_i(\sigma)$ is the ring homomorphism supplied by
[[thm-universal-property-of-a-polynomial-ring-on-a-family]]. In this way a
character polynomial is realized as one class function on each $S_n$. The
realization is not injective on a single $S_n$, since $X_i$ vanishes
identically on $S_n$ for $i>n$. It is injective in the limit:

**Uniqueness.** If $P,Q$ agree as functions on $S_n$ for infinitely many $n$,
then $P=Q$.

Indeed, put $R:=P-Q$ and let $A\subseteq\mathbb N$ be infinite with
$R|_{S_n}=0$ for every $n\in A$. Fix $m\ge0$, $\sigma\in S_m$ and $k\ge0$, and
let $\sigma^{(k)}\in S_{m+k}$ be $\sigma$ extended by $k$ fixed points outside
its domain; then $X_1(\sigma^{(k)})=X_1(\sigma)+k$ and
$X_i(\sigma^{(k)})=X_i(\sigma)$ for $i\ge2$, so
$R(\sigma^{(k)})=\sum_j\bigl(X_1(\sigma)+k\bigr)^jR_j(\sigma)$, where
$R=\sum_jX_1^jR_j$ collects the monomials of $R$ by their $X_1$-exponent $j$,
each $R_j$ involving only $X_2,X_3,\dots$. The right-hand side is given by a
polynomial in $k$ over $\mathbb Q$ of degree at most the largest $j$ with
$R_j\ne0$, and it vanishes for all $k$ with $m+k\in A$, infinitely many $k$;
by the root bound of [[thm-root-bound-for-polynomials-over-a-domain]] that
polynomial is zero, so $R(\sigma)=0$
([[def-polynomial-evaluation-and-root]]). As $\sigma\in S_m$ was arbitrary,
$R$ vanishes on every $S_m$; equivalently, $R(b_1,\dots,b_M)=0$ for every
$M\ge0$ and every tuple $(b_1,\dots,b_M)\in\mathbb N^M$, since a disjoint union
of $b_i$ cycles of length $i$, $1\le i\le M$, is a permutation with $X_i=b_i$
for $i\le M$. If $R\ne0$, then $R$ involves only $X_1,\dots,X_M$ for some $M$,
and induction on $M$ shows that such an $R$ cannot vanish at every point of
$\mathbb N^M$: for $M=0$ the polynomial is a constant evaluated at the empty
tuple; and for $M\ge1$, fixing $(b_1,\dots,b_{M-1})\in\mathbb N^{M-1}$ makes
$b_M\mapsto R(b_1,\dots,b_{M-1},b_M)$ a polynomial in one variable over
$\mathbb Q$ with infinitely many roots, hence the zero polynomial, so every
$X_M$-coefficient of $R$ vanishes at $(b_1,\dots,b_{M-1})$ and the induction
applies to each of those coefficients. Hence $R=0$.

A sequence $(\chi_n)_{n\ge0}$ of class functions with $\chi_n$ a class function
on $S_n$ is **eventually polynomial** when there are $N\ge0$ and a character
polynomial $P$ with

$$\chi_n(\sigma)=P(X_1(\sigma),X_2(\sigma),\dots)$$

for all $n\ge N$ and all $\sigma\in S_n$
([[def-class-function-and-the-space-of-complex-class-functions]]). By
uniqueness in the limit, such a $P$ is determined by $(\chi_n)$ whenever it
exists. No choice principle is used.

derivations.claim: Use Macdonald's padding identity, which combines the Frobenius formula with the $x_0=1$ homogeneity reduction (Macdonald, *Symmetric Functions and Hall Polynomials*, Chapter I §7, printed pp. 122–124; the classical input recorded in the sources): for every $N\ge\lambda_1$ and every $w\in S_{N+m}$, $\chi^{(N,\lambda)}(w)=\langle E\cdot P(w),s_\lambda\rangle_H$, where $E:=\prod_i(1-x_i)=\sum_{j\ge0}(-1)^je_j$ and $P(w):=\prod_{r\ge1}(1+p_r)^{X_r(w)}$; the pairing is read on the degree-$m$ component, where only finitely many terms occur, so no infinite sum is used.

Expanding $E=\sum_j(-1)^je_j$ and each $(1+p_r)^{X_r(w)}=\sum_{k=0}^{X_r(w)}\binom{X_r(w)}{k}p_r^{k}$ shows that the degree-$m$ component of $E\cdot P(w)$ is the finite sum of $(-1)^j\binom{X_1(w)}{k_1}\cdots\binom{X_s(w)}{k_s}\,e_jp_{r_1}^{k_1}\cdots p_{r_s}^{k_s}$ over all tuples with $j+\sum_ir_ik_i=m$; the finiteness follows because $j\le m$ and $r_ik_i\le m$.

Define $P_\lambda\in\mathbb Q[X_1,X_2,\dots]$ as the finite sum $\sum_{j+\sum_irk_i=m}(-1)^j\langle e_jp_{r_1}^{k_1}\cdots p_{r_s}^{k_s},s_\lambda\rangle_H\prod_r\binom{X_r}{k_r}$. Its coefficients are integers, it involves finitely many variables, and its weighted degree is $\sum_rr k_r\le m$. Substituting $\sigma\in S_n$ with $n\ge m+\lambda_1$ and using steps 1.1 and 1.2 with $N=n-m\ge\lambda_1$, together with the gradedness of the Hall pairing [F2], gives $\chi^{\lambda[n]}(\sigma)=\langle E\cdot P(\sigma),s_\lambda\rangle_H=\langle(E\cdot P(\sigma))_m,s_\lambda\rangle_H=P_\lambda(X_1(\sigma),X_2(\sigma),\dots)$.

The polynomial $P_\lambda$ produced in step 2.1 satisfies the required identity for all $n\ge m+\lambda_1$ and all $\sigma\in S_n$; it is unique with this property, since two character polynomials agreeing on all $S_n$ for all sufficiently large $n$ are equal [F4]. Hence for every partition $\lambda$ there is a character polynomial of weighted degree at most $|\lambda|$ representing the padded irreducible characters $\chi^{\lambda[n]}$ on the stated range.

boundaries.evidence: step 2.1: for lambda = emptyset the sum has the single term (j, k) = (0, 0) and yields P = 1, matching the trivial character of (n) for all n >= 0.
step 2.1: the defining sum is finite and contains no division; the term count is bounded by j + sum r_i k_i = m, and m = 0 gives the constant polynomial.
step 2.1: for lambda = (1) the surviving terms give P_(1) = X_1 - 1, the smallest nonconstant padded family.
step 1.1: the homogeneity reduction x_0 = 1 removes the degenerate variable and is what makes the identity polynomial in the X_r; the hypothesis N >= lambda_1 excludes the empty range.
step 1.1: the value N = lambda_1, i.e. n = m + lambda_1 at the padding threshold, is allowed, and larger N follows from the same identity.
step 2.1: P_lambda is defined as an explicit finite sum of Hall pairings indexed by tuples with j + sum r_i k_i = m; no basis of the symmetric-function ring is chosen.

Uniqueness in the limit is supplied separately by the character-polynomial definition and is not asserted here.

citations.quote:
Let $F$ be a field of characteristic $0$, let $\lambda\vdash n$, and let
$S^\lambda_F$ be the corresponding field-valued Specht module
([[def-polytabloid-specht-module-over-an-arbitrary-field]]).

(i) For every $k\ge0$ there is an isomorphism of $FS_{n+k}$-modules

$$\operatorname{Ind}_{S_n\times S_k}^{S_{n+k}}\bigl(S^\lambda_F\boxtimes F\bigr)\cong\bigoplus_{\mu}S^\mu_F,$$

summed over the partitions $\mu\vdash n+k$ obtained from $\lambda$ by adding
one box to each of $k$ different columns (equivalently, $\mu\supseteq\lambda$
and $\mu/\lambda$ is a horizontal $k$-strip).

(ii) For every $k\le n$ there is an isomorphism of $FS_{n-k}$-modules

$$\bigl(\operatorname{Res}^{S_n}_{S_{n-k}\times S_k}S^\lambda_F\bigr)_{S_k}\cong\bigoplus_{\nu}S^\nu_F,$$

summed over the partitions $\nu\vdash n-k$ obtained from $\lambda$ by removing
one box from each of $k$ different columns, where the outer subscript denotes
$S_k$-coinvariants of the restriction to the ordered block subgroup
$S_{n-k}\times S_k\le S_n$ ([[def-coinvariants-functor-of-a-group-module]]);
the left-hand side is an $FS_{n-k}$-module because the two blocks commute. All
multiplicities are $0$ or $1$. No choice principle is used.

Let $F$ be a field of characteristic $0$ and let $n\ge0$. For every partition
$\lambda\vdash n$ the field-valued Specht module $S^\lambda_F$ of
[[def-polytabloid-specht-module-over-an-arbitrary-field]] is nonzero and
irreducible, distinct partitions give non-isomorphic modules, and every
irreducible $FS_n$-module is isomorphic to exactly one of them. Consequently,
by Maschke's theorem, every finite-dimensional $FS_n$-module is a direct sum of
copies of the $S^\lambda_F$; thus the irreducible $FS_n$-modules are indexed by
the partitions of $n$ and the modules $\{S^\lambda_F:\lambda\vdash n\}$ form a
complete irredundant list.

This is the constituent convention used throughout the pair: over
$F=\mathbb C$ it specialises to the published complex classification, and over
a general characteristic-zero field $F$ it is proved by extending the rational
Specht models along $\mathbb Q\to F$, never by a scalar extension from
$\mathbb C$ to $F$.

Let $G$ be a finite group, let $k$ be a field with
$\operatorname{char} k \nmid |G|$, let $\rho:G \to \operatorname{GL}(V)$ be a
finite-dimensional representation of $G$ over $k$, and let $W \le V$ be a
subrepresentation. Then there is a subrepresentation $U \le V$ such that

$$V=W\oplus U.$$

A **graded $k[T]$-module** consists of $k$-modules $U_n$, $n\ge0$, together
with $k$-linear maps $T=T_n\colon U_n\to U_{n+1}$ for all $n\ge0$. A
**morphism** $U\to U'$ of graded $k[T]$-modules is a family of $k$-linear maps
$u_n\colon U_n\to U'_n$ with $u_{n+1}\circ T_n=T'_n\circ u_n$ for all $n$.

Fix $a\ge0$, a set $\mathbf a$ of cardinality $a$, and a functorial disjoint
union of finite sets. Let $V$ be an FI-module over $k$
([[def-fi-category-and-fi-module]]) and let $n\ge0$. Put

$$\Phi_a(V)_n:=(V_{\mathbf a\sqcup n})_{S_n},$$

the coinvariants of the $kS_n$-module $V_{\mathbf a\sqcup n}$: the quotient by
the span of the elements $\sigma\cdot v-v$, $\sigma\in S_n$, $v\in
V_{\mathbf a\sqcup n}$ ([[def-coinvariants-functor-of-a-group-module]],
[[def-quotient-module]]). Equivalently $\Phi_a(V)_n=k\otimes_{kS_n}
V_{\mathbf a\sqcup n}$, the two descriptions being identified by the balancing
argument of [[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]] and
the corresponding identification for $\mathbb Z$ in
[[def-coinvariants-functor-of-a-group-module]]; the group ring $kS_n$ is a
unital $k$-algebra with basis the group elements
([[def-group-ring]], [[thm-group-ring-is-a-unital-algebra-with-basis-g]]).

To define the transition map $T\colon\Phi_a(V)_n\to\Phi_a(V)_{n+1}$, choose an
injection $f\colon n\to n+1$. It induces the injection
$\mathrm{id}_{\mathbf a}\sqcup f\colon\mathbf a\sqcup n\to\mathbf a\sqcup n+1$
and hence a $k$-linear map $(V_{\mathbf a\sqcup n}\to
V_{\mathbf a\sqcup n+1})$. This map is $S_n$-equivariant, where $S_n$ acts on
the target through the injection $\mathrm{id}_{\mathbf a}\sqcup f$, so it
descends to the quotient map $T=T_f$ on coinvariants. The map $T_f$ is
independent of $f$: for two injections $f,g\colon n\to n+1$ the composite
$g\circ f^{-1}$ is a bijection $f(n)\to g(n)$, which extends along the
complement to a permutation $\tau\in S_{n+1}$ with $g=\tau\circ f$; then
$\mathrm{id}_{\mathbf a}\sqcup g=(\mathrm{id}_{\mathbf a}\sqcup
\tau)\circ(\mathrm{id}_{\mathbf a}\sqcup f)$, and the map induced by
$\mathrm{id}_{\mathbf a}\sqcup\tau$ on
$(V_{\mathbf a\sqcup n+1})_{S_{n+1}}$ is the identity because it comes from
the action of the group element $\tau$. Thus $T$ is well defined and
$(\Phi_a(V),T)$ is a graded $k[T]$-module.

A map of FI-modules $\alpha\colon V\to W$ gives $k$-linear maps
$\alpha_{\mathbf a\sqcup n}\colon V_{\mathbf a\sqcup n}\to W_{\mathbf
a\sqcup n}$ commuting with the $S_n$-actions and with the maps induced by
$\mathrm{id}_{\mathbf a}\sqcup f$, hence maps $(\Phi_a\alpha)_n$ of coinvariants
commuting with $T$; so $\Phi_a$ is a functor from FI-modules over $k$ to graded
$k[T]$-modules.

**Exactness.** Coinvariants of a group module are right exact
([[prop-the-coinvariants-functor-is-right-exact]]), so the functor
$M\mapsto M_{S_n}\cong k\otimes_{kS_n}M$ is right exact and each $\Phi_a$ is
right exact in every degree. If $k$ contains $\mathbb Q$, then $1/n!$ exists in $k$
and the averaging map
$s\colon\Phi_a(V)_n\to V_{\mathbf a\sqcup n}$,
$s([v])=\frac1{n!}\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\sigma\cdot v$, is a well-defined
$k$-linear section of the quotient map that is natural in $V$; it identifies
$\Phi_a(V)_n$ with the invariants $V_{\mathbf a\sqcup n}^{S_n}$. Under this
natural identification $\Phi_a$ becomes the invariants functor, which is left
exact (kernels of equivariant maps are computed pointwise), and therefore
$\Phi_a$ is exact; in that case the induced map $\Phi_a(W)\to\Phi_a(V)$ is
injective for every sub-FI-module $W\subseteq V$
([[def-submodule]], [[def-module-homomorphism-kernel-image-and-cokernel]]), so
$\Phi_a(W)$ is identified with a submodule of $\Phi_a(V)$. Finite averaging
uses only the finite groups $S_n$; no choice principle is used.

citations.quote:
Let $W$ be an FB-module over $k$, i.e. a functor from the groupoid of finite
sets and bijections to $k\text{-}\mathrm{Mod}$ ([[def-fi-category-and-fi-module]]);
thus $W(T)$ is a $k$-module for every finite set $T$, and every bijection
$\beta\colon T\to T'$ gives an isomorphism $W(\beta)\colon W(T)\to W(T')$.
Because an FB-module is defined on all finite sets, no transport choices are
needed below.

The **free FI-module** $M(W)$ assigns to a finite set $S$ the direct sum

$$M(W)_S:=\bigoplus_{T\subseteq S}W(T)$$

over all subsets $T\subseteq S$ ([[def-subset-and-proper-subset]],
[[def-direct-sum-of-a-family-of-modules]]; only finitely many summands occur).
For an injection $f\colon S\to S'$ and a subset $T\subseteq S$, the restriction
$f|_T\colon T\to f(T)$ is a bijection
([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]), and the transition map
$f_*\colon M(W)_S\to M(W)_{S'}$ is the sum of the isomorphisms
$W(f|_T)\colon W(T)\to W(f(T))$ over all $T\subseteq S$. This is $k$-linear and
functorial, since $(f'\circ f)|_T=f'|_{f(T)}\circ f|_T$; hence $M(W)$ is an
FI-module over $k$.

For $S=[n]=\{0,\dots,n-1\}$ the symmetric group $S_n$
([[def-finite-symmetric-group-and-permutation-notation]]) acts by
$\sigma\cdot T:=\sigma(T)$ and $W(\sigma|_T)$, and this is a left action
making $M(W)_n$ a left $kS_n$-module ([[def-group-ring]]). Grouping the sum by
the cardinality of $T$, the subsets of cardinality $a$ form a single $S_n$-orbit
with stabilizer the ordered block subgroup
$S_{\{0,\dots,a-1\}}\times S_{\{a,\dots,n-1\}}\cong S_a\times S_{n-a}$, so the
orbit summand is identified with an induced module
([[def-induced-r-linear-g-module-by-h-covariant-functions]]):

$$M(W)_n\cong\bigoplus_{a=0}^{n}\operatorname{Ind}_{S_a\times S_{n-a}}^{S_n}\bigl(W_a\boxtimes k\bigr),$$

where $W_a:=W(\{0,\dots,a-1\})$ is the value of the FB-module on an $a$-element
set, the first factor acts on $W_a$ through $W$ and the second factor acts
trivially, and $\boxtimes$ is the external tensor product of modules for the
two direct factors ([[def-outer-induction-product-for-symmetric-group-characters]],
[[lem-character-ring-of-a-direct-product-is-the-tensor-product]],
[[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]]).

**Adjunction.** Let $\pi$ be the functor from FI-modules to FB-modules that
forgets the maps between distinct cardinalities. The inclusion of the $T=S$
summand is a natural map $\eta_W\colon W\to\pi M(W)$, and evaluating a map
$F\colon M(W)\to V$ of FI-modules on that summand yields a map of FB-modules
$\pi F\circ\eta_W\colon W\to\pi V$. Conversely, a map of FB-modules
$\varphi\colon W\to\pi V$ extends uniquely to a map of FI-modules
$\widetilde\varphi\colon M(W)\to V$ whose value on the summand $W(T)\subseteq
M(W)_S$ is $V(\iota_{T,S})\circ\varphi_T$, with $\iota_{T,S}\colon T\to S$ the
inclusion; the components are compatible with injections and the two
constructions are inverse, so
$\operatorname{Hom}_{FI\text{-}Mod}(M(W),V)\cong
\operatorname{Hom}_{FB\text{-}Mod}(W,\pi V)$ naturally in $V$ and $W$: $M$ is
left adjoint to $\pi$, with unit $\eta$.

For $m\ge0$ write $k[S_m]$ for the FB-module with $k[S_m](T)$ the free $k$-module
on the bijections $[m]\to T$, and zero when $|T|\ne m$; its value on an
$m$-element set is the regular representation of $S_m$. Put
$M(m):=M(k[S_m])$. Then $M(m)_S$ has as $k$-basis the injections
$[m]\hookrightarrow S$ — equivalently, the ordered sequences of $m$ distinct
elements of $S$ — and for a partition $\lambda$ with $|\lambda|=m$ and a field
$k$ of characteristic $0$, put $M(\lambda):=M(S^\lambda_k)$, where the FB-module
$S^\lambda_k$ is supported on $m$-element sets and $S^\lambda_k(T):=
k[\operatorname{Iso}([m],T)]\otimes_{kS_m}S^\lambda_k$. By the adjunction, a map
$M(m)\to V$ of FI-modules corresponds naturally to the choice of an element of
$V_m$: the module $M(m)$ represents the functor $V\mapsto V_m$. All
constructions are given by finitely many canonical bijections of finite sets;
no choice principle is used.

Let $V$ be an FI-module over $k$ ([[def-fi-category-and-fi-module]]) and let
$\Sigma$ be a set of elements, each lying in $V_S$ for some finite set $S$. The
**sub-FI-module generated by $\Sigma$**, written
$\operatorname{span}_V(\Sigma)$, is the intersection of all sub-FI-modules of
$V$ that are subfunctors and contain $\Sigma$
([[def-submodule]], [[lem-submodule-criterion-sums-and-intersections]] for the
objectwise intersection of submodules). The family is nonempty because $V$
itself qualifies, and the intersection is a sub-FI-module, since each
transition map $f_*$ preserves every member and hence their intersection;
thus $\operatorname{span}_V(\Sigma)$ is the smallest sub-FI-module of $V$
containing $\Sigma$.

Explicitly, $\operatorname{span}_V(\Sigma)_T$ is the $k$-span of all elements
$f_*(v)$ with $v\in\Sigma\cap V_S$ and $f\colon S\to T$ a morphism of $FI$: the
set of all finite $k$-linear combinations of such elements is a sub-FI-module
of $V$ containing $\Sigma$, because $g_*(f_*(v))=(g\circ f)_*(v)$, and every
sub-FI-module containing $\Sigma$ contains each $f_*(v)$; hence it equals the
intersection. Call $V$ **finitely generated** when
$\operatorname{span}_V(\Sigma)=V$ for some finite $\Sigma$, and **generated in
degree $\le d$** when $\operatorname{span}_V(V_{\le d})=V$, where
$V_{\le d}=\bigsqcup_{|S|\le d}V_S$ is the set of all elements lying in the
values of $V$ at finite sets $S$ with $|S|\le d$. The **generation degree** of
$V$ is the least $d\ge0$ such that $V$ is generated in degree $\le d$, and
$\infty$ when no such $d$ exists
([[def-generated-cyclic-finitely-generated-and-free-modules]]).

Finite generation of $V$ and pointwise finite generation of the individual
$k$-modules $V_S$ are different conditions: the pointwise property is implied
by finite generation (as shown below by
[[lem-generated-in-degree-d-is-a-quotient-of-free-fi-modules]]) but does not
imply it, and no pointwise finite generation or finite-dimensionality is built
into either notion. A degree bound on a generating set is an additional
structure on $V$, not a consequence of finite generation. No choice principle
is used: $\operatorname{span}_V(\Sigma)$ is defined by an intersection of
subfunctors, and its explicit description involves only finite $k$-linear
combinations.

Let $R$ be a unital ring and $(M_i)_{i\in I}$ a family of left $R$-modules ([[def-left-and-right-modules]]). Their **direct product** is the module $\prod_{i\in I}M_i$ with coordinatewise operations. The **support** of $m=(m_i)$ is $\{i\in I:m_i\ne0\}$, and the **direct sum** is the submodule
$$\bigoplus_{i\in I}M_i=\{m\in\prod_{i\in I}M_i:\operatorname{supp}(m)\text{ is finite}\}$$
([[def-submodule]]).

This subset is a submodule because the support of a sum is contained in the union of two finite supports and scalar multiplication cannot enlarge support.

For each $i$, the coordinate inclusion $\jmath_i:M_i\to\bigoplus_jM_j$ puts its input in coordinate $i$ and zero elsewhere. If $I=\varnothing$, both product and direct sum are the zero module.

For left $R$-modules $M,N$, a function $f:M\to N$ is an **$R$-module
homomorphism** if

$$f(m+m')=f(m)+f(m')\quad\text{and}\quad f(rm)=rf(m)$$

for all $m,m'\in M$ and $r\in R$. It is a **module isomorphism** if it is a
bijective module homomorphism.

Its **kernel** and **image** are

$$\ker f:=\{m\in M:f(m)=0_N\},\qquad\operatorname{im}f:=\{f(m):m\in M\}.$$

Once [[thm-module-kernel-image-and-injectivity]] establishes that the image is a
submodule, the **cokernel** of $f$ is the quotient module
$\operatorname{coker}f:=N/\operatorname{im}f$.

Let $M$ be a left $R$-module and $S\subseteq M$. The **submodule generated by
$S$** is

$$\langle S\rangle_R:=\bigcap\{N\le M:S\subseteq N\}.$$

The family is nonempty because $M\le M$, and its intersection is a submodule by
[[lem-submodule-criterion-sums-and-intersections]]. Thus $\langle S\rangle_R$
is the smallest submodule of $M$ containing $S$, just as
[[def-generated-subgroup]] defines a generated subgroup.

The module $M$ is **cyclic** if $M=\langle m\rangle_R$ for some $m\in M$, and
**finitely generated** if $M=\langle S\rangle_R$ for some finite $S$. A subset
$B\subseteq M$ is a **basis** if every element of $M$ has a unique expression
as a finite $R$-linear combination of elements of $B$. A module possessing a
basis is a **free $R$-module**.

citations.quote:
Let $FI$ be the category ([[def-category]]) whose objects are the finite sets and
whose morphisms are the injections; composition is composition of functions and
identities are identity functions. Every finite set $S$ is in bijection with
exactly one of the sets $[n]:=\{0,1,\dots,n-1\}$, $n\ge0$, and injections
between these representatives form a full subcategory equivalent to $FI$;
under the realization $S_n=\operatorname{Sym}(\{0,\dots,n-1\})$ of
[[def-finite-symmetric-group-and-permutation-notation]] this gives
$\operatorname{End}_{FI}([n])=S_n$ for every $n\ge0$, and between different
objects there are no endomorphisms.

An **FI-module over a commutative ring $k$** ([[def-commutative-ring]]) is a
covariant functor $V\colon FI\to k\text{-}\mathrm{Mod}$
([[def-functor-and-contravariant-functor]],
[[def-left-and-right-modules]]). Write $V_S:=V(S)$, $V_n:=V([n])$ and
$f_*:=V(f)\colon V_S\to V_T$ for a morphism $f\colon S\to T$; functoriality
means $(g\circ f)_*=g_*\circ f_*$ and $(\mathrm{id}_S)_*=\mathrm{id}_{V_S}$.
Since $\operatorname{End}_{FI}([n])=S_n$, the maps $V_n\to V_n$ induced by
permutations make $V_n$ a left $kS_n$-module via the group ring
([[def-group-ring]], [[thm-group-actions-and-group-ring-modules-correspond]]):
functoriality gives $\sigma_*\tau_*=(\sigma\tau)_*$ and
${(\mathrm{id})}_*=\mathrm{id}$, and the group-ring axioms follow.

For an injection $f\colon[m]\to[n]$ define
$\Phi_f\colon S_m\to S_n$ by $\Phi_f(\sigma)(y):=f(\sigma(f^{-1}(y)))$ for
$y\in f([m])$ and $\Phi_f(\sigma)(y):=y$ for $y\notin f([m])$; then $\Phi_f$ is
a group homomorphism, because $f^{-1}(y)$ is defined on $f([m])$, the two
factors of a product commute through $f$, and both sides fix the complement
pointwise. Since $f\circ\sigma=\Phi_f(\sigma)\circ f$, functoriality gives
$f_*\circ\sigma_*=(\Phi_f(\sigma))_*\circ f_*$ for all $\sigma\in S_m$: each
$f_*\colon V_m\to V_n$ is equivariant for the conjugation homomorphism
$\Phi_f$ determined by $f$.

A **sub-FI-module** of $V$ is a subfunctor $W\subseteq V$
([[def-submodule]]): submodules $W_S\le V_S$ with $f_*(W_S)\subseteq W_T$ for
all injections $f\colon S\to T$. A **map of FI-modules** $V\to W$ is a natural
transformation, and kernels, images and cokernels of such maps are computed
pointwise, so that e.g. $\ker(F)_S=\ker(F_S\colon V_S\to W_S)$ with the
restrictions of the transition maps
([[def-quotient-module]], [[def-abelian-category]]). With these pointwise
operations the category of FI-modules over $k$ inherits its additive structure
and its abelian-category structure from $k\text{-}\mathrm{Mod}$
([[thm-modules-over-a-ring-form-an-abelian-category]]): finite direct sums,
kernels, cokernels and the compatibility axioms are checked objectwise, and a
pointwise surjective map is an epimorphism and a pointwise injective map is a
monomorphism.

An **FB-module over $k$** is a functor from the groupoid $FB$ of finite sets
and bijections to $k\text{-}\mathrm{Mod}$, with natural transformations as
maps. Since all morphisms of $FB$ are isomorphisms and every finite set is
isomorphic to exactly one $[n]$, an FB-module is determined up to isomorphism
by the $kS_n$-modules $W_n$ alone and carries no transition maps between
different $n$. No choice principle is used beyond the definable-class
conventions of [[def-category]].

Let $V$ be an FI-module over $k$ ([[def-fi-category-and-fi-module]]) and let
$\Sigma$ be a set of elements, each lying in $V_S$ for some finite set $S$. The
**sub-FI-module generated by $\Sigma$**, written
$\operatorname{span}_V(\Sigma)$, is the intersection of all sub-FI-modules of
$V$ that are subfunctors and contain $\Sigma$
([[def-submodule]], [[lem-submodule-criterion-sums-and-intersections]] for the
objectwise intersection of submodules). The family is nonempty because $V$
itself qualifies, and the intersection is a sub-FI-module, since each
transition map $f_*$ preserves every member and hence their intersection;
thus $\operatorname{span}_V(\Sigma)$ is the smallest sub-FI-module of $V$
containing $\Sigma$.

Explicitly, $\operatorname{span}_V(\Sigma)_T$ is the $k$-span of all elements
$f_*(v)$ with $v\in\Sigma\cap V_S$ and $f\colon S\to T$ a morphism of $FI$: the
set of all finite $k$-linear combinations of such elements is a sub-FI-module
of $V$ containing $\Sigma$, because $g_*(f_*(v))=(g\circ f)_*(v)$, and every
sub-FI-module containing $\Sigma$ contains each $f_*(v)$; hence it equals the
intersection. Call $V$ **finitely generated** when
$\operatorname{span}_V(\Sigma)=V$ for some finite $\Sigma$, and **generated in
degree $\le d$** when $\operatorname{span}_V(V_{\le d})=V$, where
$V_{\le d}=\bigsqcup_{|S|\le d}V_S$ is the set of all elements lying in the
values of $V$ at finite sets $S$ with $|S|\le d$. The **generation degree** of
$V$ is the least $d\ge0$ such that $V$ is generated in degree $\le d$, and
$\infty$ when no such $d$ exists
([[def-generated-cyclic-finitely-generated-and-free-modules]]).

Finite generation of $V$ and pointwise finite generation of the individual
$k$-modules $V_S$ are different conditions: the pointwise property is implied
by finite generation (as shown below by
[[lem-generated-in-degree-d-is-a-quotient-of-free-fi-modules]]) but does not
imply it, and no pointwise finite generation or finite-dimensionality is built
into either notion. A degree bound on a generating set is an additional
structure on $V$, not a consequence of finite generation. No choice principle
is used: $\operatorname{span}_V(\Sigma)$ is defined by an intersection of
subfunctors, and its explicit description involves only finite $k$-linear
combinations.

Let $A$ and $B$ be sets and let $f : A \to B$ be a function ([[def-function]]).

- $f$ is **injective** (one-to-one) if $f(x) = f(y)$ implies $x = y$, for all
  $x, y \in A$.
- $f$ is **surjective** (onto) if for every $b \in B$ there is some $x \in A$
  with $f(x) = b$; equivalently, the image $f[A] := \{ f(x) : x \in A \}$ equals
  $B$.
- $f$ is **bijective** if it is both injective and surjective.

For $S \subseteq A$ we write $f[S] = \{ f(x) : x \in S \}$ for the image of $S$,
and for $T \subseteq B$ we write $f^{-1}[T] = \{ x \in A : f(x) \in T \}$ for the
preimage of $T$; these are the image and preimage of a set under $f$ read as a
relation ([[def-image-and-preimage-under-a-relation]]).

Let $n\in\mathbb N$, so that $n=\{0,1,\dots,n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]). The
**symmetric group on $n$ letters** is

$$S_n:=\operatorname{Sym}(n)=\operatorname{Sym}(\{0,1,\dots,n-1\}),$$

the group of all bijections of $n$ under composition ([[def-symmetric-group]]),
with the composition convention

$$(\sigma\tau)(i):=(\sigma\circ\tau)(i)=\sigma(\tau(i))\qquad(i\in n),$$

so that in a product the right-hand factor acts first. An element of $S_n$ is
named by either of the two notations below.

**One-line notation.** For $\sigma\in S_n$, its **one-line form** is the list of
its values in order of their arguments,

$$\sigma=[\sigma(0),\sigma(1),\dots,\sigma(n-1)].$$

This list has length $n$ and its entries are $0,1,\dots,n-1$, each occurring
once, because $\sigma$ is a bijection of $n$. Conversely, a list
$[b_0,b_1,\dots,b_{n-1}]$ whose entries are $0,1,\dots,n-1$ each occurring once
is the one-line form of exactly one element of $S_n$, namely the map sending
each $i\in n$ to $b_i$: that map is injective because the entries are distinct,
and surjective because every element of $n$ occurs among them. So one-line
notation is a bijection from $S_n$ to the arrangements of $0,1,\dots,n-1$ in a
list. For $n=0$ the one-line form of the unique element of $S_0$ is the empty
list.

**Cycle notation.** For distinct $a_0,a_1,\dots,a_{k-1}\in n$ with $k\ge2$, the
symbol $(a_0\,a_1\,\cdots\,a_{k-1})$ denotes the element of $S_n$ that sends
$a_i$ to $a_{i+1}$ for each $i<k-1$, sends $a_{k-1}$ to $a_0$, and fixes every
element of $n$ outside $\{a_0,\dots,a_{k-1}\}$ ([[def-symmetric-group]]); it is
called a **$k$-cycle**, and a $2$-cycle is a **transposition**. Writing cycle
symbols side by side means composing them, so $(a\,b)(c\,d)$ is
$(a\,b)\circ(c\,d)$, and the empty juxtaposition of cycle symbols is the
identity $\operatorname{id}$.

Unlike one-line notation, cycle notation does not name each permutation once:
the symbol may be started at any of its entries, so

$$(a_0\,a_1\,\cdots\,a_{k-1})=(a_1\,\cdots\,a_{k-1}\,a_0)$$

and each $k$-cycle is written by exactly $k$ symbols of this shape. A cycle
symbol also does not record $n$, which must be supplied by the context.

derivations.claim: $V$ is a functor: $V(\mathrm{id}_S)$ sends $e_S$ to $e_S$ because $\mathrm{id}_S$ is a bijection; and for composable injections $f\colon S\to T$, $g\colon T\to U$ the two sides of $V(g\circ f)=V(g)V(f)$ agree on $e_S$ in each case — if $f$ and $g$ are bijections both sides send $e_S\mapsto e_U$; if $g$ fails to be a bijection then $g\circ f$ fails to be a bijection, so both sides are $0$; and if $f$ fails to be a bijection then $g\circ f$ fails to be a bijection and both sides are $0$. Hence $V$ is an FI-module and $\dim_kV_S=1$ for every finite set $S$.

Suppose $\Sigma=\{s_1,\dots,s_k\}$ is a finite set of elements that generates $V$, with $s_i\in V_{S_i}$, and put $M:=\max_i|S_i|$ (if $k=0$, then $\operatorname{span}_V(\varnothing)=0\ne V$, so $k\ge1$). For every finite set $T$ with $|T|>M$, every injection $f\colon S_i\to T$ satisfies $|S_i|\le M<|T|$, so $f$ is not a bijection and $f_*(s_i)=V(f)(s_i)=0$.

By the explicit description of the span, step 1.2 shows $\operatorname{span}_V(\Sigma)_T=0$ for every finite set $T$ with $|T|>M$. Taking $T=[M+1]$, which has $M+1>M$ elements, gives $\operatorname{span}_V(\Sigma)_T=0$ while $V_T=k\,e_T\ne0$; hence $\operatorname{span}_V(\Sigma)\ne V$ and no finite set of elements generates $V$.

Thus $V$ has $\dim_kV_S=1$ for every finite set $S$ by step 1.1, yet is not finitely generated by step 2.1: pointwise finite-dimensionality does not imply finite generation, and the refuted claim fails.

boundaries.evidence: step 1.1: on S = emptyset the module V_emptyset = k e_emptyset is one-dimensional, so the counterexample includes the empty rank.
step 1.1: non-bijections act by the zero map, and functoriality of these zero values is part of the construction; the zero action is the mechanism of the example.
step 1.1: bijections act as the identity identification and the module is one-dimensional in every rank, including rank one.
step 1.2: an arbitrary finite generating set is reduced to the single integer M = max |S_i|, covering generators spread over different ranks.
step 2.1: the span vanishes at every T with |T| > M, the first rank past the largest generating degree.
step 1.2: only the finitely many listed generators and their finite maximum are used, so no choice principle enters the refutation.

boundaries.reason: The counterexample refutes the implication pointwise finite-dimensionality implies finite generation; it asserts no biconditional.
No converse direction is claimed; the failure is one-directional and recorded as such.
