containing $\Sigma$.

Explicitly, $\operatorname{span}_V(\Sigma)_T$ is the $k$-span of all elements
$f_*(v)$ with $v\in\Sigma\cap V_S$ and $f\colon S\to T$ a morphism of $FI$: the
set of all finite $k$-linear combinations of such elements is a sub-FI-module
of $V$ containing $\Sigma$, because $g_*(f_*(v))=(g\circ f)_*(v)$, and every
sub-FI-module containing $\Sigma$ contains each $f_*(v)$; hence it equals the
intersection. Call $V$ **finitely generated** when
$\operatorname{span}_V(\Sigma)=V$ for some finite $\Sigma$, and **generated in
degree $\le d$** when $\operatorname{span}_V(V_{\le d})=V$, where
$V_{\le d}=\bigsqcup_{|S|\le d}V_S$ is the set of all elements lying in the
values of $V$ at finite sets $S$ with $|S|\le d$. The **generation degree** of
$V$ is the least $d\ge0$ such that $V$ is generated in degree $\le d$, and
$\infty$ when no such $d$ exists
([[def-generated-cyclic-finitely-generated-and-free-modules]]).

Finite generation of $V$ and pointwise finite generation of the individual
$k$-modules $V_S$ are different conditions: the pointwise property is implied
by finite generation (as shown below by
[[lem-generated-in-degree-d-is-a-quotient-of-free-fi-modules]]) but does not
imply it, and no pointwise finite generation or finite-dimensionality is built
into either notion. A degree bound on a generating set is an additional
structure on $V$, not a consequence of finite generation. No choice principle
is used: $\operatorname{span}_V(\Sigma)$ is defined by an intersection of
subfunctors, and its explicit description involves only finite $k$-linear
combinations.

For $i\ge1$ and $n\ge0$ let $X_i\colon S_n\to\mathbb N$ be the function
sending a permutation $\sigma\in S_n$ to the number
$X_i(\sigma):=c_i(\sigma)$ of $i$-element orbits in its cycle type
([[def-permutation-support-disjoint-cycles-and-cycle-type]],
[[def-finite-symmetric-group-and-permutation-notation]],
[[def-natural-numbers]]); thus $X_1(\sigma)$ is the number of fixed points of
$\sigma$, and $X_i(\sigma)=0$ whenever $i>n$. Each $X_i$ is a **class
function** on $S_n$ ([[def-class-function-and-the-space-of-complex-class-functions]]):
if $\tau\sigma\tau^{-1}$ is a conjugate of $\sigma$, then $O\mapsto\tau(O)$ is
a bijection from the orbits of $\sigma$ onto the orbits of
$\tau\sigma\tau^{-1}$ that preserves cardinalities, so
$c_i(\tau\sigma\tau^{-1})=c_i(\sigma)$.

Let $\mathbb Q[X_1,X_2,\dots]$ be the polynomial ring on the family of
indeterminates indexed by $i\ge1$
([[def-polynomial-ring-on-a-family-of-indeterminates]]); its elements are
finitely supported coefficient families on the monomials of
[[def-monomials-on-an-index-set]], so every element involves only finitely many
of the indeterminates. A **character polynomial** is an element
$P\in\mathbb Q[X_1,X_2,\dots]$. Setting $\deg X_i:=i$ gives the monomial
$X^a=\prod_iX_i^{a_i}$ the **weighted degree** $\sum_ii\,a_i$ (a finite sum); a
character polynomial has **weighted degree $\le d$** when every monomial
occurring in it has weighted degree at most $d$, and the **weighted degree** of
$P\ne0$ is the largest weighted degree of a monomial of $P$. Products and
rational linear combinations of class functions on $S_n$ are again class
functions, so every character polynomial defines for each $n\ge0$ a class
function

$$P\colon S_n\longrightarrow\mathbb Q,\qquad \sigma\longmapsto P(X_1(\sigma),X_2(\sigma),\dots),$$

the defining sum being finite because $P$ has finite support and
$X_i(\sigma)=0$ for $i>n$; equivalently, the substitution $X_i\mapsto
X_i(\sigma)$ is the ring homomorphism supplied by
[[thm-universal-property-of-a-polynomial-ring-on-a-family]]. In this way a
character polynomial is realized as one class function on each $S_n$. The
realization is not injective on a single $S_n$, since $X_i$ vanishes
identically on $S_n$ for $i>n$. It is injective in the limit:

**Uniqueness.** If $P,Q$ agree as functions on $S_n$ for infinitely many $n$,
then $P=Q$.

Indeed, put $R:=P-Q$ and let $A\subseteq\mathbb N$ be infinite with
$R|_{S_n}=0$ for every $n\in A$. Fix $m\ge0$, $\sigma\in S_m$ and $k\ge0$, and
let $\sigma^{(k)}\in S_{m+k}$ be $\sigma$ extended by $k$ fixed points outside
its domain; then $X_1(\sigma^{(k)})=X_1(\sigma)+k$ and
$X_i(\sigma^{(k)})=X_i(\sigma)$ for $i\ge2$, so
$R(\sigma^{(k)})=\sum_j\bigl(X_1(\sigma)+k\bigr)^jR_j(\sigma)$, where
$R=\sum_jX_1^jR_j$ collects the monomials of $R$ by their $X_1$-exponent $j$,
each $R_j$ involving only $X_2,X_3,\dots$. The right-hand side is given by a
polynomial in $k$ over $\mathbb Q$ of degree at most the largest $j$ with
$R_j\ne0$, and it vanishes for all $k$ with $m+k\in A$, infinitely many $k$;
by the root bound of [[thm-root-bound-for-polynomials-over-a-domain]] that
polynomial is zero, so $R(\sigma)=0$
([[def-polynomial-evaluation-and-root]]). As $\sigma\in S_m$ was arbitrary,
$R$ vanishes on every $S_m$; equivalently, $R(b_1,\dots,b_M)=0$ for every
$M\ge0$ and every tuple $(b_1,\dots,b_M)\in\mathbb N^M$, since a disjoint union
of $b_i$ cycles of length $i$, $1\le i\le M$, is a permutation with $X_i=b_i$
for $i\le M$. If $R\ne0$, then $R$ involves only $X_1,\dots,X_M$ for some $M$,
and induction on $M$ shows that such an $R$ cannot vanish at every point of
$\mathbb N^M$: for $M=0$ the polynomial is a constant evaluated at the empty
tuple; and for $M\ge1$, fixing $(b_1,\dots,b_{M-1})\in\mathbb N^{M-1}$ makes
$b_M\mapsto R(b_1,\dots,b_{M-1},b_M)$ a polynomial in one variable over
$\mathbb Q$ with infinitely many roots, hence the zero polynomial, so every
$X_M$-coefficient of $R$ vanishes at $(b_1,\dots,b_{M-1})$ and the induction
applies to each of those coefficients. Hence $R=0$.

A sequence $(\chi_n)_{n\ge0}$ of class functions with $\chi_n$ a class function
on $S_n$ is **eventually polynomial** when there are $N\ge0$ and a character
polynomial $P$ with

$$\chi_n(\sigma)=P(X_1(\sigma),X_2(\sigma),\dots)$$

for all $n\ge N$ and all $\sigma\in S_n$
([[def-class-function-and-the-space-of-complex-class-functions]]). By
uniqueness in the limit, such a $P$ is determined by $(\chi_n)$ whenever it
exists. No choice principle is used.

For a square matrix $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(F)$, its **trace** is the sum of its
diagonal entries,

$$\operatorname{tr}(A):=\sum_{i\in n}a_{ii}.$$

For $n=0$, this is the empty sum, so the unique empty matrix has trace $0$.

derivations.claim: $V$ is a functor: $V(\mathrm{id}_S)$ sends each basis element $e_s$ to $e_s$, hence is the identity, and for composable injections $f\colon S\to T$, $g\colon T\to U$ one has $V(g\circ f)(e_s)=e_{g(f(s))}=V(g)(e_{f(s)})=V(g)V(f)(e_s)$ on every basis element, so $V(g\circ f)=V(g)V(f)$; hence $V$ is an FI-module with basis $S$ of $V_S$.

Identify $V_S$ with $M(1)_S$ by sending the basis element $e_s$ to the injection $u_s\colon[1]\to S$ with $u_s(0)=s$; this is a $k$-linear isomorphism because the $u_s$ are exactly the basis injections of $M(1)_S$ [F2]. It is compatible with transition maps: for $f\colon S\to S'$, $M(1)(f)(u_s)=f\circ u_s=u_{f(s)}$ corresponds to $e_{f(s)}=V(f)(e_s)$. Hence $V\cong M(1)$; in particular $V_n\cong k^n$ with basis $[n]$, and $\sigma\in S_n$ acts by $\sigma\cdot e_s=e_{\sigma(s)}$, the permutation representation.

The element $e_0\in V_{[1]}$ generates: for any finite set $S$ and $s\in S$, the injection $u_s\colon[1]\to S$ satisfies $(u_s)_*(e_0)=e_{u_s(0)}=e_s$, so $\operatorname{span}_V(e_0)$ contains every basis element and equals $V$; thus $V$ is generated in degree $\le1$ by $V_{\{0\}}$.

For $\sigma\in S_n$ and basis elements $s,t\in[n]$, the coefficient of $e_t$ in $\sigma\cdot e_s=e_{\sigma(s)}$ is $\delta_{t,\sigma(s)}$; the diagonal entry at $s$ is therefore $\delta_{s,\sigma(s)}$, equal to $1$ if $\sigma$ fixes $s$ and to $0$ otherwise. By [F5], $\operatorname{tr}(\sigma;V_n)=\sum_{s\in[n]}\delta_{s,\sigma(s)}$, the number of fixed points of $\sigma$, which is $X_1(\sigma)$; for $n=0$ both sides are $0$. This holds for every $n$, so the trace function of $V_n$ is the character polynomial $X_1$ on the whole range.
Steps 1.1, 2.1 and 2.2 exhibit $V\cong M(1)$ as the permutation FI-module generated in degree $\le1$, and step 3.1 identifies its character with $X_1$, a character polynomial of weighted degree $1$.

boundaries.evidence: step 1.1: V_emptyset = k is the free module on the empty set, and the functor axioms are checked for it in the same computation.
step 3.1: for n = 0 the trace over the empty basis is 0 and X_1(id) = 0, so the case is recorded rather than excepted.
step 2.2: V is generated in degree <= 1 by the single element e_0 in V_{[1]}, the smallest possible generating set.
step 2.1: the identification V_S = M(1)_S is built on basis elements for every finite S, including S of size 0 and 1 without exception.
step 3.1: the endpoint n = 0 and the general value of n satisfy the same formula, so the range n >= 0 has no exceptional point.
step 2.1: the isomorphism is defined by e_s -> u_s on the given basis; no basis of an abstract space or decomposition is selected.

boundaries.reason: The example verifies a character identity and a generation degree; no if-and-only-if is asserted.
No converse claim appears; the trace identity is asserted in one direction for every n and every sigma.

citations.quote:
Let $W$ be an FB-module over $k$, i.e. a functor from the groupoid of finite
sets and bijections to $k\text{-}\mathrm{Mod}$ ([[def-fi-category-and-fi-module]]);
thus $W(T)$ is a $k$-module for every finite set $T$, and every bijection
$\beta\colon T\to T'$ gives an isomorphism $W(\beta)\colon W(T)\to W(T')$.
Because an FB-module is defined on all finite sets, no transport choices are
needed below.

The **free FI-module** $M(W)$ assigns to a finite set $S$ the direct sum

$$M(W)_S:=\bigoplus_{T\subseteq S}W(T)$$

over all subsets $T\subseteq S$ ([[def-subset-and-proper-subset]],
[[def-direct-sum-of-a-family-of-modules]]; only finitely many summands occur).
For an injection $f\colon S\to S'$ and a subset $T\subseteq S$, the restriction
$f|_T\colon T\to f(T)$ is a bijection
([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]), and the transition map
$f_*\colon M(W)_S\to M(W)_{S'}$ is the sum of the isomorphisms
$W(f|_T)\colon W(T)\to W(f(T))$ over all $T\subseteq S$. This is $k$-linear and
functorial, since $(f'\circ f)|_T=f'|_{f(T)}\circ f|_T$; hence $M(W)$ is an
FI-module over $k$.

For $S=[n]=\{0,\dots,n-1\}$ the symmetric group $S_n$
([[def-finite-symmetric-group-and-permutation-notation]]) acts by
$\sigma\cdot T:=\sigma(T)$ and $W(\sigma|_T)$, and this is a left action
making $M(W)_n$ a left $kS_n$-module ([[def-group-ring]]). Grouping the sum by
the cardinality of $T$, the subsets of cardinality $a$ form a single $S_n$-orbit
with stabilizer the ordered block subgroup
$S_{\{0,\dots,a-1\}}\times S_{\{a,\dots,n-1\}}\cong S_a\times S_{n-a}$, so the
orbit summand is identified with an induced module
([[def-induced-r-linear-g-module-by-h-covariant-functions]]):

$$M(W)_n\cong\bigoplus_{a=0}^{n}\operatorname{Ind}_{S_a\times S_{n-a}}^{S_n}\bigl(W_a\boxtimes k\bigr),$$

where $W_a:=W(\{0,\dots,a-1\})$ is the value of the FB-module on an $a$-element
set, the first factor acts on $W_a$ through $W$ and the second factor acts
trivially, and $\boxtimes$ is the external tensor product of modules for the
two direct factors ([[def-outer-induction-product-for-symmetric-group-characters]],
[[lem-character-ring-of-a-direct-product-is-the-tensor-product]],
[[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]]).

**Adjunction.** Let $\pi$ be the functor from FI-modules to FB-modules that
forgets the maps between distinct cardinalities. The inclusion of the $T=S$
summand is a natural map $\eta_W\colon W\to\pi M(W)$, and evaluating a map
$F\colon M(W)\to V$ of FI-modules on that summand yields a map of FB-modules
$\pi F\circ\eta_W\colon W\to\pi V$. Conversely, a map of FB-modules
$\varphi\colon W\to\pi V$ extends uniquely to a map of FI-modules
$\widetilde\varphi\colon M(W)\to V$ whose value on the summand $W(T)\subseteq
M(W)_S$ is $V(\iota_{T,S})\circ\varphi_T$, with $\iota_{T,S}\colon T\to S$ the
inclusion; the components are compatible with injections and the two
constructions are inverse, so
$\operatorname{Hom}_{FI\text{-}Mod}(M(W),V)\cong
\operatorname{Hom}_{FB\text{-}Mod}(W,\pi V)$ naturally in $V$ and $W$: $M$ is
left adjoint to $\pi$, with unit $\eta$.

For $m\ge0$ write $k[S_m]$ for the FB-module with $k[S_m](T)$ the free $k$-module
on the bijections $[m]\to T$, and zero when $|T|\ne m$; its value on an
$m$-element set is the regular representation of $S_m$. Put
$M(m):=M(k[S_m])$. Then $M(m)_S$ has as $k$-basis the injections
$[m]\hookrightarrow S$ — equivalently, the ordered sequences of $m$ distinct
elements of $S$ — and for a partition $\lambda$ with $|\lambda|=m$ and a field
$k$ of characteristic $0$, put $M(\lambda):=M(S^\lambda_k)$, where the FB-module
$S^\lambda_k$ is supported on $m$-element sets and $S^\lambda_k(T):=
k[\operatorname{Iso}([m],T)]\otimes_{kS_m}S^\lambda_k$. By the adjunction, a map
$M(m)\to V$ of FI-modules corresponds naturally to the choice of an element of
$V_m$: the module $M(m)$ represents the functor $V\mapsto V_m$. All
constructions are given by finitely many canonical bijections of finite sets;
no choice principle is used.

A **graded $k[T]$-module** consists of $k$-modules $U_n$, $n\ge0$, together
with $k$-linear maps $T=T_n\colon U_n\to U_{n+1}$ for all $n\ge0$. A
**morphism** $U\to U'$ of graded $k[T]$-modules is a family of $k$-linear maps
$u_n\colon U_n\to U'_n$ with $u_{n+1}\circ T_n=T'_n\circ u_n$ for all $n$.

Fix $a\ge0$, a set $\mathbf a$ of cardinality $a$, and a functorial disjoint
union of finite sets. Let $V$ be an FI-module over $k$
([[def-fi-category-and-fi-module]]) and let $n\ge0$. Put

$$\Phi_a(V)_n:=(V_{\mathbf a\sqcup n})_{S_n},$$

the coinvariants of the $kS_n$-module $V_{\mathbf a\sqcup n}$: the quotient by
the span of the elements $\sigma\cdot v-v$, $\sigma\in S_n$, $v\in
V_{\mathbf a\sqcup n}$ ([[def-coinvariants-functor-of-a-group-module]],
[[def-quotient-module]]). Equivalently $\Phi_a(V)_n=k\otimes_{kS_n}
V_{\mathbf a\sqcup n}$, the two descriptions being identified by the balancing
argument of [[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]] and
the corresponding identification for $\mathbb Z$ in
[[def-coinvariants-functor-of-a-group-module]]; the group ring $kS_n$ is a
unital $k$-algebra with basis the group elements
([[def-group-ring]], [[thm-group-ring-is-a-unital-algebra-with-basis-g]]).

To define the transition map $T\colon\Phi_a(V)_n\to\Phi_a(V)_{n+1}$, choose an
injection $f\colon n\to n+1$. It induces the injection
$\mathrm{id}_{\mathbf a}\sqcup f\colon\mathbf a\sqcup n\to\mathbf a\sqcup n+1$
and hence a $k$-linear map $(V_{\mathbf a\sqcup n}\to
V_{\mathbf a\sqcup n+1})$. This map is $S_n$-equivariant, where $S_n$ acts on
the target through the injection $\mathrm{id}_{\mathbf a}\sqcup f$, so it
descends to the quotient map $T=T_f$ on coinvariants. The map $T_f$ is
independent of $f$: for two injections $f,g\colon n\to n+1$ the composite
$g\circ f^{-1}$ is a bijection $f(n)\to g(n)$, which extends along the
complement to a permutation $\tau\in S_{n+1}$ with $g=\tau\circ f$; then
$\mathrm{id}_{\mathbf a}\sqcup g=(\mathrm{id}_{\mathbf a}\sqcup
\tau)\circ(\mathrm{id}_{\mathbf a}\sqcup f)$, and the map induced by
$\mathrm{id}_{\mathbf a}\sqcup\tau$ on
$(V_{\mathbf a\sqcup n+1})_{S_{n+1}}$ is the identity because it comes from
the action of the group element $\tau$. Thus $T$ is well defined and
$(\Phi_a(V),T)$ is a graded $k[T]$-module.

A map of FI-modules $\alpha\colon V\to W$ gives $k$-linear maps
$\alpha_{\mathbf a\sqcup n}\colon V_{\mathbf a\sqcup n}\to W_{\mathbf
a\sqcup n}$ commuting with the $S_n$-actions and with the maps induced by
$\mathrm{id}_{\mathbf a}\sqcup f$, hence maps $(\Phi_a\alpha)_n$ of coinvariants
commuting with $T$; so $\Phi_a$ is a functor from FI-modules over $k$ to graded
$k[T]$-modules.

**Exactness.** Coinvariants of a group module are right exact
([[prop-the-coinvariants-functor-is-right-exact]]), so the functor
$M\mapsto M_{S_n}\cong k\otimes_{kS_n}M$ is right exact and each $\Phi_a$ is
right exact in every degree. If $k$ contains $\mathbb Q$, then $1/n!$ exists in $k$
and the averaging map
$s\colon\Phi_a(V)_n\to V_{\mathbf a\sqcup n}$,
$s([v])=\frac1{n!}\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\sigma\cdot v$, is a well-defined
$k$-linear section of the quotient map that is natural in $V$; it identifies
$\Phi_a(V)_n$ with the invariants $V_{\mathbf a\sqcup n}^{S_n}$. Under this
natural identification $\Phi_a$ becomes the invariants functor, which is left
exact (kernels of equivariant maps are computed pointwise), and therefore
$\Phi_a$ is exact; in that case the induced map $\Phi_a(W)\to\Phi_a(V)$ is
injective for every sub-FI-module $W\subseteq V$
([[def-submodule]], [[def-module-homomorphism-kernel-image-and-cokernel]]), so
$\Phi_a(W)$ is identified with a submodule of $\Phi_a(V)$. Finite averaging
uses only the finite groups $S_n$; no choice principle is used.

Let $F$ be a field of characteristic $0$, let $\lambda\vdash n$, and let
$S^\lambda_F$ be the corresponding field-valued Specht module
([[def-polytabloid-specht-module-over-an-arbitrary-field]]).

(i) For every $k\ge0$ there is an isomorphism of $FS_{n+k}$-modules

$$\operatorname{Ind}_{S_n\times S_k}^{S_{n+k}}\bigl(S^\lambda_F\boxtimes F\bigr)\cong\bigoplus_{\mu}S^\mu_F,$$

summed over the partitions $\mu\vdash n+k$ obtained from $\lambda$ by adding
one box to each of $k$ different columns (equivalently, $\mu\supseteq\lambda$
and $\mu/\lambda$ is a horizontal $k$-strip).

(ii) For every $k\le n$ there is an isomorphism of $FS_{n-k}$-modules

$$\bigl(\operatorname{Res}^{S_n}_{S_{n-k}\times S_k}S^\lambda_F\bigr)_{S_k}\cong\bigoplus_{\nu}S^\nu_F,$$

summed over the partitions $\nu\vdash n-k$ obtained from $\lambda$ by removing
one box from each of $k$ different columns, where the outer subscript denotes
$S_k$-coinvariants of the restriction to the ordered block subgroup
$S_{n-k}\times S_k\le S_n$ ([[def-coinvariants-functor-of-a-group-module]]);
the left-hand side is an $FS_{n-k}$-module because the two blocks commute. All
multiplicities are $0$ or $1$. No choice principle is used.

Let $F$ be a field of characteristic $0$ and let $n\ge0$. For every partition
$\lambda\vdash n$ the field-valued Specht module $S^\lambda_F$ of
[[def-polytabloid-specht-module-over-an-arbitrary-field]] is nonzero and
irreducible, distinct partitions give non-isomorphic modules, and every
irreducible $FS_n$-module is isomorphic to exactly one of them. Consequently,
by Maschke's theorem, every finite-dimensional $FS_n$-module is a direct sum of
copies of the $S^\lambda_F$; thus the irreducible $FS_n$-modules are indexed by
the partitions of $n$ and the modules $\{S^\lambda_F:\lambda\vdash n\}$ form a
complete irredundant list.

This is the constituent convention used throughout the pair: over
$F=\mathbb C$ it specialises to the published complex classification, and over
a general characteristic-zero field $F$ it is proved by extending the rational
Specht models along $\mathbb Q\to F$, never by a scalar extension from
$\mathbb C$ to $F$.

Let $\alpha=(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_k)$ be a partition with $|\alpha|=\alpha_1+\cdots+\alpha_k$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]), and let $n\ge0$ be
an integer. Whenever

$$n\;\ge\;|\alpha|+\alpha_1,$$

define the **first-row padding** of $\alpha$ to size $n$ to be
$$\alpha[n]:=\bigl(n-|\alpha|,\ \alpha_1,\ \alpha_2,\ \dots,\ \alpha_k\bigr).$$

The threshold is exact.

**Above the threshold.** Suppose $n\ge|\alpha|+\alpha_1$. Then
$n-|\alpha|\ge\alpha_1\ge0$, so every entry of the displayed sequence is a
nonnegative integer, the entries sum to $(n-|\alpha|)+|\alpha|=n$, and the
sequence is weakly decreasing because $n-|\alpha|\ge\alpha_1$ and $\alpha$ is
weakly decreasing ([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]).
If $\alpha$ is nonempty then $\alpha_1\ge1$, hence $n-|\alpha|\ge1$ and the
displayed sequence is a partition of $n$ with positive parts. If
$\alpha=\varnothing$ then the displayed sequence is $(n)$; this is a partition
of $n$ for every $n\ge1$, while for $n=0$ one takes $\varnothing[0]:=\varnothing$,
the unique partition of $0$. Thus the padding is defined and is a partition of
$n$ on the whole displayed range.

**Below the threshold.** If $\alpha$ is nonempty and $n<|\alpha|+\alpha_1$,
then $n-|\alpha|<\alpha_1$; if also $n\ge|\alpha|$ the leading entry is
nonnegative but smaller than the second entry $\alpha_1$, and if $n<|\alpha|$
it is negative. In both cases the displayed sequence is not a partition, so
$\alpha[n]$ is left undefined. The threshold $|\alpha|+\alpha_1$ is therefore
the exact size at which the padded family begins: at
$n=|\alpha|+\alpha_1$ the padding equals $(\alpha_1,\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\dots)$,
which is a partition with a repeated first part when $\alpha$ is nonempty.

**Neutrality of the notation.** This definition records a family of partitions;
it asserts no constancy of any quantity along the family and no stability
property. The same notation is used by the FI-module and
representation-stability developments, where the padding threshold reappears as
the generation degree of the family under consideration.

Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $0$ and let $V$ be an FI-module over $k$
([[def-fi-category-and-fi-module]]). For a partition $\lambda$ and
$n\ge|\lambda|+\lambda_1$ put $\lambda[n]:=(n-|\lambda|,\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\dots)$,
the first-row padding ([[def-first-row-padding-of-a-partition]]), and let

$$V(\lambda)_n:=k\otimes_{\mathbb Q}S^{\lambda[n]}_{\mathbb Q}$$

be the scalar extension of the rational Specht model of $\lambda[n]$
([[thm-complex-specht-modules-are-irreducible]],
[[lem-specht-modules-classify-irreducibles-over-characteristic-zero-fields]]).
By the classification lemma, $V(\lambda)_n$ is the irreducible $kS_n$-module
with label $\lambda[n]$, and every irreducible $kS_n$-module is isomorphic to
exactly one $V(\lambda)_n$: indeed, every partition $\mu=(\mu_1,\mu_2,\dots)$
of $n$ is uniquely $\lambda[n]$ for the partition
$\lambda=(\mu_2,\mu_3,\dots)$ obtained by deleting the first row, and
$n\ge|\lambda|+\lambda_1$ holds precisely because $\mu_1\ge\mu_2$;
consequently the labels $\lambda[n]$ run over the partitions of $n$ without
repetition.

Say that $V(\lambda)_n$ **occurs as a constituent** of $V_n$ when there are
$kS_n$-submodules $U\subseteq W\subseteq V_n$ with
$W/U\cong V(\lambda)_n$ ([[def-submodule]], [[def-quotient-module]]); this is a
condition on subquotients and requires no decomposition or finite-dimensionality
of $V_n$. The **weight** of $V$ is

$$\operatorname{weight}(V):=\sup\bigl\{|\lambda|:V(\lambda)_n\text{ occurs as a constituent of }V_n\text{ for some }n\ge|\lambda|+\lambda_1\bigr\},$$

the supremum over all pairs $(\lambda,n)$ as displayed. The set of integers
displayed is a set of nonnegative integers, so the supremum is well defined in
$\mathbb N\cup\{\infty\}$; it is $0$ for $V=0$, and $\operatorname{weight}(V)=\infty$
exactly when the displayed set is unbounded. No finiteness of
$\operatorname{weight}(V)$ is asserted.

If $W$ is a **subquotient** of $V$, meaning that $W\cong U'/U$ for sub-FI-modules
$U\subseteq U'\subseteq V$ computed pointwise, then
$\operatorname{weight}(W)\le\operatorname{weight}(V)$: a constituent of $W_n$ is
a subquotient of the subquotient $U'_n/U_n$ of $V_n$, hence a subquotient of
$V_n$, so it contributes the same label $|\lambda|$ to the supremum for $V$. No
choice principle is used: the labels $\lambda[n]$, constituents and the
supremum are set-theoretic data, and no bases or decompositions are chosen.

Let $G$ be a finite group, let $k$ be a field with
$\operatorname{char} k \nmid |G|$, let $\rho:G \to \operatorname{GL}(V)$ be a
finite-dimensional representation of $G$ over $k$, and let $W \le V$ be a
subrepresentation. Then there is a subrepresentation $U \le V$ such that

$$V=W\oplus U.$$

derivations.claim:
Decompose $M(W)_{\mathbf a\sqcup n}=\bigoplus_{T\subseteq\mathbf a\sqcup n}W(T)$ under the action of $S_n$ (fixing $\mathbf a$) [F1]. The $S_n$-orbits of subsets are classified by the pair $(U,k)$ with $U\subseteq\mathbf a$ and $0\le k\le n$, where $U=T\cap\mathbf a$ and $k=|T\cap n|$; a representative is $T_{U,k}=U\sqcup\{a_0,\dots,a_0+k-1\}$, and its stabilizer is the copy of $S_k\times S_{n-k}$ permuting the chosen $k$-element block of $n$ and its complement. Therefore the coinvariants split as
$$\Phi_aM(W)_n\cong\bigoplus_{U\subseteq\mathbf a}\bigoplus_{k=0}^{n}\Phi_{|U|}(W)_k,$$
because on the summand $W(T_{U,k})$ the complement factor $S_{n-k}$ acts trivially and the block factor $S_k$ acts by permutations of the last $k$ points of $U\sqcup\{a_0,\dots,a_0+k-1\}\cong[|U|+k]$, so that its coinvariants are exactly $\Phi_{|U|}(W)_k$ [F2]. The transition map $T$ is induced by an injection fixing $\mathbf a$ that sends the standard $k$-block of $n$ into the standard $k$-block of $n+1$; it preserves $U$ and $k$ and acts as the identity on each factor $\Phi_{|U|}(W)_k$.

Let $k$ have characteristic $0$ and let $|\lambda|=m$. For $n\ge m$ the identification $M(S^\lambda_k)_n\cong\operatorname{Ind}^{S_n}_{S_m	imes S_{n-m}}(S^\lambda_k oxtimes k)$ of [F1] together with the branching rule [F3] shows that the constituents of $M(\lambda)_n$ are the Specht modules $S^{
u}$ over the partitions $
u\vdash n$ obtained from $\lambda$ by adding one box in each of $n-m$ different columns; for $n<m$ the value is $0$. For such a $
u$, the added boxes occupy $n-m$ distinct columns, so $
u_1\ge n-m$; writing $
u=\eta[n]$ this gives $|\eta|=n-
u_1\le m$. Hence every constituent $V(\eta)_n$ of any $M(\lambda)_n$ has $|\eta|\le m$, so $\operatorname{weight}(M(\lambda))\le m$ by [F5].

By step 1.1 the map $T\colon\Phi_aM(W)_n\to\Phi_aM(W)_{n+1}$ is injective for all $a,n$, since it is the identity on every direct summand and maps distinct summands to distinct summands; hence $\operatorname{inj-deg}(M(W))=0$. If $W_i=0$ for $i>m$, then $\Phi_{|U|}(W)_k=0$ for $k>m$, so for $n\ge m$ the direct-sum decomposition of step 1.1 is independent of $n$ and $T$ is an isomorphism; hence $\operatorname{surj-deg}(M(W))\le m$. For $M(m)=M(k[S_m])$ the factor $\Phi_0(k[S_m])_m=(k[S_m])_{S_m}\cong k$ is nonzero, and it occurs in $\Phi_0(M(m))_n$ only when $n\ge m$; so $T\colon\Phi_0(M(m))_{m-1}\to\Phi_0(M(m))_m$ (with the convention that the empty direct sum is $0$ when $m=0$) is not surjective, giving $\operatorname{surj-deg}(M(m))\ge m$ and hence equality, and $\operatorname{stab-deg}(M(m))=m$.

Conversely, for $n\ge m+\lambda_1$ the padded partition $\lambda[n]=(n-m,\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\dots)$ is obtained from $\lambda$ by adding one box in each of the first $n-m$ columns, so $V(\lambda)_n$ occurs in $M(\lambda)_n$ by step 1.2; therefore $\operatorname{weight}(M(\lambda))\ge m$, and with step 1.2, $\operatorname{weight}(M(\lambda))=m$.

For the stability degree, fix $a\ge0$ and use the decomposition of step 1.1 for $W=S^\lambda_k$: the factor indexed by $U\subseteq\mathbf a$ is $\Phi_{|U|}(S^\lambda_k)_k=(S^\lambda_k)_{S_k}$ when $|U|+k=m$ (and $0$ otherwise), where $S_k$ acts on the last $k$ points. By the branching rule [F3], $(S^\lambda_k)_{S_k}$ is the sum of the Specht modules obtained from $\lambda$ by removing one box from each of $k$ different columns, and by the strip criterion [F4] such a removal exists exactly when $k\le\lambda_1$; hence $(S^\lambda_k)_{S_k}=0$ for $k>\lambda_1$ and is nonzero for $k=\lambda_1$ provided $m\ge\lambda_1$. Consequently, for every $n\ge\lambda_1$ all nonzero factors of $\Phi_aM(\lambda)_n$ already occur in $\Phi_aM(\lambda)_{\lambda_1}$, and $T$ acts as the identity on them, so $T$ is surjective for all $n\ge\lambda_1$; thus $\operatorname{surj-deg}(M(\lambda))\le\lambda_1$.

Sharpness: if $\lambda_1>0$, take $a=m-\lambda_1\ge0$. The factor with $U=\mathbf a$ and $k=\lambda_1$ equals $(S^\lambda_k)_{S_{\lambda_1}}\ne0$ and occurs in $\Phi_aM(\lambda)_n$ exactly when $n\ge\lambda_1$; in particular $T\colon\Phi_aM(\lambda)_{\lambda_1-1}\to\Phi_aM(\lambda)_{\lambda_1}$ has a nonzero target summand not met by $T$, so it is not surjective and $\operatorname{surj-deg}(M(\lambda))\ge\lambda_1$. Hence $\operatorname{surj-deg}(M(\lambda))=\lambda_1$, and by step 2.1, which gives injectivity degree $0$, $\operatorname{stab-deg}(M(\lambda))=\lambda_1$. For $\lambda=\varnothing$ we have $m=\lambda_1=0$, $M(\varnothing)=M(k)$ has all transition maps isomorphisms and stability degree $0$.

Step 2.1 gives the general injectivity and surjectivity bounds and the exact stability degree of $M(m)$; steps 1.2 and 2.2 give $\operatorname{weight}(M(\lambda))=|\lambda|$; steps 2.3 and 3.1 give $\operatorname{stab-deg}(M(\lambda))=\lambda_1$.

citations.quote:
Let $V$ be an FI-module over $k$ ([[def-fi-category-and-fi-module]]) and let
$\Sigma$ be a set of elements, each lying in $V_S$ for some finite set $S$. The
**sub-FI-module generated by $\Sigma$**, written
$\operatorname{span}_V(\Sigma)$, is the intersection of all sub-FI-modules of
$V$ that are subfunctors and contain $\Sigma$
([[def-submodule]], [[lem-submodule-criterion-sums-and-intersections]] for the
objectwise intersection of submodules). The family is nonempty because $V$
itself qualifies, and the intersection is a sub-FI-module, since each
transition map $f_*$ preserves every member and hence their intersection;
thus $\operatorname{span}_V(\Sigma)$ is the smallest sub-FI-module of $V$
containing $\Sigma$.

Explicitly, $\operatorname{span}_V(\Sigma)_T$ is the $k$-span of all elements
$f_*(v)$ with $v\in\Sigma\cap V_S$ and $f\colon S\to T$ a morphism of $FI$: the
set of all finite $k$-linear combinations of such elements is a sub-FI-module
of $V$ containing $\Sigma$, because $g_*(f_*(v))=(g\circ f)_*(v)$, and every
sub-FI-module containing $\Sigma$ contains each $f_*(v)$; hence it equals the
intersection. Call $V$ **finitely generated** when
$\operatorname{span}_V(\Sigma)=V$ for some finite $\Sigma$, and **generated in
degree $\le d$** when $\operatorname{span}_V(V_{\le d})=V$, where
$V_{\le d}=\bigsqcup_{|S|\le d}V_S$ is the set of all elements lying in the
values of $V$ at finite sets $S$ with $|S|\le d$. The **generation degree** of
$V$ is the least $d\ge0$ such that $V$ is generated in degree $\le d$, and
$\infty$ when no such $d$ exists
([[def-generated-cyclic-finitely-generated-and-free-modules]]).

Finite generation of $V$ and pointwise finite generation of the individual
$k$-modules $V_S$ are different conditions: the pointwise property is implied
by finite generation (as shown below by
[[lem-generated-in-degree-d-is-a-quotient-of-free-fi-modules]]) but does not
imply it, and no pointwise finite generation or finite-dimensionality is built
into either notion. A degree bound on a generating set is an additional
structure on $V$, not a consequence of finite generation. No choice principle
is used: $\operatorname{span}_V(\Sigma)$ is defined by an intersection of
subfunctors, and its explicit description involves only finite $k$-linear
combinations.

Let $W$ be an FB-module over $k$, i.e. a functor from the groupoid of finite
sets and bijections to $k\text{-}\mathrm{Mod}$ ([[def-fi-category-and-fi-module]]);
thus $W(T)$ is a $k$-module for every finite set $T$, and every bijection
$\beta\colon T\to T'$ gives an isomorphism $W(\beta)\colon W(T)\to W(T')$.
Because an FB-module is defined on all finite sets, no transport choices are
needed below.

The **free FI-module** $M(W)$ assigns to a finite set $S$ the direct sum

$$M(W)_S:=\bigoplus_{T\subseteq S}W(T)$$

over all subsets $T\subseteq S$ ([[def-subset-and-proper-subset]],
[[def-direct-sum-of-a-family-of-modules]]; only finitely many summands occur).
For an injection $f\colon S\to S'$ and a subset $T\subseteq S$, the restriction
$f|_T\colon T\to f(T)$ is a bijection
([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]), and the transition map
$f_*\colon M(W)_S\to M(W)_{S'}$ is the sum of the isomorphisms
$W(f|_T)\colon W(T)\to W(f(T))$ over all $T\subseteq S$. This is $k$-linear and
functorial, since $(f'\circ f)|_T=f'|_{f(T)}\circ f|_T$; hence $M(W)$ is an
FI-module over $k$.

For $S=[n]=\{0,\dots,n-1\}$ the symmetric group $S_n$
([[def-finite-symmetric-group-and-permutation-notation]]) acts by
$\sigma\cdot T:=\sigma(T)$ and $W(\sigma|_T)$, and this is a left action
making $M(W)_n$ a left $kS_n$-module ([[def-group-ring]]). Grouping the sum by
the cardinality of $T$, the subsets of cardinality $a$ form a single $S_n$-orbit
with stabilizer the ordered block subgroup
$S_{\{0,\dots,a-1\}}\times S_{\{a,\dots,n-1\}}\cong S_a\times S_{n-a}$, so the
orbit summand is identified with an induced module
([[def-induced-r-linear-g-module-by-h-covariant-functions]]):

$$M(W)_n\cong\bigoplus_{a=0}^{n}\operatorname{Ind}_{S_a\times S_{n-a}}^{S_n}\bigl(W_a\boxtimes k\bigr),$$

where $W_a:=W(\{0,\dots,a-1\})$ is the value of the FB-module on an $a$-element
set, the first factor acts on $W_a$ through $W$ and the second factor acts
trivially, and $\boxtimes$ is the external tensor product of modules for the
two direct factors ([[def-outer-induction-product-for-symmetric-group-characters]],
[[lem-character-ring-of-a-direct-product-is-the-tensor-product]],
[[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]]).

**Adjunction.** Let $\pi$ be the functor from FI-modules to FB-modules that
forgets the maps between distinct cardinalities. The inclusion of the $T=S$
summand is a natural map $\eta_W\colon W\to\pi M(W)$, and evaluating a map
$F\colon M(W)\to V$ of FI-modules on that summand yields a map of FB-modules
$\pi F\circ\eta_W\colon W\to\pi V$. Conversely, a map of FB-modules
$\varphi\colon W\to\pi V$ extends uniquely to a map of FI-modules
$\widetilde\varphi\colon M(W)\to V$ whose value on the summand $W(T)\subseteq
M(W)_S$ is $V(\iota_{T,S})\circ\varphi_T$, with $\iota_{T,S}\colon T\to S$ the
inclusion; the components are compatible with injections and the two
constructions are inverse, so
$\operatorname{Hom}_{FI\text{-}Mod}(M(W),V)\cong
\operatorname{Hom}_{FB\text{-}Mod}(W,\pi V)$ naturally in $V$ and $W$: $M$ is
left adjoint to $\pi$, with unit $\eta$.

For $m\ge0$ write $k[S_m]$ for the FB-module with $k[S_m](T)$ the free $k$-module
on the bijections $[m]\to T$, and zero when $|T|\ne m$; its value on an
$m$-element set is the regular representation of $S_m$. Put
$M(m):=M(k[S_m])$. Then $M(m)_S$ has as $k$-basis the injections
$[m]\hookrightarrow S$ — equivalently, the ordered sequences of $m$ distinct
elements of $S$ — and for a partition $\lambda$ with $|\lambda|=m$ and a field
$k$ of characteristic $0$, put $M(\lambda):=M(S^\lambda_k)$, where the FB-module
$S^\lambda_k$ is supported on $m$-element sets and $S^\lambda_k(T):=
k[\operatorname{Iso}([m],T)]\otimes_{kS_m}S^\lambda_k$. By the adjunction, a map
$M(m)\to V$ of FI-modules corresponds naturally to the choice of an element of
$V_m$: the module $M(m)$ represents the functor $V\mapsto V_m$. All
constructions are given by finitely many canonical bijections of finite sets;
no choice principle is used.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring. If $M$ is free with basis $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ and $N$ is free with basis $(f_j)_{j\in J}$, then $M\otimes_RN$ is free with basis

$$\bigl(e_i\otimes f_j\bigr)_{(i,j)\in I\times J}.$$

Equivalently, the canonical map $R^{(I\times J)}\to M\otimes_RN$ sending the standard basis vector at $(i,j)$ to $e_i\otimes f_j$ is an isomorphism. This includes an empty basis in either factor.

Let $V$ be an FI-module over $k$
([[def-fi-category-and-fi-module]]), with free FI-modules $M(m)$ as in
[[def-free-fi-module-generated-by-an-sm-module]] and span as in
[[def-finite-generation-and-generation-degree-of-an-fi-module]].

(a) For $v\in V_m$ the map of FI-modules $M(m)\to V$ sending the canonical
generator $\mathrm{id}_m\in M(m)_m$ to $v$ has image $\operatorname{span}_V(v)$;
more generally, for any set $\Sigma$ of elements, each lying in some $V_S$, the
canonical map $\bigoplus_{s\in\Sigma}M(|S_s|)\to V$ sending the generator of
the summand indexed by $s$ to $s$ has image $\operatorname{span}_V(\Sigma)$.

(b) $V$ is finitely generated if and only if there is a finite family
$m_1,\dots,m_k\ge0$ with a surjection

$$M(m_1)\oplus\cdots\oplus M(m_k)\twoheadrightarrow V;$$

$V$ is generated in degree $\le d$ if and only if there is a surjection
$\bigoplus_{i\in I}M(m_i)\twoheadrightarrow V$ with $m_i\le d$ for all $i$. In
particular, if $V$ is generated in degree $\le d$, then the evaluation map
$\bigoplus_{m\le d}M(V_m)\to V$, whose restriction to each copy of $M(m)$
indexed by an element $v\in V_m$ sends $\mathrm{id}_m\mapsto v$, is surjective.

(c) If $V$ is finitely generated, then $V_S$ is a finitely generated $k$-module
for every finite set $S$
([[def-generated-cyclic-finitely-generated-and-free-modules]]).

No choice principle is used: all maps come from a finite or explicitly indexed
set of generators, and the image computations are linear algebra on the values
at a fixed finite set.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let

$$A\xrightarrow{f}B\xrightarrow{g}C\longrightarrow0$$

be an exact sequence of $R$-modules, and let $N$ be an $R$-module. Then

$$A\otimes_RN\xrightarrow{f\otimes1}B\otimes_RN\xrightarrow{g\otimes1}C\otimes_RN\longrightarrow0$$

is exact. Thus tensoring preserves cokernels and surjections, but no injectivity at the left is asserted.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $(M_i)_{i\in I}$ be any family of $R$-modules, and let $N$ be an $R$-module. The homomorphism induced by the coordinate inclusions is a natural $R$-module isomorphism

$$\Phi:\bigoplus_{i\in I}(M_i\otimes_RN)\longrightarrow\left(\bigoplus_{i\in I}M_i\right)\otimes_RN,$$

$$\Phi\bigl(\jmath_i(m\otimes n)\bigr)=\jmath_i(m)\otimes n.$$

The same holds with the direct sum in the second variable: there is a natural $R$-module isomorphism

$$\Phi':\bigoplus_{i\in I}(N\otimes_RM_i)\longrightarrow N\otimes_R\left(\bigoplus_{i\in I}M_i\right),\qquad \Phi'\bigl(\jmath_i(n\otimes m)\bigr)=n\otimes\jmath_i(m).$$

The assertion includes $I=\varnothing$, when both sides are zero.

Let $R$ be a unital ring, $M$ a right $R$-module, and $N$ a left $R$-module. Let

$$F:=\mathbb Z^{(M\times N)}$$

be the free $\mathbb Z$-module on the set $M\times N$ ([[def-free-module-on-a-set-and-standard-basis]], [[thm-universal-property-of-free-modules]]), and write $e_{(m,n)}$ for its standard basis elements. The additive group of $F$ is abelian. Let $H$ be the subgroup generated ([[def-generated-subgroup]]) by all elements

$$e_{(m+m',n)}-e_{(m,n)}-e_{(m',n)},$$

$$e_{(m,n+n')}-e_{(m,n)}-e_{(m,n')},$$

and

$$e_{(mr,n)}-e_{(m,rn)}$$

as $m,m'$ range over $M$, $n,n'$ over $N$, and $r$ over $R$. Since every subgroup of an abelian group is normal, the quotient group $F/H$ is defined ([[def-quotient-group]]). The **tensor product of $M$ and $N$ over $R$** is

$$M\otimes_RN:=F/H.$$

The coset of $e_{(m,n)}$ is the **elementary tensor** $m\otimes n$. Every tensor is a finite sum of elementary tensors, because every element of $F$ is a finite $\mathbb Z$-linear combination of basis elements and integer coefficients may be absorbed into either additive variable. The defining relations give

$$(m+m')\otimes n=m\otimes n+m'\otimes n,\qquad m\otimes(n+n')=m\otimes n+m\otimes n',$$

and

$$(mr)\otimes n=m\otimes(rn).$$

In particular $0\otimes n=0=m\otimes0$. No $R$-module structure on $M\otimes_RN$ is part of this arbitrary-ring definition; at this stage it is an abelian group.

derivations.claim: $V\otimes W$ is an FI-module: $(V\otimes W)(\mathrm{id}_S)=\mathrm{id}_{V_S}\otimes\mathrm{id}_{W_S}=\mathrm{id}_{V_S\otimes W_S}$, and $(g\circ f)_*\otimes(g\circ f)_*=(g_*\otimes g_*)(f_*\otimes f_*)$ for composable injections; the pointwise tensor product of $k$-linear maps and the functor axioms in each variable give the claim.

Let $U:=M(m_1)\otimes M(m_2)$, with $(U)_S$ having $k$-basis the pairs $(f_1,f_2)$ of injections $f_1\colon[m_1]\hookrightarrow S$, $f_2\colon[m_2]\hookrightarrow S$ [F2]. For a basis element $(f_1,f_2)$, put $T:=\operatorname{im}(f_1)\cup\operatorname{im}(f_2)\subseteq S$, so $|T|\le m_1+m_2$; the maps $f_i$ factor as $f_i=\iota\circ g_i$ with $g_i\colon[m_i]\hookrightarrow T$ injective and $\iota\colon T\hookrightarrow S$ the inclusion, and functoriality gives $(f_1,f_2)=(\iota_*\otimes\iota_*)(g_1,g_2)$ with $(g_1,g_2)\in U_T$. Hence every basis element of $U_S$ lies in the span of the images of the $U_T$ with $|T|\le m_1+m_2$, so $\operatorname{span}_U(U_{\le m_1+m_2})=U$ by [F1]: $U$ is generated in degree $\le m_1+m_2$.

Now let $V$ be generated in degree $\le m_1$ and $W$ in degree $\le m_2$, so that by [F3] there are surjections $\bigoplus_{i=1}^rM(m_i)\twoheadrightarrow V$ and $\bigoplus_{j=1}^sM(n_j)\twoheadrightarrow W$ with $m_i\le m_1$, $n_j\le m_2$. Tensoring them pointwise and distributing the finite direct sums [F4] gives a surjection $\bigoplus_{i,j}\bigl(M(m_i)\otimes M(n_j)\bigr)\twoheadrightarrow V\otimes W$.

Each summand $U_{ij}:=M(m_i)\otimes M(n_j)$ is generated in degree $\le m_i+n_j\le m_1+m_2$ by step 2.1, hence so is their finite direct sum; and a quotient of a module generated in degree $\le d$ is generated in degree $\le d$, because the image of $\operatorname{span}(U_{\le d})=U$ under a surjective map of FI-modules is $\operatorname{span}$ of the images of $U_{\le d}$, which is the whole quotient. Therefore $V\otimes W$, being a quotient of the sum of the $U_{ij}$, is generated in degree $\le m_1+m_2$.

If $V$ and $W$ are finitely generated, they are generated in degrees $\le m_1$ and $\le m_2$ for suitable finite $m_1,m_2$, and step 3.1 exhibits a finite generating set of $V\otimes W$ of degrees at most $m_1+m_2$; hence $V\otimes W$ is finitely generated, with the stated degree bound.

boundaries.evidence: step 2.1: m_1 = 0 or m_2 = 0 makes one factor M(0) = M(k), and the union T of images covers the empty-image case without exception.
step 1.1: V = 0 or W = 0 yields V_S tensor W_S = 0 and the zero FI-module, included in the functoriality verification.
step 2.1: for m_1 = m_2 = 1 the module U = M(1) tensor M(1) is generated by the single basis pair (id, id) in degree 2.
step 2.2: the surjections supplied by the presentation lemma may have zero summands when a factor is 0, and empty finite sums of modules are allowed.
step 3.1: the degree bound m_1 + m_2 is inclusive, with equality in T = im f_1 union im f_2 when the two images are disjoint.
step 4.1: the generating set is the explicit finite set of tensor products of the chosen generators; no basis of V or W is selected.

No converse necessary condition is stated or used in the proof.

citations.quote:
Let $FI$ be the category ([[def-category]]) whose objects are the finite sets and
whose morphisms are the injections; composition is composition of functions and
identities are identity functions. Every finite set $S$ is in bijection with
exactly one of the sets $[n]:=\{0,1,\dots,n-1\}$, $n\ge0$, and injections
between these representatives form a full subcategory equivalent to $FI$;
under the realization $S_n=\operatorname{Sym}(\{0,\dots,n-1\})$ of
[[def-finite-symmetric-group-and-permutation-notation]] this gives
$\operatorname{End}_{FI}([n])=S_n$ for every $n\ge0$, and between different
objects there are no endomorphisms.

An **FI-module over a commutative ring $k$** ([[def-commutative-ring]]) is a
covariant functor $V\colon FI\to k\text{-}\mathrm{Mod}$
([[def-functor-and-contravariant-functor]],
[[def-left-and-right-modules]]). Write $V_S:=V(S)$, $V_n:=V([n])$ and
$f_*:=V(f)\colon V_S\to V_T$ for a morphism $f\colon S\to T$; functoriality
means $(g\circ f)_*=g_*\circ f_*$ and $(\mathrm{id}_S)_*=\mathrm{id}_{V_S}$.
Since $\operatorname{End}_{FI}([n])=S_n$, the maps $V_n\to V_n$ induced by
permutations make $V_n$ a left $kS_n$-module via the group ring
([[def-group-ring]], [[thm-group-actions-and-group-ring-modules-correspond]]):
functoriality gives $\sigma_*\tau_*=(\sigma\tau)_*$ and
${(\mathrm{id})}_*=\mathrm{id}$, and the group-ring axioms follow.

For an injection $f\colon[m]\to[n]$ define
$\Phi_f\colon S_m\to S_n$ by $\Phi_f(\sigma)(y):=f(\sigma(f^{-1}(y)))$ for
$y\in f([m])$ and $\Phi_f(\sigma)(y):=y$ for $y\notin f([m])$; then $\Phi_f$ is
a group homomorphism, because $f^{-1}(y)$ is defined on $f([m])$, the two
factors of a product commute through $f$, and both sides fix the complement
pointwise. Since $f\circ\sigma=\Phi_f(\sigma)\circ f$, functoriality gives
$f_*\circ\sigma_*=(\Phi_f(\sigma))_*\circ f_*$ for all $\sigma\in S_m$: each
$f_*\colon V_m\to V_n$ is equivariant for the conjugation homomorphism
$\Phi_f$ determined by $f$.

A **sub-FI-module** of $V$ is a subfunctor $W\subseteq V$
([[def-submodule]]): submodules $W_S\le V_S$ with $f_*(W_S)\subseteq W_T$ for
all injections $f\colon S\to T$. A **map of FI-modules** $V\to W$ is a natural
transformation, and kernels, images and cokernels of such maps are computed
pointwise, so that e.g. $\ker(F)_S=\ker(F_S\colon V_S\to W_S)$ with the
restrictions of the transition maps
([[def-quotient-module]], [[def-abelian-category]]). With these pointwise
operations the category of FI-modules over $k$ inherits its additive structure
and its abelian-category structure from $k\text{-}\mathrm{Mod}$
([[thm-modules-over-a-ring-form-an-abelian-category]]): finite direct sums,
kernels, cokernels and the compatibility axioms are checked objectwise, and a
pointwise surjective map is an epimorphism and a pointwise injective map is a
monomorphism.

An **FB-module over $k$** is a functor from the groupoid $FB$ of finite sets
and bijections to $k\text{-}\mathrm{Mod}$, with natural transformations as
maps. Since all morphisms of $FB$ are isomorphisms and every finite set is
isomorphic to exactly one $[n]$, an FB-module is determined up to isomorphism
by the $kS_n$-modules $W_n$ alone and carries no transition maps between
different $n$. No choice principle is used beyond the definable-class
conventions of [[def-category]].

For every finite set $S$ let $V_S$ be the free $k$-module on $S$, and for an
injection $f\colon S\to S'$ let $V(f)$ be the linear extension of $f$. Then
$V$ is an FI-module ([[def-fi-category-and-fi-module]]), isomorphic to $M(1)$
in the notation of [[def-free-fi-module-generated-by-an-sm-module]]; it
satisfies $V_n\cong k^n$ with the permutation action of $S_n$
([[def-finite-symmetric-group-and-permutation-notation]]) and is generated by
$V_{\{0\}}$ in degree $\le1$
([[def-finite-generation-and-generation-degree-of-an-fi-module]]). Its
character is the character polynomial $X_1$ of weighted degree $1$
([[def-character-polynomial-in-cycle-counts]]): for every $n\ge0$ and every
$\sigma\in S_n$ the trace $\operatorname{tr}(\sigma;V_n)$
([[def-trace-of-a-square-matrix]]) equals $X_1(\sigma)$, the number of fixed
points of $\sigma$. No choice principle is used.

Let $T:V\to W$ be linear. Iterating the induced map of [[prop-functoriality-of-module-tensor-products]] gives the **$k$-fold tensor power**

$$T^{\otimes k}:V^{\otimes k}\longrightarrow W^{\otimes k},\qquad T^{\otimes k}(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_k)=T(v_1)\otimes\cdots\otimes T(v_k),$$

with $T^{\otimes0}=\operatorname{id}_F$ and $T^{\otimes1}=T$. A pure tensor with $v_i=v_j$ maps to the pure tensor with $T(v_i)=T(v_j)$, so $T^{\otimes k}(W_k(V))\subseteq W_k(W)$ for the relation subspaces of [[def-kth-exterior-power-by-quotient]]. Hence $T^{\otimes k}$ descends to the quotient, defining the **$k$th exterior power**

$$\Lambda^kT:\Lambda^kV\longrightarrow\Lambda^kW,\qquad \Lambda^kT(v_1\wedge\cdots\wedge v_k)=T(v_1)\wedge\cdots\wedge T(v_k).$$

For $k=0$ this is $\Lambda^0T=\operatorname{id}_F$, and for $k=1$ it is $T$ itself under $\Lambda^1V=V$.

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ and let $k\ge0$. The **$k$-fold tensor power** is $V^{\otimes0}=F$, $V^{\otimes1}=V$, and for $k\ge2$ the iterated tensor product of $k$ copies of $V$ under any parenthesization. By [[cor-finite-iterated-tensor-products-represent-multilinear-maps]] every parenthesization represents the $k$-linear maps out of $V^k$, and different parenthesizations are joined by the unique isomorphism preserving pure tensors, so $V^{\otimes k}$ is determined up to that isomorphism.

Let $W_k\subseteq V^{\otimes k}$ be the subspace **spanned** by all pure tensors $v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_k$ for which $v_i=v_j$ for some pair $1\le i<j\le k$ (so $W_0=W_1=0$). The **$k$th exterior power** of $V$ is the quotient vector space

$$\Lambda^kV:=V^{\otimes k}/W_k,$$

and the **basic wedge map** is

$$\wedge:V^k\longrightarrow\Lambda^kV,\qquad (v_1,\ldots,v_k)\longmapsto v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_k+W_k.$$

Let $R$ be a commutative unital ring and let $F$ be a finite free $R$-module
with ordered basis $e_1,\ldots,e_n$. Define
$\bigwedge F=T_R(F)/(v\otimes v:v\in F)$, graded by tensor degree; write
$e_I=e_{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge e_{i_p}$ for
$I=\{i_1<\cdots<i_p\}$.
For every $p$, the wedges $e_I$ with $|I|=p$ form an $R$-basis of $\bigwedge^pF$; in particular it is zero for $p>n$.

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ and let $k\ge0$. The **$k$-fold tensor power** is $V^{\otimes0}=F$, $V^{\otimes1}=V$, and for $k\ge2$ the iterated tensor product of $k$ copies of $V$ under any parenthesization. By [[cor-finite-iterated-tensor-products-represent-multilinear-maps]] every parenthesization represents the $k$-linear maps out of $V^k$, and different parenthesizations are joined by the unique isomorphism preserving pure tensors, so $V^{\otimes k}$ is determined up to that isomorphism.

Let $W_k\subseteq V^{\otimes k}$ be the subspace **spanned** by all pure tensors $v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_k$ for which $v_i=v_j$ for some pair $1\le i<j\le k$ (so $W_0=W_1=0$). The **$k$th exterior power** of $V$ is the quotient vector space

$$\Lambda^kV:=V^{\otimes k}/W_k,$$

and the **basic wedge map** is

$$\wedge:V^k\longrightarrow\Lambda^kV,\qquad (v_1,\ldots,v_k)\longmapsto v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_k+W_k.$$

For $i\ge1$ and $n\ge0$ let $X_i\colon S_n\to\mathbb N$ be the function
sending a permutation $\sigma\in S_n$ to the number
$X_i(\sigma):=c_i(\sigma)$ of $i$-element orbits in its cycle type
([[def-permutation-support-disjoint-cycles-and-cycle-type]],
[[def-finite-symmetric-group-and-permutation-notation]],
[[def-natural-numbers]]); thus $X_1(\sigma)$ is the number of fixed points of
$\sigma$, and $X_i(\sigma)=0$ whenever $i>n$. Each $X_i$ is a **class
function** on $S_n$ ([[def-class-function-and-the-space-of-complex-class-functions]]):
if $\tau\sigma\tau^{-1}$ is a conjugate of $\sigma$, then $O\mapsto\tau(O)$ is
a bijection from the orbits of $\sigma$ onto the orbits of
$\tau\sigma\tau^{-1}$ that preserves cardinalities, so
$c_i(\tau\sigma\tau^{-1})=c_i(\sigma)$.

Let $\mathbb Q[X_1,X_2,\dots]$ be the polynomial ring on the family of
indeterminates indexed by $i\ge1$
([[def-polynomial-ring-on-a-family-of-indeterminates]]); its elements are
finitely supported coefficient families on the monomials of
[[def-monomials-on-an-index-set]], so every element involves only finitely many
of the indeterminates. A **character polynomial** is an element
$P\in\mathbb Q[X_1,X_2,\dots]$. Setting $\deg X_i:=i$ gives the monomial
$X^a=\prod_iX_i^{a_i}$ the **weighted degree** $\sum_ii\,a_i$ (a finite sum); a
character polynomial has **weighted degree $\le d$** when every monomial
occurring in it has weighted degree at most $d$, and the **weighted degree** of
$P\ne0$ is the largest weighted degree of a monomial of $P$. Products and
rational linear combinations of class functions on $S_n$ are again class
functions, so every character polynomial defines for each $n\ge0$ a class
function

$$P\colon S_n\longrightarrow\mathbb Q,\qquad \sigma\longmapsto P(X_1(\sigma),X_2(\sigma),\dots),$$

the defining sum being finite because $P$ has finite support and
$X_i(\sigma)=0$ for $i>n$; equivalently, the substitution $X_i\mapsto
X_i(\sigma)$ is the ring homomorphism supplied by
[[thm-universal-property-of-a-polynomial-ring-on-a-family]]. In this way a
character polynomial is realized as one class function on each $S_n$. The
realization is not injective on a single $S_n$, since $X_i$ vanishes
identically on $S_n$ for $i>n$. It is injective in the limit:

**Uniqueness.** If $P,Q$ agree as functions on $S_n$ for infinitely many $n$,
then $P=Q$.

Indeed, put $R:=P-Q$ and let $A\subseteq\mathbb N$ be infinite with
$R|_{S_n}=0$ for every $n\in A$. Fix $m\ge0$, $\sigma\in S_m$ and $k\ge0$, and
let $\sigma^{(k)}\in S_{m+k}$ be $\sigma$ extended by $k$ fixed points outside
its domain; then $X_1(\sigma^{(k)})=X_1(\sigma)+k$ and
$X_i(\sigma^{(k)})=X_i(\sigma)$ for $i\ge2$, so
$R(\sigma^{(k)})=\sum_j\bigl(X_1(\sigma)+k\bigr)^jR_j(\sigma)$, where
$R=\sum_jX_1^jR_j$ collects the monomials of $R$ by their $X_1$-exponent $j$,
each $R_j$ involving only $X_2,X_3,\dots$. The right-hand side is given by a
polynomial in $k$ over $\mathbb Q$ of degree at most the largest $j$ with
$R_j\ne0$, and it vanishes for all $k$ with $m+k\in A$, infinitely many $k$;
by the root bound of [[thm-root-bound-for-polynomials-over-a-domain]] that
polynomial is zero, so $R(\sigma)=0$
([[def-polynomial-evaluation-and-root]]). As $\sigma\in S_m$ was arbitrary,
$R$ vanishes on every $S_m$; equivalently, $R(b_1,\dots,b_M)=0$ for every
$M\ge0$ and every tuple $(b_1,\dots,b_M)\in\mathbb N^M$, since a disjoint union
of $b_i$ cycles of length $i$, $1\le i\le M$, is a permutation with $X_i=b_i$
for $i\le M$. If $R\ne0$, then $R$ involves only $X_1,\dots,X_M$ for some $M$,
and induction on $M$ shows that such an $R$ cannot vanish at every point of
$\mathbb N^M$: for $M=0$ the polynomial is a constant evaluated at the empty
tuple; and for $M\ge1$, fixing $(b_1,\dots,b_{M-1})\in\mathbb N^{M-1}$ makes
$b_M\mapsto R(b_1,\dots,b_{M-1},b_M)$ a polynomial in one variable over
$\mathbb Q$ with infinitely many roots, hence the zero polynomial, so every
$X_M$-coefficient of $R$ vanishes at $(b_1,\dots,b_{M-1})$ and the induction
applies to each of those coefficients. Hence $R=0$.

A sequence $(\chi_n)_{n\ge0}$ of class functions with $\chi_n$ a class function
on $S_n$ is **eventually polynomial** when there are $N\ge0$ and a character
polynomial $P$ with

$$\chi_n(\sigma)=P(X_1(\sigma),X_2(\sigma),\dots)$$

for all $n\ge N$ and all $\sigma\in S_n$
([[def-class-function-and-the-space-of-complex-class-functions]]). By
uniqueness in the limit, such a $P$ is determined by $(\chi_n)$ whenever it
exists. No choice principle is used.

Let $X$ be a finite set and let $\sigma\in\operatorname{Sym}(X)$, with cycle
notation and composition as in [[def-symmetric-group]].

The **support** and **fixed-point set** of $\sigma$ are

$$\operatorname{supp}(\sigma):=\{x\in X:\sigma(x)\ne x\},\qquad \operatorname{Fix}(\sigma):=\{x\in X:\sigma(x)=x\}.$$

A cycle $(a_0\,a_1\,\ldots\,a_{k-1})$ has **length** $k$ and support
$\{a_0,\ldots,a_{k-1}\}$. Two cycles are **disjoint** when their supports are
disjoint. A **disjoint-cycle decomposition** of $\sigma$ is an expression for
$\sigma$ as a product of pairwise disjoint cycles of length at least $2$.
One-cycles are omitted, and the empty product is the identity permutation.

When $|X|=n$, the **cycle type** of $\sigma$ is the list of natural numbers
$c_1(\sigma),\ldots,c_n(\sigma)$, where $c_k(\sigma)$ is the number of
$k$-element orbits of the action generated by $\sigma$. Thus $c_1(\sigma)$ is
the number of fixed points. Equivalently, the cycle type records the lengths of
all cycles after each fixed point is inserted as a one-cycle.

For a square matrix $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(F)$, its **trace** is the sum of its
diagonal entries,

$$\operatorname{tr}(A):=\sum_{i\in n}a_{ii}.$$

For $n=0$, this is the empty sum, so the unique empty matrix has trace $0$.

derivations.claim: $W$ is a functor: $W(\mathrm{id}_S)=\Lambda^2(\mathrm{id}_{V_S})=\mathrm{id}_{W_S}$ and $W(g\circ f)=\Lambda^2(V(g)V(f))=\Lambda^2V(g)\circ\Lambda^2V(f)=W(g)W(f)$, using that $V$ satisfies the functor axioms [F1] and that $\Lambda^2$ preserves identities and composites [F2]; hence $W$ is an FI-module with values $W_S=\Lambda^2V_S$, and for $S=[n]$ this is $W_n=\Lambda^2(k^n)$ with the action induced by the permutation action of $S_n$ on $k^n$.

Fix $n$ and $\sigma\in S_n$. By [F3], applied to the free module $V_n$ with basis $e_0,\dots,e_{n-1}$, the elements $e_i\wedge e_j$ with $i<j$ form a $k$-basis of $W_n$; and $\sigma\cdot(e_i\wedge e_j)=e_{\sigma(i)}\wedge e_{\sigma(j)}$. Hence the diagonal entry of the matrix of $\sigma$ at the basis element $e_i\wedge e_j$ is the coefficient of $e_i\wedge e_j$ in $e_{\sigma(i)}\wedge e_{\sigma(j)}$, which can be nonzero only when $\{\sigma(i),\sigma(j)\}=\{i,j\}$. In that case $\sigma$ restricts to a bijection of the two-element set $\{i,j\}$: it is either the identity, giving coefficient $+1$, or the transposition $(\,i\ j\,)$, giving $e_j\wedge e_i=-e_i\wedge e_j$ and coefficient $-1$. There is no other possibility, so the diagonal entry is $+1$ exactly for the unordered pairs of distinct fixed points of $\sigma$, is $-1$ exactly for the $2$-cycles of $\sigma$, and is $0$ otherwise.

By [F5] the trace of $\sigma$ on $W_n$ is the sum of the diagonal entries computed in step 1.2, namely the number $\binom{X_1(\sigma)}{2}$ of unordered pairs of distinct fixed points minus the number $X_2(\sigma)$ of $2$-cycles: $\operatorname{tr}(\sigma;W_n)=\binom{X_1(\sigma)}{2}-X_2(\sigma)$. For $n=0$ and $n=1$ the module $W_n$ is $0$ and both sides are $0$, since then $X_1(\sigma)\le1$. This holds for every $n$, and $\binom{X_1}{2}-X_2$ is a character polynomial of weighted degree $2$, so the trace function of $W$ is given by that character polynomial.
Steps 1.1, 1.2 and 2.1 show that $W=\Lambda^2V$ is an FI-module with $W_n\cong\Lambda^2(k^n)$ whose character is the weighted-degree-two character polynomial $\binom{X_1}{2}-X_2$.

boundaries.evidence: step 1.1: W_S is defined for every finite S, including S = emptyset where Lambda^2(k^0) = 0 and the functor axioms hold trivially.
step 2.1: for n <= 1 the module W_n = 0 and both sides of the character formula vanish because X_1(sigma) <= 1.
step 1.2: the wedge basis e_i ^ e_j with i < j is empty for n = 1, so the rank-one case is covered by an empty sum.
step 1.2: the two possible behaviours of sigma on the two-element set {i, j}, identity and transposition, are the complete list and give coefficients +1 and -1.
step 2.1: the range n >= 0 is treated including the endpoint n = 0, where both sides equal 0.
step 1.2: the basis of wedges is the standard one supplied by the exterior-algebra basis lemma, so no basis of a quotient is chosen.

No converse of the character computation is claimed.

A **graded $k[T]$-module** consists of $k$-modules $U_n$, $n\ge0$, together
with $k$-linear maps $T=T_n\colon U_n\to U_{n+1}$ for all $n\ge0$. A
**morphism** $U\to U'$ of graded $k[T]$-modules is a family of $k$-linear maps
$u_n\colon U_n\to U'_n$ with $u_{n+1}\circ T_n=T'_n\circ u_n$ for all $n$.

Fix $a\ge0$, a set $\mathbf a$ of cardinality $a$, and a functorial disjoint
union of finite sets. Let $V$ be an FI-module over $k$
([[def-fi-category-and-fi-module]]) and let $n\ge0$. Put

$$\Phi_a(V)_n:=(V_{\mathbf a\sqcup n})_{S_n},$$

the coinvariants of the $kS_n$-module $V_{\mathbf a\sqcup n}$: the quotient by
the span of the elements $\sigma\cdot v-v$, $\sigma\in S_n$, $v\in
V_{\mathbf a\sqcup n}$ ([[def-coinvariants-functor-of-a-group-module]],
[[def-quotient-module]]). Equivalently $\Phi_a(V)_n=k\otimes_{kS_n}
V_{\mathbf a\sqcup n}$, the two descriptions being identified by the balancing
argument of [[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]] and
the corresponding identification for $\mathbb Z$ in
[[def-coinvariants-functor-of-a-group-module]]; the group ring $kS_n$ is a
unital $k$-algebra with basis the group elements
([[def-group-ring]], [[thm-group-ring-is-a-unital-algebra-with-basis-g]]).

To define the transition map $T\colon\Phi_a(V)_n\to\Phi_a(V)_{n+1}$, choose an
injection $f\colon n\to n+1$. It induces the injection
$\mathrm{id}_{\mathbf a}\sqcup f\colon\mathbf a\sqcup n\to\mathbf a\sqcup n+1$
and hence a $k$-linear map $(V_{\mathbf a\sqcup n}\to
V_{\mathbf a\sqcup n+1})$. This map is $S_n$-equivariant, where $S_n$ acts on
the target through the injection $\mathrm{id}_{\mathbf a}\sqcup f$, so it
descends to the quotient map $T=T_f$ on coinvariants. The map $T_f$ is
independent of $f$: for two injections $f,g\colon n\to n+1$ the composite
$g\circ f^{-1}$ is a bijection $f(n)\to g(n)$, which extends along the
complement to a permutation $\tau\in S_{n+1}$ with $g=\tau\circ f$; then
$\mathrm{id}_{\mathbf a}\sqcup g=(\mathrm{id}_{\mathbf a}\sqcup
\tau)\circ(\mathrm{id}_{\mathbf a}\sqcup f)$, and the map induced by
$\mathrm{id}_{\mathbf a}\sqcup\tau$ on
$(V_{\mathbf a\sqcup n+1})_{S_{n+1}}$ is the identity because it comes from
the action of the group element $\tau$. Thus $T$ is well defined and
$(\Phi_a(V),T)$ is a graded $k[T]$-module.

A map of FI-modules $\alpha\colon V\to W$ gives $k$-linear maps
$\alpha_{\mathbf a\sqcup n}\colon V_{\mathbf a\sqcup n}\to W_{\mathbf
a\sqcup n}$ commuting with the $S_n$-actions and with the maps induced by
$\mathrm{id}_{\mathbf a}\sqcup f$, hence maps $(\Phi_a\alpha)_n$ of coinvariants
commuting with $T$; so $\Phi_a$ is a functor from FI-modules over $k$ to graded
$k[T]$-modules.

**Exactness.** Coinvariants of a group module are right exact
([[prop-the-coinvariants-functor-is-right-exact]]), so the functor
$M\mapsto M_{S_n}\cong k\otimes_{kS_n}M$ is right exact and each $\Phi_a$ is
right exact in every degree. If $k$ contains $\mathbb Q$, then $1/n!$ exists in $k$
and the averaging map
$s\colon\Phi_a(V)_n\to V_{\mathbf a\sqcup n}$,
$s([v])=\frac1{n!}\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\sigma\cdot v$, is a well-defined
$k$-linear section of the quotient map that is natural in $V$; it identifies
$\Phi_a(V)_n$ with the invariants $V_{\mathbf a\sqcup n}^{S_n}$. Under this
natural identification $\Phi_a$ becomes the invariants functor, which is left
exact (kernels of equivariant maps are computed pointwise), and therefore
$\Phi_a$ is exact; in that case the induced map $\Phi_a(W)\to\Phi_a(V)$ is
injective for every sub-FI-module $W\subseteq V$
([[def-submodule]], [[def-module-homomorphism-kernel-image-and-cokernel]]), so
$\Phi_a(W)$ is identified with a submodule of $\Phi_a(V)$. Finite averaging
uses only the finite groups $S_n$; no choice principle is used.

Let $R$ be a unital ring and $(M_i)_{i\in I}$ a family of left $R$-modules ([[def-left-and-right-modules]]). Their **direct product** is the module $\prod_{i\in I}M_i$ with coordinatewise operations. The **support** of $m=(m_i)$ is $\{i\in I:m_i\ne0\}$, and the **direct sum** is the submodule
$$\bigoplus_{i\in I}M_i=\{m\in\prod_{i\in I}M_i:\operatorname{supp}(m)\text{ is finite}\}$$
([[def-submodule]]).

This subset is a submodule because the support of a sum is contained in the union of two finite supports and scalar multiplication cannot enlarge support.

For each $i$, the coordinate inclusion $\jmath_i:M_i\to\bigoplus_jM_j$ puts its input in coordinate $i$ and zero elsewhere. If $I=\varnothing$, both product and direct sum are the zero module.

Let $V$ be an FI-module over $k$
([[def-fi-category-and-fi-module]]), with free FI-modules $M(m)$ as in
[[def-free-fi-module-generated-by-an-sm-module]] and span as in
[[def-finite-generation-and-generation-degree-of-an-fi-module]].

(a) For $v\in V_m$ the map of FI-modules $M(m)\to V$ sending the canonical
generator $\mathrm{id}_m\in M(m)_m$ to $v$ has image $\operatorname{span}_V(v)$;
more generally, for any set $\Sigma$ of elements, each lying in some $V_S$, the
canonical map $\bigoplus_{s\in\Sigma}M(|S_s|)\to V$ sending the generator of
the summand indexed by $s$ to $s$ has image $\operatorname{span}_V(\Sigma)$.

(b) $V$ is finitely generated if and only if there is a finite family
$m_1,\dots,m_k\ge0$ with a surjection

$$M(m_1)\oplus\cdots\oplus M(m_k)\twoheadrightarrow V;$$

$V$ is generated in degree $\le d$ if and only if there is a surjection
$\bigoplus_{i\in I}M(m_i)\twoheadrightarrow V$ with $m_i\le d$ for all $i$. In
particular, if $V$ is generated in degree $\le d$, then the evaluation map
$\bigoplus_{m\le d}M(V_m)\to V$, whose restriction to each copy of $M(m)$
indexed by an element $v\in V_m$ sends $\mathrm{id}_m\mapsto v$, is surjective.

(c) If $V$ is finitely generated, then $V_S$ is a finitely generated $k$-module
for every finite set $S$
([[def-generated-cyclic-finitely-generated-and-free-modules]]).

No choice principle is used: all maps come from a finite or explicitly indexed
set of generators, and the image computations are linear algebra on the values
at a fixed finite set.

Let $W$ be an FB-module over $k$, i.e. a functor from the groupoid of finite
sets and bijections to $k\text{-}\mathrm{Mod}$ ([[def-fi-category-and-fi-module]]);
thus $W(T)$ is a $k$-module for every finite set $T$, and every bijection
$\beta\colon T\to T'$ gives an isomorphism $W(\beta)\colon W(T)\to W(T')$.
Because an FB-module is defined on all finite sets, no transport choices are
needed below.

The **free FI-module** $M(W)$ assigns to a finite set $S$ the direct sum

$$M(W)_S:=\bigoplus_{T\subseteq S}W(T)$$

over all subsets $T\subseteq S$ ([[def-subset-and-proper-subset]],
[[def-direct-sum-of-a-family-of-modules]]; only finitely many summands occur).
For an injection $f\colon S\to S'$ and a subset $T\subseteq S$, the restriction
$f|_T\colon T\to f(T)$ is a bijection
([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]), and the transition map
$f_*\colon M(W)_S\to M(W)_{S'}$ is the sum of the isomorphisms
$W(f|_T)\colon W(T)\to W(f(T))$ over all $T\subseteq S$. This is $k$-linear and
functorial, since $(f'\circ f)|_T=f'|_{f(T)}\circ f|_T$; hence $M(W)$ is an
FI-module over $k$.

For $S=[n]=\{0,\dots,n-1\}$ the symmetric group $S_n$
([[def-finite-symmetric-group-and-permutation-notation]]) acts by
$\sigma\cdot T:=\sigma(T)$ and $W(\sigma|_T)$, and this is a left action
making $M(W)_n$ a left $kS_n$-module ([[def-group-ring]]). Grouping the sum by
the cardinality of $T$, the subsets of cardinality $a$ form a single $S_n$-orbit
with stabilizer the ordered block subgroup
$S_{\{0,\dots,a-1\}}\times S_{\{a,\dots,n-1\}}\cong S_a\times S_{n-a}$, so the
orbit summand is identified with an induced module
([[def-induced-r-linear-g-module-by-h-covariant-functions]]):

$$M(W)_n\cong\bigoplus_{a=0}^{n}\operatorname{Ind}_{S_a\times S_{n-a}}^{S_n}\bigl(W_a\boxtimes k\bigr),$$

where $W_a:=W(\{0,\dots,a-1\})$ is the value of the FB-module on an $a$-element
set, the first factor acts on $W_a$ through $W$ and the second factor acts
trivially, and $\boxtimes$ is the external tensor product of modules for the
two direct factors ([[def-outer-induction-product-for-symmetric-group-characters]],
[[lem-character-ring-of-a-direct-product-is-the-tensor-product]],
[[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]]).

forgets the maps between distinct cardinalities. The inclusion of the $T=S$
summand is a natural map $\eta_W\colon W\to\pi M(W)$, and evaluating a map
$F\colon M(W)\to V$ of FI-modules on that summand yields a map of FB-modules
$\pi F\circ\eta_W\colon W\to\pi V$. Conversely, a map of FB-modules
$\varphi\colon W\to\pi V$ extends uniquely to a map of FI-modules
$\widetilde\varphi\colon M(W)\to V$ whose value on the summand $W(T)\subseteq
M(W)_S$ is $V(\iota_{T,S})\circ\varphi_T$, with $\iota_{T,S}\colon T\to S$ the
inclusion; the components are compatible with injections and the two
constructions are inverse, so
$\operatorname{Hom}_{FI\text{-}Mod}(M(W),V)\cong
\operatorname{Hom}_{FB\text{-}Mod}(W,\pi V)$ naturally in $V$ and $W$: $M$ is
left adjoint to $\pi$, with unit $\eta$.

For $m\ge0$ write $k[S_m]$ for the FB-module with $k[S_m](T)$ the free $k$-module
on the bijections $[m]\to T$, and zero when $|T|\ne m$; its value on an
$m$-element set is the regular representation of $S_m$. Put
$M(m):=M(k[S_m])$. Then $M(m)_S$ has as $k$-basis the injections
$[m]\hookrightarrow S$ — equivalently, the ordered sequences of $m$ distinct
elements of $S$ — and for a partition $\lambda$ with $|\lambda|=m$ and a field
$k$ of characteristic $0$, put $M(\lambda):=M(S^\lambda_k)$, where the FB-module
$S^\lambda_k$ is supported on $m$-element sets and $S^\lambda_k(T):=
k[\operatorname{Iso}([m],T)]\otimes_{kS_m}S^\lambda_k$. By the adjunction, a map
$M(m)\to V$ of FI-modules corresponds naturally to the choice of an element of
$V_m$: the module $M(m)$ represents the functor $V\mapsto V_m$. All
constructions are given by finitely many canonical bijections of finite sets;
no choice principle is used.

Let $W$ be an FB-module over $k$ and let $M(W)$ be the free FI-module of
[[def-free-fi-module-generated-by-an-sm-module]]. Then
$\operatorname{inj-deg}(M(W))=0$, and if $W_i=0$ for all $i>m$ then
$\operatorname{surj-deg}(M(W))\le m$; in particular
$M(m)=M(k[S_m])$ satisfies $\operatorname{inj-deg}(M(m))=0$ and
$\operatorname{stab-deg}(M(m))=m$
([[def-injectivity-surjectivity-and-stability-degree-of-an-fi-module]]).
If moreover $k$ is a field of characteristic $0$ and $\lambda$ is a partition,
then $\operatorname{weight}(M(\lambda))=|\lambda|$
([[def-weight-of-a-characteristic-zero-fi-module]]) and
$\operatorname{stab-deg}(M(\lambda))=\lambda_1$. No choice principle is used.

Let $F$ be a field of characteristic $0$ and let $n\ge0$. For every partition
$\lambda\vdash n$ the field-valued Specht module $S^\lambda_F$ of
[[def-polytabloid-specht-module-over-an-arbitrary-field]] is nonzero and
irreducible, distinct partitions give non-isomorphic modules, and every
irreducible $FS_n$-module is isomorphic to exactly one of them. Consequently,
by Maschke's theorem, every finite-dimensional $FS_n$-module is a direct sum of
copies of the $S^\lambda_F$; thus the irreducible $FS_n$-modules are indexed by
the partitions of $n$ and the modules $\{S^\lambda_F:\lambda\vdash n\}$ form a
complete irredundant list.

This is the constituent convention used throughout the pair: over
$F=\mathbb C$ it specialises to the published complex classification, and over
a general characteristic-zero field $F$ it is proved by extending the rational
Specht models along $\mathbb Q\to F$, never by a scalar extension from
$\mathbb C$ to $F$.

Let $G$ be a finite group, let $k$ be a field with
$\operatorname{char} k \nmid |G|$, let $\rho:G \to \operatorname{GL}(V)$ be a
finite-dimensional representation of $G$ over $k$, and let $W \le V$ be a
subrepresentation. Then there is a subrepresentation $U \le V$ such that

$$V=W\oplus U.$$

Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $0$ and let $V$ be an FI-module over $k$
([[def-fi-category-and-fi-module]]). For a partition $\lambda$ and
$n\ge|\lambda|+\lambda_1$ put $\lambda[n]:=(n-|\lambda|,\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\dots)$,
the first-row padding ([[def-first-row-padding-of-a-partition]]), and let

$$V(\lambda)_n:=k\otimes_{\mathbb Q}S^{\lambda[n]}_{\mathbb Q}$$

be the scalar extension of the rational Specht model of $\lambda[n]$
([[thm-complex-specht-modules-are-irreducible]],
[[lem-specht-modules-classify-irreducibles-over-characteristic-zero-fields]]).
By the classification lemma, $V(\lambda)_n$ is the irreducible $kS_n$-module
with label $\lambda[n]$, and every irreducible $kS_n$-module is isomorphic to
exactly one $V(\lambda)_n$: indeed, every partition $\mu=(\mu_1,\mu_2,\dots)$
of $n$ is uniquely $\lambda[n]$ for the partition
$\lambda=(\mu_2,\mu_3,\dots)$ obtained by deleting the first row, and
$n\ge|\lambda|+\lambda_1$ holds precisely because $\mu_1\ge\mu_2$;
consequently the labels $\lambda[n]$ run over the partitions of $n$ without
repetition.

Say that $V(\lambda)_n$ **occurs as a constituent** of $V_n$ when there are
$kS_n$-submodules $U\subseteq W\subseteq V_n$ with
$W/U\cong V(\lambda)_n$ ([[def-submodule]], [[def-quotient-module]]); this is a
condition on subquotients and requires no decomposition or finite-dimensionality
of $V_n$. The **weight** of $V$ is

$$\operatorname{weight}(V):=\sup\bigl\{|\lambda|:V(\lambda)_n\text{ occurs as a constituent of }V_n\text{ for some }n\ge|\lambda|+\lambda_1\bigr\},$$

the supremum over all pairs $(\lambda,n)$ as displayed. The set of integers
displayed is a set of nonnegative integers, so the supremum is well defined in
$\mathbb N\cup\{\infty\}$; it is $0$ for $V=0$, and $\operatorname{weight}(V)=\infty$
exactly when the displayed set is unbounded. No finiteness of
$\operatorname{weight}(V)$ is asserted.

If $W$ is a **subquotient** of $V$, meaning that $W\cong U'/U$ for sub-FI-modules
$U\subseteq U'\subseteq V$ computed pointwise, then
$\operatorname{weight}(W)\le\operatorname{weight}(V)$: a constituent of $W_n$ is
a subquotient of the subquotient $U'_n/U_n$ of $V_n$, hence a subquotient of
$V_n$, so it contributes the same label $|\lambda|$ to the supremum for $V$. No
choice principle is used: the labels $\lambda[n]$, constituents and the
supremum are set-theoretic data, and no bases or decompositions are chosen.

Let $W$ be an FB-module over $k$ and let $M(W)$ be the free FI-module of
[[def-free-fi-module-generated-by-an-sm-module]]. Then
$\operatorname{inj-deg}(M(W))=0$, and if $W_i=0$ for all $i>m$ then
$\operatorname{surj-deg}(M(W))\le m$; in particular
$M(m)=M(k[S_m])$ satisfies $\operatorname{inj-deg}(M(m))=0$ and
$\operatorname{stab-deg}(M(m))=m$
([[def-injectivity-surjectivity-and-stability-degree-of-an-fi-module]]).
If moreover $k$ is a field of characteristic $0$ and $\lambda$ is a partition,
then $\operatorname{weight}(M(\lambda))=|\lambda|$
([[def-weight-of-a-characteristic-zero-fi-module]]) and
$\operatorname{stab-deg}(M(\lambda))=\lambda_1$. No choice principle is used.

derivations.claim: For (a), let $q\colon V\twoheadrightarrow W$ be a quotient. By [F1] each $q_n$ is surjective on $\Phi_a$, and naturality gives $T_{\Phi_a(W)}\circ q_n=q_{n+1}\circ T_{\Phi_a(V)}$. If $T_{\Phi_a(V)}$ is surjective, then $T_{\Phi_a(W)}$ is surjective as well, because every element of $\Phi_a(W)_{n+1}$ is the image under the surjection $q_{n+1}$ of an element hit by $T_{\Phi_a(V)}$. Hence the threshold controlling surjectivity of $T$ for $W$ is at most that for $V$, i.e. $\operatorname{surj-deg}(W)\le\operatorname{surj-deg}(V)$.

Let $k$ have characteristic $0$ and let $W$ be a finite-dimensional $kS_m$-module regarded as an FB-module supported on cardinality $m$. By [F5] $W\cong\bigoplus_\lambda c_\lambda S^\lambda_k$ (finite sum), and by the additivity in [F3] $M(W)\cong\bigoplus_\lambda M(S^\lambda_k)^{\oplus c_\lambda}$; hence $\operatorname{weight}(M(W))=\max\{|\lambda|:c_\lambda\ne0\}\le m$ by [F4] and [F6].

Let $W$ be an arbitrary $kS_m$-module (characteristic zero) and let $V(\eta)_N$ be a constituent of $M(W)_N$. Let $P/Q\subseteq M(W)_N$ be a subquotient isomorphic to $V(\eta)_N$ and choose $x\in P\setminus Q$. The $S_N$-orbit span $X$ of $x$ is a finite-dimensional $S_N$-submodule of $M(W)_N$, and $X/(X\cap Q)$ is a nonzero submodule of the simple $V(\eta)_N$, hence is isomorphic to $V(\eta)_N$; in particular $V(\eta)_N$ is a constituent of $X$. Now $X$ lies in the direct sum $\bigoplus_{T\subseteq[N]}W(T)$ of [F3] over finitely many $T$, and for each of those $T$ the projection of $X$ to $W(T)$ is finite-dimensional; let $W'$ be the $kS_m$-submodule of $W$ generated by the finitely many images of these projections under the canonical identifications $W(T)\cong W$. Then $W'$ is finite-dimensional and $X\subseteq M(W')_N$, so $V(\eta)_N$ is a constituent of $M(W')_N$; by step 1.2 and [F6], $|\eta|\le m$. Therefore $\operatorname{weight}(M(W))\le m$ for every $kS_m$-module $W$.

For (b), suppose $V$ is generated in degree $\le d$. By [F3] the evaluation map $\bigoplus_{m\le d}M(V_m)\twoheadrightarrow V$ is surjective, and each $V_m$ is supported in degree $m\le d$, so $\operatorname{surj-deg}(M(V_m))\le m\le d$ by [F4]; by [F2] the finite direct sum has surjectivity degree at most $d$, and step 1.1 applied to the quotient gives $\operatorname{surj-deg}(V)\le d$.

For (c), the same surjection $\bigoplus_{m\le d}M(V_m)\twoheadrightarrow V$ and [F6] give $\operatorname{weight}(V)\le\operatorname{weight}\bigl(\bigoplus_{m\le d}M(V_m)\bigr)$. A constituent of a direct sum is a constituent of one summand (a simple subquotient of $\bigoplus_iU_i$ projects nontrivially to some $U_i$), so the weight of the finite direct sum is $\max_{m\le d}\operatorname{weight}(M(V_m))\le d$ by step 2.1. Hence $\operatorname{weight}(V)\le d$.
Step 1.1 proves (a); step 2.2 proves (b); step 3.1 proves (c).

boundaries.evidence: step 2.1: the empty label eta = emptyset, the trivial constituent, is included and contributes |eta| = 0 <= m to the weight bound.
step 1.2: the finite-dimensional case permits c_lambda = 0 for absent labels and W = 0, where the maximum defining the weight is 0.
step 3.1: the finite direct sum may consist of a single summand with m <= d, including the value d = 0.
step 1.1: the quotient bound is meaningful for the zero quotient and allows surj-deg = 0; the degenerate identifications are not excluded.
step 3.1: the bound weight(V) <= d is inclusive, and the case d = 0 from step 2.2 covers constant modules at the endpoint.
step 2.1: an arbitrary module is reduced to a finite-dimensional submodule generated by finitely many projections, so no decomposition of the whole module or infinite basis is chosen.
step 4.1: the three asserted implications (a), (b), (c) are each proved in steps 1.1, 2.2 and 3.1 and summarised there.

boundaries.reason: The lemma is a collection of upper bounds on degrees and weights, not an optimality or converse statement for general V.

Let $F$ be a field of characteristic $0$, let $\lambda\vdash n$, and let
$S^\lambda_F$ be the corresponding field-valued Specht module
([[def-polytabloid-specht-module-over-an-arbitrary-field]]).

(i) For every $k\ge0$ there is an isomorphism of $FS_{n+k}$-modules

$$\operatorname{Ind}_{S_n\times S_k}^{S_{n+k}}\bigl(S^\lambda_F\boxtimes F\bigr)\cong\bigoplus_{\mu}S^\mu_F,$$

summed over the partitions $\mu\vdash n+k$ obtained from $\lambda$ by adding
one box to each of $k$ different columns (equivalently, $\mu\supseteq\lambda$
and $\mu/\lambda$ is a horizontal $k$-strip).

(ii) For every $k\le n$ there is an isomorphism of $FS_{n-k}$-modules

$$\bigl(\operatorname{Res}^{S_n}_{S_{n-k}\times S_k}S^\lambda_F\bigr)_{S_k}\cong\bigoplus_{\nu}S^\nu_F,$$

summed over the partitions $\nu\vdash n-k$ obtained from $\lambda$ by removing
one box from each of $k$ different columns, where the outer subscript denotes
$S_k$-coinvariants of the restriction to the ordered block subgroup
$S_{n-k}\times S_k\le S_n$ ([[def-coinvariants-functor-of-a-group-module]]);
the left-hand side is an $FS_{n-k}$-module because the two blocks commute. All
multiplicities are $0$ or $1$. No choice principle is used.

Let $F$ be a field of characteristic $0$ and let $n\ge0$. For every partition
$\lambda\vdash n$ the field-valued Specht module $S^\lambda_F$ of
[[def-polytabloid-specht-module-over-an-arbitrary-field]] is nonzero and
irreducible, distinct partitions give non-isomorphic modules, and every
