No reverse implication is claimed; the item does not characterise which modules have all submodules finitely generated.

citations.quote:
Let $\alpha=(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_k)$ be a partition with $|\alpha|=\alpha_1+\cdots+\alpha_k$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]), and let $n\ge0$ be
an integer. Whenever

$$n\;\ge\;|\alpha|+\alpha_1,$$

define the **first-row padding** of $\alpha$ to size $n$ to be
$$\alpha[n]:=\bigl(n-|\alpha|,\ \alpha_1,\ \alpha_2,\ \dots,\ \alpha_k\bigr).$$

The threshold is exact.

**Above the threshold.** Suppose $n\ge|\alpha|+\alpha_1$. Then
$n-|\alpha|\ge\alpha_1\ge0$, so every entry of the displayed sequence is a
nonnegative integer, the entries sum to $(n-|\alpha|)+|\alpha|=n$, and the
sequence is weakly decreasing because $n-|\alpha|\ge\alpha_1$ and $\alpha$ is
weakly decreasing ([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]).
If $\alpha$ is nonempty then $\alpha_1\ge1$, hence $n-|\alpha|\ge1$ and the
displayed sequence is a partition of $n$ with positive parts. If
$\alpha=\varnothing$ then the displayed sequence is $(n)$; this is a partition
of $n$ for every $n\ge1$, while for $n=0$ one takes $\varnothing[0]:=\varnothing$,
the unique partition of $0$. Thus the padding is defined and is a partition of
$n$ on the whole displayed range.

**Below the threshold.** If $\alpha$ is nonempty and $n<|\alpha|+\alpha_1$,
then $n-|\alpha|<\alpha_1$; if also $n\ge|\alpha|$ the leading entry is
nonnegative but smaller than the second entry $\alpha_1$, and if $n<|\alpha|$
it is negative. In both cases the displayed sequence is not a partition, so
$\alpha[n]$ is left undefined. The threshold $|\alpha|+\alpha_1$ is therefore
the exact size at which the padded family begins: at
$n=|\alpha|+\alpha_1$ the padding equals $(\alpha_1,\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\dots)$,
which is a partition with a repeated first part when $\alpha$ is nonempty.

**Neutrality of the notation.** This definition records a family of partitions;
it asserts no constancy of any quantity along the family and no stability
property. The same notation is used by the FI-module and
representation-stability developments, where the padding threshold reappears as
the generation degree of the family under consideration.

Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $0$, let $\lambda$ be a partition with
$m:=|\lambda|$ and first part $\lambda_1$, and put $d:=m+\lambda_1$. For a
partition $\mu\vdash n$ write $V_\mu$ for the irreducible $kS_n$-module with
label $\mu$
([[lem-specht-modules-classify-irreducibles-over-characteristic-zero-fields]]),
and for $n\ge d$ let $\lambda[n]$ be the first-row padding of $\lambda$ to $n$
([[def-first-row-padding-of-a-partition]]).

Then there is a sub-FI-module $V(\lambda)$ of the free FI-module $M(\lambda)$
([[def-free-fi-module-generated-by-an-sm-module]]) with

$$V(\lambda)_n\cong V_{\lambda[n]}\quad(n\ge d),\qquad V(\lambda)_n=0\quad(n<d),$$

so that the value of this FI-module at $[n]$ is the irreducible $kS_n$-module
denoted $V(\lambda)_n$ in [[def-weight-of-a-characteristic-zero-fi-module]].
This FI-module is generated in degree $\le d$
([[def-finite-generation-and-generation-degree-of-an-fi-module]]), and its
generation degree is exactly $d$. It has

$$\operatorname{weight}(V(\lambda))=m,\qquad\operatorname{inj-deg}(V(\lambda))=0,\qquad\operatorname{surj-deg}(V(\lambda))=\operatorname{stab-deg}(V(\lambda))=\lambda_1,$$

where weight is as in [[def-weight-of-a-characteristic-zero-fi-module]] and the
three degrees are as in
[[def-injectivity-surjectivity-and-stability-degree-of-an-fi-module]]. No
choice principle is used.

Let $F$ be a field of characteristic $0$ and let $n\ge0$. For every partition
$\lambda\vdash n$ the field-valued Specht module $S^\lambda_F$ of
[[def-polytabloid-specht-module-over-an-arbitrary-field]] is nonzero and
irreducible, distinct partitions give non-isomorphic modules, and every
irreducible $FS_n$-module is isomorphic to exactly one of them. Consequently,
by Maschke's theorem, every finite-dimensional $FS_n$-module is a direct sum of
copies of the $S^\lambda_F$; thus the irreducible $FS_n$-modules are indexed by
the partitions of $n$ and the modules $\{S^\lambda_F:\lambda\vdash n\}$ form a
complete irredundant list.

This is the constituent convention used throughout the pair: over
$F=\mathbb C$ it specialises to the published complex classification, and over
a general characteristic-zero field $F$ it is proved by extending the rational
Specht models along $\mathbb Q\to F$, never by a scalar extension from
$\mathbb C$ to $F$.

Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $0$ and let $V$ be an FI-module over $k$
([[def-fi-category-and-fi-module]]). For a partition $\lambda$ and
$n\ge|\lambda|+\lambda_1$ put $\lambda[n]:=(n-|\lambda|,\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\dots)$,
the first-row padding ([[def-first-row-padding-of-a-partition]]), and let

$$V(\lambda)_n:=k\otimes_{\mathbb Q}S^{\lambda[n]}_{\mathbb Q}$$

be the scalar extension of the rational Specht model of $\lambda[n]$
([[thm-complex-specht-modules-are-irreducible]],
[[lem-specht-modules-classify-irreducibles-over-characteristic-zero-fields]]).
By the classification lemma, $V(\lambda)_n$ is the irreducible $kS_n$-module
with label $\lambda[n]$, and every irreducible $kS_n$-module is isomorphic to
exactly one $V(\lambda)_n$: indeed, every partition $\mu=(\mu_1,\mu_2,\dots)$
of $n$ is uniquely $\lambda[n]$ for the partition
$\lambda=(\mu_2,\mu_3,\dots)$ obtained by deleting the first row, and
$n\ge|\lambda|+\lambda_1$ holds precisely because $\mu_1\ge\mu_2$;
consequently the labels $\lambda[n]$ run over the partitions of $n$ without
repetition.

Say that $V(\lambda)_n$ **occurs as a constituent** of $V_n$ when there are
$kS_n$-submodules $U\subseteq W\subseteq V_n$ with
$W/U\cong V(\lambda)_n$ ([[def-submodule]], [[def-quotient-module]]); this is a
condition on subquotients and requires no decomposition or finite-dimensionality
of $V_n$. The **weight** of $V$ is

$$\operatorname{weight}(V):=\sup\bigl\{|\lambda|:V(\lambda)_n\text{ occurs as a constituent of }V_n\text{ for some }n\ge|\lambda|+\lambda_1\bigr\},$$

the supremum over all pairs $(\lambda,n)$ as displayed. The set of integers
displayed is a set of nonnegative integers, so the supremum is well defined in
$\mathbb N\cup\{\infty\}$; it is $0$ for $V=0$, and $\operatorname{weight}(V)=\infty$
exactly when the displayed set is unbounded. No finiteness of
$\operatorname{weight}(V)$ is asserted.

If $W$ is a **subquotient** of $V$, meaning that $W\cong U'/U$ for sub-FI-modules
$U\subseteq U'\subseteq V$ computed pointwise, then
$\operatorname{weight}(W)\le\operatorname{weight}(V)$: a constituent of $W_n$ is
a subquotient of the subquotient $U'_n/U_n$ of $V_n$, hence a subquotient of
$V_n$, so it contributes the same label $|\lambda|$ to the supremum for $V$. No
choice principle is used: the labels $\lambda[n]$, constituents and the
supremum are set-theoretic data, and no bases or decompositions are chosen.

Let $V$ be an FI-module over $k$ and let $\Phi_a$ and $T$ be the coinvariant
functors and transition maps of
[[def-fi-coinvariant-functors-and-transition-maps]]. The **injectivity degree**
$\operatorname{inj-deg}(V)$ is the least $s\ge0$ such that for every $a\ge0$
the transition map $T\colon\Phi_a(V)_n\to\Phi_a(V)_{n+1}$ is injective for all
$n\ge s$; the **surjectivity degree** $\operatorname{surj-deg}(V)$ is the least
$s\ge0$ such that for every $a\ge0$ the map $T$ is surjective for all $n\ge s$.
The **stability degree** is

$$\operatorname{stab-deg}(V):=\max\bigl(\operatorname{inj-deg}(V),\operatorname{surj-deg}(V)\bigr).$$

Each of the three is $+\infty$ when no such $s$ exists; here the bounds are
read as elements of the extended nonnegative integers
$\mathbb N\cup\{+\infty\}$ with the evident order, in which every nonempty
subset of $\mathbb N$ has a least element
([[def-natural-numbers]]), so "the least $s$" is well defined. Equivalently,
$T\colon\Phi_a(V)_n\to\Phi_a(V)_{n+1}$ is an isomorphism for all $a\ge0$ and
all $n\ge\operatorname{stab-deg}(V)$: the map is an isomorphism exactly when it
is both injective and surjective, and for finite bounds a threshold that
controls all $a$ simultaneously is the larger of the two thresholds, while
each of the two stated bounds remains the least threshold controlling its own
property.

The three bounds are kept distinct: $\operatorname{stab-deg}(V)$ is the maximum
of the other two, and nothing in the definition requires
$\operatorname{inj-deg}(V)=\operatorname{surj-deg}(V)$. No finiteness is
asserted: each bound is allowed to be $+\infty$. No choice principle is used.

derivations.claim: Substituting $\lambda=(2,1)$ gives $\lambda[n]=(n-3,2,1)$: for $n<3$ the first entry is negative, for $n=3$ it is $0<2$ and for $n=4$ it is $1<2$, so in these cases the sequence is not a partition; for $n\ge5$ the first entry is at least $2$, the entries are nonnegative and weakly decreasing and their sum is $(n-3)+2+1=n$. Hence $\lambda[n]$ is a partition exactly for $n\ge5=|\lambda|+\lambda_1$.

Apply [F2] with $\alpha=\lambda=(2,1)$, so $m'=3$ and $d'=5$: there is a sub-FI-module $V((2,1))$ of $M((2,1))$ with $V((2,1))_n\cong V_{\lambda[n]}=V_{(n-3,2,1)}$ for $n\ge5$ and $V((2,1))_n=0$ for $n<5$, of generation degree exactly $5$, weight $3$, injectivity degree $0$ and surjectivity degree $2$, so that its stability degree is $2$.

Steps 1.1 and 2.1 show that the padded family $V((2,1))$ begins at rank five, not at $|\lambda|=3$, is generated in degree $5$, and has weight $3$ and stability degree $2$; the second row of each constituent diagram $\lambda[n]=(n-3,2,1)$ remains $2$ while the first row grows. No choice principle is used.

No converse claim, such as uniqueness of the partition realising this family, is made.

citations.quote:
Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $0$. A **consistent sequence** is a
sequence $(V_n,\varphi_n)_{n\ge0}$ in which each $V_n$ is a finite-dimensional
left $kS_n$-module and each $\varphi_n\colon V_n\to V_{n+1}$ is
$S_n$-equivariant, the target being regarded as an $S_n$-module by restriction
along the standard inclusion $S_n\hookrightarrow S_{n+1}$ that fixes $n$. An
FI-module $V$ over $k$ with finite-dimensional values
([[def-fi-category-and-fi-module]]) determines such a sequence by
$V_n:=V([n])$ and $\varphi_n:=f_*$ for the standard inclusions
$f\colon[n]\to[n+1]$; these maps are $S_n$-equivariant by functoriality and the
conjugation action, since $f\circ\sigma=\Phi_f(\sigma)\circ f$ with
$\Phi_f(\sigma)$ the extension of $\sigma$ by the fixed point $n$.

The sequence is **uniformly representation stable with stable range $n\ge N$**
when all three of the following hold.

1. **(I) Injectivity.** The map $\varphi_n\colon V_n\to V_{n+1}$ is injective for
   every $n\ge N$.
2. **(II) Surjectivity.** The $S_{n+1}$-span of the image $\varphi_n(V_n)$ is
   all of $V_{n+1}$ for every $n\ge N$.
3. **(III) Multiplicities.** For each partition $\lambda$ and each $n$ with
   $n\ge|\lambda|+\lambda_1$, let $V(\lambda)_n$ be the irreducible $kS_n$-module
   indexed by the first-row padding $\lambda[n]=(n-|\lambda|,\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\dots)$
   ([[def-first-row-padding-of-a-partition]]), namely the scalar extension
   $k\otimes_{\mathbb Q}S^{\lambda[n]}_{\mathbb Q}$ of the rational Specht model,
   which is the unique irreducible $kS_n$-module with that label
   ([[lem-specht-modules-classify-irreducibles-over-characteristic-zero-fields]];
   over $\mathbb C$ this is the published complex Specht classification
   [[thm-complex-specht-modules-are-irreducible]]). Decompose
   $V_n\cong\bigoplus_{\lambda}c_{\lambda,n}V(\lambda)_n$ with multiplicities
   $c_{\lambda,n}\ge0$, the sum over those $\lambda$ with
   $n\ge|\lambda|+\lambda_1$. Then for every fixed $\lambda$ the multiplicity
   $c_{\lambda,n}$ is independent of $n$ for all $n\ge N$.

The sequence is **uniformly representation stable** when it is so for some
$N\ge0$. All three conditions are part of the definition, and (II) is not a
consequence of (I) and (III): the sequence with $V_n=k^2$ carrying the trivial
$S_n$-action and $\varphi_n$ the inclusion of the first coordinate is injective
and has constant multiplicities $c_{\varnothing,n}=2$, but its images span only
a one-dimensional subspace of $V_{n+1}$. No choice principle is used.

Let $V$ be an FI-module over $k$ and let $\Phi_a$ and $T$ be the coinvariant
functors and transition maps of
[[def-fi-coinvariant-functors-and-transition-maps]]. The **injectivity degree**
$\operatorname{inj-deg}(V)$ is the least $s\ge0$ such that for every $a\ge0$
the transition map $T\colon\Phi_a(V)_n\to\Phi_a(V)_{n+1}$ is injective for all
$n\ge s$; the **surjectivity degree** $\operatorname{surj-deg}(V)$ is the least
$s\ge0$ such that for every $a\ge0$ the map $T$ is surjective for all $n\ge s$.
The **stability degree** is

$$\operatorname{stab-deg}(V):=\max\bigl(\operatorname{inj-deg}(V),\operatorname{surj-deg}(V)\bigr).$$

Each of the three is $+\infty$ when no such $s$ exists; here the bounds are
read as elements of the extended nonnegative integers
$\mathbb N\cup\{+\infty\}$ with the evident order, in which every nonempty
subset of $\mathbb N$ has a least element
([[def-natural-numbers]]), so "the least $s$" is well defined. Equivalently,
$T\colon\Phi_a(V)_n\to\Phi_a(V)_{n+1}$ is an isomorphism for all $a\ge0$ and
all $n\ge\operatorname{stab-deg}(V)$: the map is an isomorphism exactly when it
is both injective and surjective, and for finite bounds a threshold that
controls all $a$ simultaneously is the larger of the two thresholds, while
each of the two stated bounds remains the least threshold controlling its own
property.

The three bounds are kept distinct: $\operatorname{stab-deg}(V)$ is the maximum
of the other two, and nothing in the definition requires
$\operatorname{inj-deg}(V)=\operatorname{surj-deg}(V)$. No finiteness is
asserted: each bound is allowed to be $+\infty$. No choice principle is used.

A **graded $k[T]$-module** consists of $k$-modules $U_n$, $n\ge0$, together
with $k$-linear maps $T=T_n\colon U_n\to U_{n+1}$ for all $n\ge0$. A
**morphism** $U\to U'$ of graded $k[T]$-modules is a family of $k$-linear maps
$u_n\colon U_n\to U'_n$ with $u_{n+1}\circ T_n=T'_n\circ u_n$ for all $n$.

Fix $a\ge0$, a set $\mathbf a$ of cardinality $a$, and a functorial disjoint
union of finite sets. Let $V$ be an FI-module over $k$
([[def-fi-category-and-fi-module]]) and let $n\ge0$. Put

$$\Phi_a(V)_n:=(V_{\mathbf a\sqcup n})_{S_n},$$

the coinvariants of the $kS_n$-module $V_{\mathbf a\sqcup n}$: the quotient by
the span of the elements $\sigma\cdot v-v$, $\sigma\in S_n$, $v\in
V_{\mathbf a\sqcup n}$ ([[def-coinvariants-functor-of-a-group-module]],
[[def-quotient-module]]). Equivalently $\Phi_a(V)_n=k\otimes_{kS_n}
V_{\mathbf a\sqcup n}$, the two descriptions being identified by the balancing
argument of [[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]] and
the corresponding identification for $\mathbb Z$ in
[[def-coinvariants-functor-of-a-group-module]]; the group ring $kS_n$ is a
unital $k$-algebra with basis the group elements
([[def-group-ring]], [[thm-group-ring-is-a-unital-algebra-with-basis-g]]).

To define the transition map $T\colon\Phi_a(V)_n\to\Phi_a(V)_{n+1}$, choose an
injection $f\colon n\to n+1$. It induces the injection
$\mathrm{id}_{\mathbf a}\sqcup f\colon\mathbf a\sqcup n\to\mathbf a\sqcup n+1$
and hence a $k$-linear map $(V_{\mathbf a\sqcup n}\to
V_{\mathbf a\sqcup n+1})$. This map is $S_n$-equivariant, where $S_n$ acts on
the target through the injection $\mathrm{id}_{\mathbf a}\sqcup f$, so it
descends to the quotient map $T=T_f$ on coinvariants. The map $T_f$ is
independent of $f$: for two injections $f,g\colon n\to n+1$ the composite
$g\circ f^{-1}$ is a bijection $f(n)\to g(n)$, which extends along the
complement to a permutation $\tau\in S_{n+1}$ with $g=\tau\circ f$; then
$\mathrm{id}_{\mathbf a}\sqcup g=(\mathrm{id}_{\mathbf a}\sqcup
\tau)\circ(\mathrm{id}_{\mathbf a}\sqcup f)$, and the map induced by
$\mathrm{id}_{\mathbf a}\sqcup\tau$ on
$(V_{\mathbf a\sqcup n+1})_{S_{n+1}}$ is the identity because it comes from
the action of the group element $\tau$. Thus $T$ is well defined and
$(\Phi_a(V),T)$ is a graded $k[T]$-module.

A map of FI-modules $\alpha\colon V\to W$ gives $k$-linear maps
$\alpha_{\mathbf a\sqcup n}\colon V_{\mathbf a\sqcup n}\to W_{\mathbf
a\sqcup n}$ commuting with the $S_n$-actions and with the maps induced by
$\mathrm{id}_{\mathbf a}\sqcup f$, hence maps $(\Phi_a\alpha)_n$ of coinvariants
commuting with $T$; so $\Phi_a$ is a functor from FI-modules over $k$ to graded
$k[T]$-modules.

**Exactness.** Coinvariants of a group module are right exact
([[prop-the-coinvariants-functor-is-right-exact]]), so the functor
$M\mapsto M_{S_n}\cong k\otimes_{kS_n}M$ is right exact and each $\Phi_a$ is
right exact in every degree. If $k$ contains $\mathbb Q$, then $1/n!$ exists in $k$
and the averaging map
$s\colon\Phi_a(V)_n\to V_{\mathbf a\sqcup n}$,
$s([v])=\frac1{n!}\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\sigma\cdot v$, is a well-defined
$k$-linear section of the quotient map that is natural in $V$; it identifies
$\Phi_a(V)_n$ with the invariants $V_{\mathbf a\sqcup n}^{S_n}$. Under this
natural identification $\Phi_a$ becomes the invariants functor, which is left
exact (kernels of equivariant maps are computed pointwise), and therefore
$\Phi_a$ is exact; in that case the induced map $\Phi_a(W)\to\Phi_a(V)$ is
injective for every sub-FI-module $W\subseteq V$
([[def-submodule]], [[def-module-homomorphism-kernel-image-and-cokernel]]), so
$\Phi_a(W)$ is identified with a submodule of $\Phi_a(V)$. Finite averaging
uses only the finite groups $S_n$; no choice principle is used.

Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $0$ and let $V$ be an FI-module over $k$
([[def-fi-category-and-fi-module]]). For a partition $\lambda$ and
$n\ge|\lambda|+\lambda_1$ put $\lambda[n]:=(n-|\lambda|,\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\dots)$,
the first-row padding ([[def-first-row-padding-of-a-partition]]), and let

$$V(\lambda)_n:=k\otimes_{\mathbb Q}S^{\lambda[n]}_{\mathbb Q}$$

be the scalar extension of the rational Specht model of $\lambda[n]$
([[thm-complex-specht-modules-are-irreducible]],
[[lem-specht-modules-classify-irreducibles-over-characteristic-zero-fields]]).
By the classification lemma, $V(\lambda)_n$ is the irreducible $kS_n$-module
with label $\lambda[n]$, and every irreducible $kS_n$-module is isomorphic to
exactly one $V(\lambda)_n$: indeed, every partition $\mu=(\mu_1,\mu_2,\dots)$
of $n$ is uniquely $\lambda[n]$ for the partition
$\lambda=(\mu_2,\mu_3,\dots)$ obtained by deleting the first row, and
$n\ge|\lambda|+\lambda_1$ holds precisely because $\mu_1\ge\mu_2$;
consequently the labels $\lambda[n]$ run over the partitions of $n$ without
repetition.

Say that $V(\lambda)_n$ **occurs as a constituent** of $V_n$ when there are
$kS_n$-submodules $U\subseteq W\subseteq V_n$ with
$W/U\cong V(\lambda)_n$ ([[def-submodule]], [[def-quotient-module]]); this is a
condition on subquotients and requires no decomposition or finite-dimensionality
of $V_n$. The **weight** of $V$ is

$$\operatorname{weight}(V):=\sup\bigl\{|\lambda|:V(\lambda)_n\text{ occurs as a constituent of }V_n\text{ for some }n\ge|\lambda|+\lambda_1\bigr\},$$

the supremum over all pairs $(\lambda,n)$ as displayed. The set of integers
displayed is a set of nonnegative integers, so the supremum is well defined in
$\mathbb N\cup\{\infty\}$; it is $0$ for $V=0$, and $\operatorname{weight}(V)=\infty$
exactly when the displayed set is unbounded. No finiteness of
$\operatorname{weight}(V)$ is asserted.

If $W$ is a **subquotient** of $V$, meaning that $W\cong U'/U$ for sub-FI-modules
$U\subseteq U'\subseteq V$ computed pointwise, then
$\operatorname{weight}(W)\le\operatorname{weight}(V)$: a constituent of $W_n$ is
a subquotient of the subquotient $U'_n/U_n$ of $V_n$, hence a subquotient of
$V_n$, so it contributes the same label $|\lambda|$ to the supremum for $V$. No
choice principle is used: the labels $\lambda[n]$, constituents and the
supremum are set-theoretic data, and no bases or decompositions are chosen.

Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $0$, let $\mu\vdash n$, and write
$\mu=\lambda[n]$ as in [[def-first-row-padding-of-a-partition]]; set
$V(\lambda)_n:=V_\mu$, the irreducible $kS_n$-module with label $\mu$
([[lem-specht-modules-classify-irreducibles-over-characteristic-zero-fields]]).
For a vector space carrying an action of a product $S_a\times S_k$ and
$k_0=n-a$, write $(\,\cdot\,)_{S_{k_0}}$ for $S_{k_0}$-coinvariants of the
restriction to that product ([[def-fi-coinvariant-functors-and-transition-maps]]).

(i) For $a\le n$, with $k_0=n-a$, the $S_a$-representation
$(V_\mu)_{S_{k_0}}$ is zero if and only if $n-a>\mu_1$, equivalently
$(V(\lambda)_n)_{S_{n-a}}=0$ if and only if $a<|\lambda|$.

(ii) If $n-a=\mu_1$ (that is, $a=|\lambda|$), then
$(V(\lambda)_n)_{S_{n-a}}\cong V_\lambda$ as $S_{|\lambda|}$-modules.

(iii) For fixed $\lambda$ and $a\ge|\lambda|$, the $S_a$-module
$(V(\lambda)_n)_{S_{n-a}}$ is independent of $n$ once $n\ge a+\lambda_1$; in
fact $(V(\lambda)_n)_{S_{n-a}}\cong\operatorname{Ind}_{S_{|\lambda|}\times
S_{a-|\lambda|}}^{S_a}(V_\lambda\boxtimes k)$ throughout that range.

(iv) If $V$ is an FI-module over $k$ with $\operatorname{weight}(V)\le a$
([[def-weight-of-a-characteristic-zero-fi-module]]), then every subquotient
$W_n$ ([[def-submodule]]) of the $S_n$-module $V_n$ satisfies
$W_n=0\iff(W_n)_{S_{n-a}}=0$.

No choice principle is used.

Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $0$, let $V$ be an FI-module over $k$
([[def-fi-category-and-fi-module]]), and put
$s:=\operatorname{stab-deg}(V)<\infty$
([[def-injectivity-surjectivity-and-stability-degree-of-an-fi-module]]). Then
for every $n\ge0$, every irreducible constituent $V(\lambda)_n$ of the
$kS_n$-module $V_n$ satisfies

$$\lambda_1\le s.$$

Equivalently, since the padded partition is
$\lambda[n]=(n-|\lambda|,\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\dots)$, the second row of the
Specht diagram $\lambda[n]$ has length at most $s$; the first row of the
padding tail is the second row of the full diagram
([[def-first-row-padding-of-a-partition]],
[[def-weight-of-a-characteristic-zero-fi-module]]). No choice principle is
used.

A **graded $k[T]$-module** consists of $k$-modules $U_n$, $n\ge0$, together
with $k$-linear maps $T=T_n\colon U_n\to U_{n+1}$ for all $n\ge0$. A
**morphism** $U\to U'$ of graded $k[T]$-modules is a family of $k$-linear maps
$u_n\colon U_n\to U'_n$ with $u_{n+1}\circ T_n=T'_n\circ u_n$ for all $n$.

Fix $a\ge0$, a set $\mathbf a$ of cardinality $a$, and a functorial disjoint
union of finite sets. Let $V$ be an FI-module over $k$
([[def-fi-category-and-fi-module]]) and let $n\ge0$. Put

$$\Phi_a(V)_n:=(V_{\mathbf a\sqcup n})_{S_n},$$

the coinvariants of the $kS_n$-module $V_{\mathbf a\sqcup n}$: the quotient by
the span of the elements $\sigma\cdot v-v$, $\sigma\in S_n$, $v\in
V_{\mathbf a\sqcup n}$ ([[def-coinvariants-functor-of-a-group-module]],
[[def-quotient-module]]). Equivalently $\Phi_a(V)_n=k\otimes_{kS_n}
V_{\mathbf a\sqcup n}$, the two descriptions being identified by the balancing
argument of [[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]] and
the corresponding identification for $\mathbb Z$ in
[[def-coinvariants-functor-of-a-group-module]]; the group ring $kS_n$ is a
unital $k$-algebra with basis the group elements
([[def-group-ring]], [[thm-group-ring-is-a-unital-algebra-with-basis-g]]).

To define the transition map $T\colon\Phi_a(V)_n\to\Phi_a(V)_{n+1}$, choose an
injection $f\colon n\to n+1$. It induces the injection
$\mathrm{id}_{\mathbf a}\sqcup f\colon\mathbf a\sqcup n\to\mathbf a\sqcup n+1$
and hence a $k$-linear map $(V_{\mathbf a\sqcup n}\to
V_{\mathbf a\sqcup n+1})$. This map is $S_n$-equivariant, where $S_n$ acts on
the target through the injection $\mathrm{id}_{\mathbf a}\sqcup f$, so it
descends to the quotient map $T=T_f$ on coinvariants. The map $T_f$ is
independent of $f$: for two injections $f,g\colon n\to n+1$ the composite
$g\circ f^{-1}$ is a bijection $f(n)\to g(n)$, which extends along the
complement to a permutation $\tau\in S_{n+1}$ with $g=\tau\circ f$; then
$\mathrm{id}_{\mathbf a}\sqcup g=(\mathrm{id}_{\mathbf a}\sqcup
\tau)\circ(\mathrm{id}_{\mathbf a}\sqcup f)$, and the map induced by
$\mathrm{id}_{\mathbf a}\sqcup\tau$ on
$(V_{\mathbf a\sqcup n+1})_{S_{n+1}}$ is the identity because it comes from
the action of the group element $\tau$. Thus $T$ is well defined and
$(\Phi_a(V),T)$ is a graded $k[T]$-module.

A map of FI-modules $\alpha\colon V\to W$ gives $k$-linear maps
$\alpha_{\mathbf a\sqcup n}\colon V_{\mathbf a\sqcup n}\to W_{\mathbf
a\sqcup n}$ commuting with the $S_n$-actions and with the maps induced by
$\mathrm{id}_{\mathbf a}\sqcup f$, hence maps $(\Phi_a\alpha)_n$ of coinvariants
commuting with $T$; so $\Phi_a$ is a functor from FI-modules over $k$ to graded
$k[T]$-modules.

**Exactness.** Coinvariants of a group module are right exact
([[prop-the-coinvariants-functor-is-right-exact]]), so the functor
$M\mapsto M_{S_n}\cong k\otimes_{kS_n}M$ is right exact and each $\Phi_a$ is
right exact in every degree. If $k$ contains $\mathbb Q$, then $1/n!$ exists in $k$
and the averaging map
$s\colon\Phi_a(V)_n\to V_{\mathbf a\sqcup n}$,
$s([v])=\frac1{n!}\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\sigma\cdot v$, is a well-defined
$k$-linear section of the quotient map that is natural in $V$; it identifies
$\Phi_a(V)_n$ with the invariants $V_{\mathbf a\sqcup n}^{S_n}$. Under this
natural identification $\Phi_a$ becomes the invariants functor, which is left
exact (kernels of equivariant maps are computed pointwise), and therefore
$\Phi_a$ is exact; in that case the induced map $\Phi_a(W)\to\Phi_a(V)$ is
injective for every sub-FI-module $W\subseteq V$
([[def-submodule]], [[def-module-homomorphism-kernel-image-and-cokernel]]), so
$\Phi_a(W)$ is identified with a submodule of $\Phi_a(V)$. Finite averaging
uses only the finite groups $S_n$; no choice principle is used.

For a left $G$-module $M$, its coinvariants are
$M_G=M/\langle gm-m:g\in G,m\in M\rangle$. If
$f:M\to N$ is $G$-linear, define $f_G:M_G\to N_G$ by
$f_G([m])=[f(m)]$. Equivariance makes this well defined, and identities and
composites are preserved, so $M\mapsto M_G$ is a functor. The map
$1\otimes m\mapsto[m]$ naturally identifies
$\mathbb Z\otimes_{\mathbb Z[G]}M$ (with right trivial $\mathbb Z$) with
$M_G$.

Let $G$ be a finite group, let $k$ be a field with
$\operatorname{char} k \nmid |G|$, let $\rho:G \to \operatorname{GL}(V)$ be a
finite-dimensional representation of $G$ over $k$, and let $W \le V$ be a
subrepresentation. Then there is a subrepresentation $U \le V$ such that

$$V=W\oplus U.$$

Let $F$ be a field of characteristic $0$ and let $n\ge0$. For every partition
$\lambda\vdash n$ the field-valued Specht module $S^\lambda_F$ of
[[def-polytabloid-specht-module-over-an-arbitrary-field]] is nonzero and
irreducible, distinct partitions give non-isomorphic modules, and every
irreducible $FS_n$-module is isomorphic to exactly one of them. Consequently,
by Maschke's theorem, every finite-dimensional $FS_n$-module is a direct sum of
copies of the $S^\lambda_F$; thus the irreducible $FS_n$-modules are indexed by
the partitions of $n$ and the modules $\{S^\lambda_F:\lambda\vdash n\}$ form a
complete irredundant list.

This is the constituent convention used throughout the pair: over
$F=\mathbb C$ it specialises to the published complex classification, and over
a general characteristic-zero field $F$ it is proved by extending the rational
Specht models along $\mathbb Q\to F$, never by a scalar extension from
$\mathbb C$ to $F$.

derivations.claim: Let $K_n:=\ker\varphi_n\subseteq V_n$ and let $\varphi'_n:=\operatorname{Ind}_{S_n}^{S_{n+1}}\varphi_n\colon\operatorname{Ind}_{S_n}^{S_{n+1}}V_n\to V_{n+1}$ with cokernel $C_{n+1}$, so that $C_{n+1}$ is a quotient of $V_{n+1}$. The image of $\varphi'_n$ is the $S_{n+1}$-span of $\varphi_n(V_n)$, since $\varphi'_n(\sigma\otimes v)=\sigma\cdot\varphi_n(v)$; hence condition (I) is $K_n=0$ for all $n\ge N$ and condition (II) is $C_{n+1}=0$ for all $n\ge N$.
If $|\lambda|>d$, then $c_{\lambda,n}=0$ for every $n$ for which $c_{\lambda,n}$ is defined, so condition (III) is automatic for such $\lambda$; it remains to treat $|\lambda|\le d$.

Vanishing criteria: for $n\ge d$ one has $K_n=0\iff(K_n)_{S_{n-d}}=0$, and for $n+1\ge d$ one has $C_{n+1}=0\iff(C_{n+1})_{S_{n+1-d}}=0$. Indeed $K_n$ is a submodule of $V_n$ and $C_{n+1}$ is a quotient of $V_{n+1}$, both are subquotients of modules of weight $d$ ([[def-weight-of-a-characteristic-zero-fi-module]]), and [F4](iv) applies with $a=d$.

Factorization: for $n\ge d$, identify $\Phi_d(V)_{n-d}$ with $(V_n)_{S_{n-d}}$ and $\Phi_d(V)_{n+1-d}$ with $(V_{n+1})_{S_{n+1-d}}$ along the standard identifications of $\mathbf d\sqcup(n-d)$ with $[n]$ and of $\mathbf d\sqcup(n+1-d)$ with $[n+1]$. The transition map $T\colon(V_n)_{S_{n-d}}\to(V_{n+1})_{S_{n+1-d}}$ factors in two ways: $T=q\circ(\varphi_n)_{S_{n-d}}$, where $q$ is the quotient map onto coinvariants of the larger subgroup $S_{n+1-d}\ge S_{n-d}$, and $T=(\varphi'_n)_{S_{n+1-d}}\circ\psi$, where $\psi$ is induced by $v\mapsto1\otimes v$. Exactness of coinvariants over $k$ gives $(K_n)_{S_{n-d}}=\ker\bigl((\varphi_n)_{S_{n-d}}\bigr)$ and $(C_{n+1})_{S_{n+1-d}}=\operatorname{coker}\bigl((\varphi'_n)_{S_{n+1-d}}\bigr)$.

We prove (III) by induction on $m=|\lambda|$ in the range $m\le d$. Fix $m\le d$, let $n\ge s+d$ (so $n-m\ge s\ge0$), and assume the multiplicities $c_{\mu,n'}$ are independent of $n'$ in the range for all $|\mu|<m$. Since $n-m\ge s$, the transition maps give isomorphisms $\Phi_m(V)_{n-m}\cong\Phi_m(V)_i$ for all $i\ge s$, so the isomorphism class of $(V_n)_{S_{n-m}}=\Phi_m(V)_{n-m}$ is independent of $n$. By [F7] $V_n=\bigoplus_\lambda c_{\lambda,n}V(\lambda)_n$ is a finite direct sum of irreducibles, and [F6] gives $(V_n)_{S_{n-m}}=\bigoplus_\lambda c_{\lambda,n}(V(\lambda)_n)_{S_{n-m}}$; by [F4](i) with $a=m$ only the labels with $|\lambda|\le m$ contribute, and by [F4](ii) with $a=m$ those with $|\lambda|=m$ contribute $(V(\lambda)_n)_{S_{n-m}}\cong V_\lambda$. For $|\lambda|<m$, [F4](iii) gives $(V(\lambda)_n)_{S_{n-m}}\cong\operatorname{Ind}_{S_{|\lambda|}\times S_{m-|\lambda|}}^{S_m}(V_\lambda\boxtimes k)$, independent of $n$, provided $n\ge m+\lambda_1$; this holds because $\lambda_1\le s$ for every occurring constituent by [F5] and $m+\lambda_1\le d+s\le n$. Hence in the decomposition $(V_n)_{S_{n-m}}=\bigoplus_{|\lambda|<m}c_{\lambda,n}(V(\lambda)_n)_{S_{n-m}}\oplus\bigoplus_{|\lambda|=m}c_{\lambda,n}V_\lambda$ the first summand has an isomorphism class independent of $n$ (each factor is independent of $n$ and each multiplicity is constant by the induction hypothesis), and the total has an isomorphism class independent of $n$, so the second summand does too; as the $V_\lambda$ with $|\lambda|=m$ are pairwise non-isomorphic, every multiplicity $c_{\lambda,n}$ with $|\lambda|=m$ is independent of $n$ in the range. This proves (III) for all $\lambda$ with $|\lambda|\le d$ and hence, with step 2.1, for all $\lambda$.

Let $n\ge s+d$, so that $n-d\ge s$ and $T\colon\Phi_d(V)_{n-d}\to\Phi_d(V)_{n+1-d}$ is an isomorphism by [F2]. The first factorization in step 2.3 then forces $(\varphi_n)_{S_{n-d}}$ to be injective, and the second forces $(\varphi'_n)_{S_{n+1-d}}$ to be surjective; by the exactness identifications in step 2.3 and the criteria in step 2.2, $K_n=0$ and $C_{n+1}=0$. By step 1.1, conditions (I) and (II) hold for all $n\ge s+d$.

Steps 2.1 and 3.1 give condition (III) for $n\ge d+s$ and steps 2.2, 2.3 and 3.2 give conditions (I) and (II) for $n\ge d+s$; hence the consistent sequence $(V_n,\varphi_n)$ is uniformly representation stable with stable range $n\ge d+s$.

boundaries.evidence: step 2.1: the label lambda = emptyset is included; since |lambda| = 0 <= d it is never excluded by the weight argument.
step 1.1: the kernel K_n and the cokernel C_{n+1} may be zero, and the equivalences remain true in that case since coinvariants of 0 are 0.
step 3.1: the induction on m starts at m = 0 with the single trivial label, and there is no base case beyond it.
step 3.1: the induction admits both m = 0 (only the trivial label) and m = d (the top weight), the two degenerate ends of the range.
step 3.2: n = s + d is the inclusive endpoint at which T is an isomorphism and both the injectivity of (phi_n)_{S_{n-d}} and the surjectivity of (phi_n)_{S_{n+1-d}} are concluded.
step 1.1: K_n and C_{n+1} are defined by kernels and cokernels of the given maps; no generating set, basis or decomposition is selected anywhere in the proof.
step 2.2: the only-if halves of the two vanishing criteria, module = 0 implies coinvariants vanish, are the trivial directions used there.
step 2.2: the if halves, coinvariant vanishing implies module vanishing under weight <= d, are the statements ultimately applied in step 3.2 via the exactness identifications.

citations.quote:
Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $0$. A **consistent sequence** is a
sequence $(V_n,\varphi_n)_{n\ge0}$ in which each $V_n$ is a finite-dimensional
left $kS_n$-module and each $\varphi_n\colon V_n\to V_{n+1}$ is
$S_n$-equivariant, the target being regarded as an $S_n$-module by restriction
along the standard inclusion $S_n\hookrightarrow S_{n+1}$ that fixes $n$. An
FI-module $V$ over $k$ with finite-dimensional values
([[def-fi-category-and-fi-module]]) determines such a sequence by
$V_n:=V([n])$ and $\varphi_n:=f_*$ for the standard inclusions
$f\colon[n]\to[n+1]$; these maps are $S_n$-equivariant by functoriality and the
conjugation action, since $f\circ\sigma=\Phi_f(\sigma)\circ f$ with
$\Phi_f(\sigma)$ the extension of $\sigma$ by the fixed point $n$.

The sequence is **uniformly representation stable with stable range $n\ge N$**
when all three of the following hold.

1. **(I) Injectivity.** The map $\varphi_n\colon V_n\to V_{n+1}$ is injective for
   every $n\ge N$.
2. **(II) Surjectivity.** The $S_{n+1}$-span of the image $\varphi_n(V_n)$ is
   all of $V_{n+1}$ for every $n\ge N$.
3. **(III) Multiplicities.** For each partition $\lambda$ and each $n$ with
   $n\ge|\lambda|+\lambda_1$, let $V(\lambda)_n$ be the irreducible $kS_n$-module
   indexed by the first-row padding $\lambda[n]=(n-|\lambda|,\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\dots)$
   ([[def-first-row-padding-of-a-partition]]), namely the scalar extension
   $k\otimes_{\mathbb Q}S^{\lambda[n]}_{\mathbb Q}$ of the rational Specht model,
   which is the unique irreducible $kS_n$-module with that label
   ([[lem-specht-modules-classify-irreducibles-over-characteristic-zero-fields]];
   over $\mathbb C$ this is the published complex Specht classification
   [[thm-complex-specht-modules-are-irreducible]]). Decompose
   $V_n\cong\bigoplus_{\lambda}c_{\lambda,n}V(\lambda)_n$ with multiplicities
   $c_{\lambda,n}\ge0$, the sum over those $\lambda$ with
   $n\ge|\lambda|+\lambda_1$. Then for every fixed $\lambda$ the multiplicity
   $c_{\lambda,n}$ is independent of $n$ for all $n\ge N$.

The sequence is **uniformly representation stable** when it is so for some
$N\ge0$. All three conditions are part of the definition, and (II) is not a
consequence of (I) and (III): the sequence with $V_n=k^2$ carrying the trivial
$S_n$-action and $\varphi_n$ the inclusion of the first coordinate is injective
and has constant multiplicities $c_{\varnothing,n}=2$, but its images span only
a one-dimensional subspace of $V_{n+1}$. No choice principle is used.

Let $V$ be an FI-module over $k$ ([[def-fi-category-and-fi-module]]) and let
$\Sigma$ be a set of elements, each lying in $V_S$ for some finite set $S$. The
**sub-FI-module generated by $\Sigma$**, written
$\operatorname{span}_V(\Sigma)$, is the intersection of all sub-FI-modules of
$V$ that are subfunctors and contain $\Sigma$
([[def-submodule]], [[lem-submodule-criterion-sums-and-intersections]] for the
objectwise intersection of submodules). The family is nonempty because $V$
itself qualifies, and the intersection is a sub-FI-module, since each
transition map $f_*$ preserves every member and hence their intersection;
thus $\operatorname{span}_V(\Sigma)$ is the smallest sub-FI-module of $V$
containing $\Sigma$.

Explicitly, $\operatorname{span}_V(\Sigma)_T$ is the $k$-span of all elements
$f_*(v)$ with $v\in\Sigma\cap V_S$ and $f\colon S\to T$ a morphism of $FI$: the
set of all finite $k$-linear combinations of such elements is a sub-FI-module
of $V$ containing $\Sigma$, because $g_*(f_*(v))=(g\circ f)_*(v)$, and every
sub-FI-module containing $\Sigma$ contains each $f_*(v)$; hence it equals the
intersection. Call $V$ **finitely generated** when
$\operatorname{span}_V(\Sigma)=V$ for some finite $\Sigma$, and **generated in
degree $\le d$** when $\operatorname{span}_V(V_{\le d})=V$, where
$V_{\le d}=\bigsqcup_{|S|\le d}V_S$ is the set of all elements lying in the
values of $V$ at finite sets $S$ with $|S|\le d$. The **generation degree** of
$V$ is the least $d\ge0$ such that $V$ is generated in degree $\le d$, and
$\infty$ when no such $d$ exists
([[def-generated-cyclic-finitely-generated-and-free-modules]]).

Finite generation of $V$ and pointwise finite generation of the individual
$k$-modules $V_S$ are different conditions: the pointwise property is implied
by finite generation (as shown below by
[[lem-generated-in-degree-d-is-a-quotient-of-free-fi-modules]]) but does not
imply it, and no pointwise finite generation or finite-dimensionality is built
into either notion. A degree bound on a generating set is an additional
structure on $V$, not a consequence of finite generation. No choice principle
is used: $\operatorname{span}_V(\Sigma)$ is defined by an intersection of
subfunctors, and its explicit description involves only finite $k$-linear
combinations.

Let $V$ be an FI-module over $k$
([[def-fi-category-and-fi-module]]), with free FI-modules $M(m)$ as in
[[def-free-fi-module-generated-by-an-sm-module]] and span as in
[[def-finite-generation-and-generation-degree-of-an-fi-module]].

(a) For $v\in V_m$ the map of FI-modules $M(m)\to V$ sending the canonical
generator $\mathrm{id}_m\in M(m)_m$ to $v$ has image $\operatorname{span}_V(v)$;
more generally, for any set $\Sigma$ of elements, each lying in some $V_S$, the
canonical map $\bigoplus_{s\in\Sigma}M(|S_s|)\to V$ sending the generator of
the summand indexed by $s$ to $s$ has image $\operatorname{span}_V(\Sigma)$.

(b) $V$ is finitely generated if and only if there is a finite family
$m_1,\dots,m_k\ge0$ with a surjection

$$M(m_1)\oplus\cdots\oplus M(m_k)\twoheadrightarrow V;$$

$V$ is generated in degree $\le d$ if and only if there is a surjection
$\bigoplus_{i\in I}M(m_i)\twoheadrightarrow V$ with $m_i\le d$ for all $i$. In
particular, if $V$ is generated in degree $\le d$, then the evaluation map
$\bigoplus_{m\le d}M(V_m)\to V$, whose restriction to each copy of $M(m)$
indexed by an element $v\in V_m$ sends $\mathrm{id}_m\mapsto v$, is surjective.

(c) If $V$ is finitely generated, then $V_S$ is a finitely generated $k$-module
for every finite set $S$
([[def-generated-cyclic-finitely-generated-and-free-modules]]).

No choice principle is used: all maps come from a finite or explicitly indexed
set of generators, and the image computations are linear algebra on the values
at a fixed finite set.

Let $W$ be an FB-module over $k$, i.e. a functor from the groupoid of finite
sets and bijections to $k\text{-}\mathrm{Mod}$ ([[def-fi-category-and-fi-module]]);
thus $W(T)$ is a $k$-module for every finite set $T$, and every bijection
$\beta\colon T\to T'$ gives an isomorphism $W(\beta)\colon W(T)\to W(T')$.
Because an FB-module is defined on all finite sets, no transport choices are
needed below.

The **free FI-module** $M(W)$ assigns to a finite set $S$ the direct sum

$$M(W)_S:=\bigoplus_{T\subseteq S}W(T)$$

over all subsets $T\subseteq S$ ([[def-subset-and-proper-subset]],
[[def-direct-sum-of-a-family-of-modules]]; only finitely many summands occur).
For an injection $f\colon S\to S'$ and a subset $T\subseteq S$, the restriction
$f|_T\colon T\to f(T)$ is a bijection
([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]), and the transition map
$f_*\colon M(W)_S\to M(W)_{S'}$ is the sum of the isomorphisms
$W(f|_T)\colon W(T)\to W(f(T))$ over all $T\subseteq S$. This is $k$-linear and
functorial, since $(f'\circ f)|_T=f'|_{f(T)}\circ f|_T$; hence $M(W)$ is an
FI-module over $k$.

For $S=[n]=\{0,\dots,n-1\}$ the symmetric group $S_n$
([[def-finite-symmetric-group-and-permutation-notation]]) acts by
$\sigma\cdot T:=\sigma(T)$ and $W(\sigma|_T)$, and this is a left action
making $M(W)_n$ a left $kS_n$-module ([[def-group-ring]]). Grouping the sum by
the cardinality of $T$, the subsets of cardinality $a$ form a single $S_n$-orbit
with stabilizer the ordered block subgroup
$S_{\{0,\dots,a-1\}}\times S_{\{a,\dots,n-1\}}\cong S_a\times S_{n-a}$, so the
orbit summand is identified with an induced module
([[def-induced-r-linear-g-module-by-h-covariant-functions]]):

$$M(W)_n\cong\bigoplus_{a=0}^{n}\operatorname{Ind}_{S_a\times S_{n-a}}^{S_n}\bigl(W_a\boxtimes k\bigr),$$

where $W_a:=W(\{0,\dots,a-1\})$ is the value of the FB-module on an $a$-element
set, the first factor acts on $W_a$ through $W$ and the second factor acts
trivially, and $\boxtimes$ is the external tensor product of modules for the
two direct factors ([[def-outer-induction-product-for-symmetric-group-characters]],
[[lem-character-ring-of-a-direct-product-is-the-tensor-product]],
[[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]]).

**Adjunction.** Let $\pi$ be the functor from FI-modules to FB-modules that
forgets the maps between distinct cardinalities. The inclusion of the $T=S$
summand is a natural map $\eta_W\colon W\to\pi M(W)$, and evaluating a map
$F\colon M(W)\to V$ of FI-modules on that summand yields a map of FB-modules
$\pi F\circ\eta_W\colon W\to\pi V$. Conversely, a map of FB-modules
$\varphi\colon W\to\pi V$ extends uniquely to a map of FI-modules
$\widetilde\varphi\colon M(W)\to V$ whose value on the summand $W(T)\subseteq
M(W)_S$ is $V(\iota_{T,S})\circ\varphi_T$, with $\iota_{T,S}\colon T\to S$ the
inclusion; the components are compatible with injections and the two
constructions are inverse, so
$\operatorname{Hom}_{FI\text{-}Mod}(M(W),V)\cong
\operatorname{Hom}_{FB\text{-}Mod}(W,\pi V)$ naturally in $V$ and $W$: $M$ is
left adjoint to $\pi$, with unit $\eta$.

For $m\ge0$ write $k[S_m]$ for the FB-module with $k[S_m](T)$ the free $k$-module
on the bijections $[m]\to T$, and zero when $|T|\ne m$; its value on an
$m$-element set is the regular representation of $S_m$. Put
$M(m):=M(k[S_m])$. Then $M(m)_S$ has as $k$-basis the injections
$[m]\hookrightarrow S$ — equivalently, the ordered sequences of $m$ distinct
elements of $S$ — and for a partition $\lambda$ with $|\lambda|=m$ and a field
$k$ of characteristic $0$, put $M(\lambda):=M(S^\lambda_k)$, where the FB-module
$S^\lambda_k$ is supported on $m$-element sets and $S^\lambda_k(T):=
k[\operatorname{Iso}([m],T)]\otimes_{kS_m}S^\lambda_k$. By the adjunction, a map
$M(m)\to V$ of FI-modules corresponds naturally to the choice of an element of
$V_m$: the module $M(m)$ represents the functor $V\mapsto V_m$. All
constructions are given by finitely many canonical bijections of finite sets;
no choice principle is used.

Let $V$ be an FI-module over $k$, with surjectivity degree and stability degree
as in [[def-injectivity-surjectivity-and-stability-degree-of-an-fi-module]] and
weight as in [[def-weight-of-a-characteristic-zero-fi-module]].

(a) Every quotient $V\twoheadrightarrow W$ of FI-modules satisfies
$\operatorname{surj-deg}(W)\le\operatorname{surj-deg}(V)$.

(b) If $V$ is generated in degree $\le d$
([[def-free-fi-module-generated-by-an-sm-module]] is the source of the
notation), then $\operatorname{surj-deg}(V)\le d$.

(c) If moreover $k$ is a field of characteristic $0$ and $V$ is generated in
degree $\le d$, then $\operatorname{weight}(V)\le d$.

No choice principle is used.

Let $V$ be an FI-module over $k$ and let $\Phi_a$ and $T$ be the coinvariant
functors and transition maps of
[[def-fi-coinvariant-functors-and-transition-maps]]. The **injectivity degree**
$\operatorname{inj-deg}(V)$ is the least $s\ge0$ such that for every $a\ge0$
the transition map $T\colon\Phi_a(V)_n\to\Phi_a(V)_{n+1}$ is injective for all
$n\ge s$; the **surjectivity degree** $\operatorname{surj-deg}(V)$ is the least
$s\ge0$ such that for every $a\ge0$ the map $T$ is surjective for all $n\ge s$.
The **stability degree** is

$$\operatorname{stab-deg}(V):=\max\bigl(\operatorname{inj-deg}(V),\operatorname{surj-deg}(V)\bigr).$$

Each of the three is $+\infty$ when no such $s$ exists; here the bounds are
read as elements of the extended nonnegative integers
$\mathbb N\cup\{+\infty\}$ with the evident order, in which every nonempty
subset of $\mathbb N$ has a least element
([[def-natural-numbers]]), so "the least $s$" is well defined. Equivalently,
$T\colon\Phi_a(V)_n\to\Phi_a(V)_{n+1}$ is an isomorphism for all $a\ge0$ and
all $n\ge\operatorname{stab-deg}(V)$: the map is an isomorphism exactly when it
is both injective and surjective, and for finite bounds a threshold that
controls all $a$ simultaneously is the larger of the two thresholds, while
each of the two stated bounds remains the least threshold controlling its own
property.

The three bounds are kept distinct: $\operatorname{stab-deg}(V)$ is the maximum
of the other two, and nothing in the definition requires
$\operatorname{inj-deg}(V)=\operatorname{surj-deg}(V)$. No finiteness is
asserted: each bound is allowed to be $+\infty$. No choice principle is used.

Let $W$ be an FB-module over $k$ and let $M(W)$ be the free FI-module of
[[def-free-fi-module-generated-by-an-sm-module]]. Then
$\operatorname{inj-deg}(M(W))=0$, and if $W_i=0$ for all $i>m$ then
$\operatorname{surj-deg}(M(W))\le m$; in particular
$M(m)=M(k[S_m])$ satisfies $\operatorname{inj-deg}(M(m))=0$ and
$\operatorname{stab-deg}(M(m))=m$
([[def-injectivity-surjectivity-and-stability-degree-of-an-fi-module]]).
If moreover $k$ is a field of characteristic $0$ and $\lambda$ is a partition,
then $\operatorname{weight}(M(\lambda))=|\lambda|$
([[def-weight-of-a-characteristic-zero-fi-module]]) and
$\operatorname{stab-deg}(M(\lambda))=\lambda_1$. No choice principle is used.

Let $k$ be a commutative Noetherian ring containing $\mathbb Q$
([[def-noetherian-ring]], [[def-restriction-and-extension-of-scalars]]), and
let $V$ be a finitely generated FI-module over $k$
([[def-finite-generation-and-generation-degree-of-an-fi-module]],
[[def-fi-category-and-fi-module]]). Then every sub-FI-module
$W\subseteq V$ is again finitely generated: the category of FI-modules over
$k$ is Noetherian, in the sense that every subobject of a finitely generated
object is finitely generated. The hypothesis that $k$ contains $\mathbb Q$ is
used only through the exactness of the functors $\Phi_a$ and through
restriction of scalars to $\mathbb Q$
([[def-fi-coinvariant-functors-and-transition-maps]]). No choice principle is
used.

A **graded $k[T]$-module** consists of $k$-modules $U_n$, $n\ge0$, together
with $k$-linear maps $T=T_n\colon U_n\to U_{n+1}$ for all $n\ge0$. A
**morphism** $U\to U'$ of graded $k[T]$-modules is a family of $k$-linear maps
$u_n\colon U_n\to U'_n$ with $u_{n+1}\circ T_n=T'_n\circ u_n$ for all $n$.

Fix $a\ge0$, a set $\mathbf a$ of cardinality $a$, and a functorial disjoint
union of finite sets. Let $V$ be an FI-module over $k$
([[def-fi-category-and-fi-module]]) and let $n\ge0$. Put

$$\Phi_a(V)_n:=(V_{\mathbf a\sqcup n})_{S_n},$$

the coinvariants of the $kS_n$-module $V_{\mathbf a\sqcup n}$: the quotient by
the span of the elements $\sigma\cdot v-v$, $\sigma\in S_n$, $v\in
V_{\mathbf a\sqcup n}$ ([[def-coinvariants-functor-of-a-group-module]],
[[def-quotient-module]]). Equivalently $\Phi_a(V)_n=k\otimes_{kS_n}
V_{\mathbf a\sqcup n}$, the two descriptions being identified by the balancing
argument of [[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]] and
the corresponding identification for $\mathbb Z$ in
[[def-coinvariants-functor-of-a-group-module]]; the group ring $kS_n$ is a
unital $k$-algebra with basis the group elements
([[def-group-ring]], [[thm-group-ring-is-a-unital-algebra-with-basis-g]]).

To define the transition map $T\colon\Phi_a(V)_n\to\Phi_a(V)_{n+1}$, choose an
injection $f\colon n\to n+1$. It induces the injection
$\mathrm{id}_{\mathbf a}\sqcup f\colon\mathbf a\sqcup n\to\mathbf a\sqcup n+1$
and hence a $k$-linear map $(V_{\mathbf a\sqcup n}\to
V_{\mathbf a\sqcup n+1})$. This map is $S_n$-equivariant, where $S_n$ acts on
the target through the injection $\mathrm{id}_{\mathbf a}\sqcup f$, so it
descends to the quotient map $T=T_f$ on coinvariants. The map $T_f$ is
independent of $f$: for two injections $f,g\colon n\to n+1$ the composite
$g\circ f^{-1}$ is a bijection $f(n)\to g(n)$, which extends along the
complement to a permutation $\tau\in S_{n+1}$ with $g=\tau\circ f$; then
$\mathrm{id}_{\mathbf a}\sqcup g=(\mathrm{id}_{\mathbf a}\sqcup
\tau)\circ(\mathrm{id}_{\mathbf a}\sqcup f)$, and the map induced by
$\mathrm{id}_{\mathbf a}\sqcup\tau$ on
$(V_{\mathbf a\sqcup n+1})_{S_{n+1}}$ is the identity because it comes from
the action of the group element $\tau$. Thus $T$ is well defined and
$(\Phi_a(V),T)$ is a graded $k[T]$-module.

A map of FI-modules $\alpha\colon V\to W$ gives $k$-linear maps
$\alpha_{\mathbf a\sqcup n}\colon V_{\mathbf a\sqcup n}\to W_{\mathbf
a\sqcup n}$ commuting with the $S_n$-actions and with the maps induced by
$\mathrm{id}_{\mathbf a}\sqcup f$, hence maps $(\Phi_a\alpha)_n$ of coinvariants
commuting with $T$; so $\Phi_a$ is a functor from FI-modules over $k$ to graded
$k[T]$-modules.

**Exactness.** Coinvariants of a group module are right exact
([[prop-the-coinvariants-functor-is-right-exact]]), so the functor
$M\mapsto M_{S_n}\cong k\otimes_{kS_n}M$ is right exact and each $\Phi_a$ is
right exact in every degree. If $k$ contains $\mathbb Q$, then $1/n!$ exists in $k$
and the averaging map
$s\colon\Phi_a(V)_n\to V_{\mathbf a\sqcup n}$,
$s([v])=\frac1{n!}\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\sigma\cdot v$, is a well-defined
$k$-linear section of the quotient map that is natural in $V$; it identifies
$\Phi_a(V)_n$ with the invariants $V_{\mathbf a\sqcup n}^{S_n}$. Under this
natural identification $\Phi_a$ becomes the invariants functor, which is left
exact (kernels of equivariant maps are computed pointwise), and therefore
$\Phi_a$ is exact; in that case the induced map $\Phi_a(W)\to\Phi_a(V)$ is
injective for every sub-FI-module $W\subseteq V$
([[def-submodule]], [[def-module-homomorphism-kernel-image-and-cokernel]]), so
$\Phi_a(W)$ is identified with a submodule of $\Phi_a(V)$. Finite averaging
uses only the finite groups $S_n$; no choice principle is used.

Let $V$ be an FI-module over $k$ and let $\Phi_a$ and $T$ be the coinvariant
functors and transition maps of
[[def-fi-coinvariant-functors-and-transition-maps]]. The **injectivity degree**
$\operatorname{inj-deg}(V)$ is the least $s\ge0$ such that for every $a\ge0$
the transition map $T\colon\Phi_a(V)_n\to\Phi_a(V)_{n+1}$ is injective for all
$n\ge s$; the **surjectivity degree** $\operatorname{surj-deg}(V)$ is the least
$s\ge0$ such that for every $a\ge0$ the map $T$ is surjective for all $n\ge s$.
The **stability degree** is

$$\operatorname{stab-deg}(V):=\max\bigl(\operatorname{inj-deg}(V),\operatorname{surj-deg}(V)\bigr).$$

Each of the three is $+\infty$ when no such $s$ exists; here the bounds are
read as elements of the extended nonnegative integers
$\mathbb N\cup\{+\infty\}$ with the evident order, in which every nonempty
subset of $\mathbb N$ has a least element
([[def-natural-numbers]]), so "the least $s$" is well defined. Equivalently,
$T\colon\Phi_a(V)_n\to\Phi_a(V)_{n+1}$ is an isomorphism for all $a\ge0$ and
all $n\ge\operatorname{stab-deg}(V)$: the map is an isomorphism exactly when it
is both injective and surjective, and for finite bounds a threshold that
controls all $a$ simultaneously is the larger of the two thresholds, while
each of the two stated bounds remains the least threshold controlling its own
property.

The three bounds are kept distinct: $\operatorname{stab-deg}(V)$ is the maximum
of the other two, and nothing in the definition requires
$\operatorname{inj-deg}(V)=\operatorname{surj-deg}(V)$. No finiteness is
asserted: each bound is allowed to be $+\infty$. No choice principle is used.

Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $0$ and let $V$ be an FI-module over $k$
with finite-dimensional values, weight $d:=\operatorname{weight}(V)<\infty$ and
stability degree $s:=\operatorname{stab-deg}(V)<\infty$
([[def-weight-of-a-characteristic-zero-fi-module]],
[[def-injectivity-surjectivity-and-stability-degree-of-an-fi-module]]). Let
$(V_n,\varphi_n)$ be the consistent sequence determined by $V$
([[def-uniform-representation-stability-for-consistent-sn-sequences]]). Then
$(V_n,\varphi_n)$ is uniformly representation stable with stable range
$n\ge d+s$: the maps $\varphi_n$ are injective for all $n\ge d+s$, the
$S_{n+1}$-span of $\varphi_n(V_n)$ is all of $V_{n+1}$ for all $n\ge d+s$, and
for every partition $\lambda$ the multiplicity $c_{\lambda,n}$ of $V(\lambda)_n$
in $V_n$ is independent of $n$ for all $n\ge d+s$. No choice principle is
used.

derivations.claim: $(\Rightarrow)$ Assume that $V$ is finitely generated, say generated in degree $\le g$. By [F3] $\operatorname{surj-deg}(V)\le g$, and by [F2] there is a finite surjection $M:=\bigoplus_{i=0}^{g}M(i)^{\oplus b_i}\twoheadrightarrow V$; let $K$ be its kernel. The module $M$ is finitely generated (each $M(i)$ is generated in degree $\le i$ by [F2]), so $K$ is finitely generated by [F5] applied over the field $k$; say $K$ is generated in degree $\le r$. These data will bound the injectivity degree of $V$ below.

$(\Leftarrow)$ Conversely, assume that $(V_n,\varphi_n)$ is uniformly representation stable with range $n\ge N$. For $n\ge N$ condition (II) says that the $S_{n+1}$-span of $\varphi_n(V_n)$ is all of $V_{n+1}$, and every injection $f\colon[n]\to[n+1]$ equals $\sigma\circ f_0$ for the standard inclusion $f_0$ and some $\sigma\in S_{n+1}$, so $V_{n+1}$ is spanned by the images $f_*(V_n)$ over all injections $f\colon[n]\to[n+1]$. The values in degrees $\le N$ lie in $\operatorname{span}_V(V_{\le N})$ by [F2], and if $V_m\subseteq\operatorname{span}_V(V_{\le N})_m$ for some $m\ge N$, then every $f_*(V_m)$ lies in $\operatorname{span}_V(V_{\le N})_{m+1}$ because the span is a sub-FI-module; the displayed spanning property of condition (II) then gives $V_{m+1}\subseteq\operatorname{span}_V(V_{\le N})_{m+1}$. By induction $V_m\subseteq\operatorname{span}_V(V_{\le N})_m$ for every $m\ge0$, hence $V=\operatorname{span}_V(V_{\le N})$. Each $V_{[m]}$ with $m\le N$ is finite-dimensional, hence generated by finitely many elements; let $\Sigma$ be the finite union of these finitely many finite generating sets, so that $\operatorname{span}_V(\Sigma)\supseteq V_{[m]}$ for every $m\le N$. For a finite set $S$ with $|S|=m\le N$ and a bijection $\beta\colon[m]\to S$ one has $V_S=\beta_*(V_{[m]})\subseteq\operatorname{span}_V(\Sigma)_S$, so $\operatorname{span}_V(\Sigma)\supseteq V_{\le N}$ and therefore $\operatorname{span}_V(\Sigma)=V$; thus $V$ is finitely generated.

Returning to $(\Rightarrow)$: for every $a$, the exactness of $\Phi_a$ over the characteristic-zero field $k$ gives an exact sequence $0\to\Phi_a(K)\to\Phi_a(M)\to\Phi_a(V)\to0$ by [F6]. The module $M$ is a finite direct sum of copies of the free modules $M(i)$, each of injectivity degree $0$ by [F4], so $T\colon\Phi_a(M)_n\to\Phi_a(M)_{n+1}$ is injective for all $n$ by [F6] and [F7]; and $T\colon\Phi_a(K)_n\to\Phi_a(K)_{n+1}$ is surjective for $n\ge r$ by [F3]. Hence $T\colon\Phi_a(V)_n\to\Phi_a(V)_{n+1}$ is injective for $n\ge r$: a lift $\tilde x\in\Phi_a(M)_n$ of $x$ with $Tx=0$ has $T\tilde x$ in the image of $\Phi_a(K)$, so $T\tilde x=T\tilde y$ for some $\tilde y\in\Phi_a(K)_n$, and injectivity on $\Phi_a(M)$ gives $\tilde x=\tilde y$, whence $x=0$. Therefore $\operatorname{inj-deg}(V)\le r$ by [F7], and $\operatorname{stab-deg}(V)\le\max(g,r)$ since $\operatorname{surj-deg}(V)\le g$.

Under the assumption of step 1.1 the weight is finite, indeed $\operatorname{weight}(V)\le g$ by [F3] over the characteristic-zero field $k$, and $\operatorname{stab-deg}(V)\le\max(g,r)<\infty$ by step 2.1. By [F8] the sequence $(V_n,\varphi_n)$ is uniformly representation stable, with stable range $n\ge g+\max(g,r)$.

Steps 1.1, 2.1 and 3.1 prove that finite generation implies uniform representation stability (through finiteness of stability degree and weight and the preceding proposition), and step 1.2 proves the converse; hence for an FI-module with finite-dimensional values over a characteristic-zero field the two properties are equivalent.

boundaries.evidence: step 1.2: the range N >= 0 is inclusive and the finite set Sigma of generators of the values up to degree N may be empty when V = 0.
step 1.1: for V = 0 the degree g = 0 works, the free presentation has zero summands and K = 0 is finitely generated.
step 2.1: the exact sequence is applied for one fixed a at a time and the chase uses one lift x-tilde and one correction y-tilde.
step 1.2: the stability range N may be 0, and the induction over m >= N then covers every rank without a base-case exception.
step 2.1: the threshold n >= r-prime is inclusive and yields inj-deg(V) <= r-prime; the endpoint n = r-prime is part of the chase.
step 1.2: finite generating sets of the finite-dimensional values V_{[m]} for m <= N are combined into a single finite Sigma; only finitely many choices occur.
step 3.1: the forward implication from finite generation to uniform representation stability is concluded from the finiteness of weight and stability degree.
step 1.2: the reverse implication from uniform representation stability to finite generation is proved by spanning every value from V_{<= N}.

citations.quote:
Let $V$ be an FI-module over $k$
([[def-fi-category-and-fi-module]]), with free FI-modules $M(m)$ as in
[[def-free-fi-module-generated-by-an-sm-module]] and span as in
[[def-finite-generation-and-generation-degree-of-an-fi-module]].

(a) For $v\in V_m$ the map of FI-modules $M(m)\to V$ sending the canonical
generator $\mathrm{id}_m\in M(m)_m$ to $v$ has image $\operatorname{span}_V(v)$;
more generally, for any set $\Sigma$ of elements, each lying in some $V_S$, the
canonical map $\bigoplus_{s\in\Sigma}M(|S_s|)\to V$ sending the generator of
the summand indexed by $s$ to $s$ has image $\operatorname{span}_V(\Sigma)$.

(b) $V$ is finitely generated if and only if there is a finite family
$m_1,\dots,m_k\ge0$ with a surjection

$$M(m_1)\oplus\cdots\oplus M(m_k)\twoheadrightarrow V;$$

$V$ is generated in degree $\le d$ if and only if there is a surjection
$\bigoplus_{i\in I}M(m_i)\twoheadrightarrow V$ with $m_i\le d$ for all $i$. In
particular, if $V$ is generated in degree $\le d$, then the evaluation map
$\bigoplus_{m\le d}M(V_m)\to V$, whose restriction to each copy of $M(m)$
indexed by an element $v\in V_m$ sends $\mathrm{id}_m\mapsto v$, is surjective.

(c) If $V$ is finitely generated, then $V_S$ is a finitely generated $k$-module
for every finite set $S$
([[def-generated-cyclic-finitely-generated-and-free-modules]]).

No choice principle is used: all maps come from a finite or explicitly indexed
set of generators, and the image computations are linear algebra on the values
at a fixed finite set.

Let $W$ be an FB-module over $k$, i.e. a functor from the groupoid of finite
sets and bijections to $k\text{-}\mathrm{Mod}$ ([[def-fi-category-and-fi-module]]);
thus $W(T)$ is a $k$-module for every finite set $T$, and every bijection
$\beta\colon T\to T'$ gives an isomorphism $W(\beta)\colon W(T)\to W(T')$.
Because an FB-module is defined on all finite sets, no transport choices are
needed below.

The **free FI-module** $M(W)$ assigns to a finite set $S$ the direct sum

$$M(W)_S:=\bigoplus_{T\subseteq S}W(T)$$

over all subsets $T\subseteq S$ ([[def-subset-and-proper-subset]],
[[def-direct-sum-of-a-family-of-modules]]; only finitely many summands occur).
For an injection $f\colon S\to S'$ and a subset $T\subseteq S$, the restriction
$f|_T\colon T\to f(T)$ is a bijection
([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]), and the transition map
$f_*\colon M(W)_S\to M(W)_{S'}$ is the sum of the isomorphisms
$W(f|_T)\colon W(T)\to W(f(T))$ over all $T\subseteq S$. This is $k$-linear and
functorial, since $(f'\circ f)|_T=f'|_{f(T)}\circ f|_T$; hence $M(W)$ is an
FI-module over $k$.

For $S=[n]=\{0,\dots,n-1\}$ the symmetric group $S_n$
([[def-finite-symmetric-group-and-permutation-notation]]) acts by
$\sigma\cdot T:=\sigma(T)$ and $W(\sigma|_T)$, and this is a left action
making $M(W)_n$ a left $kS_n$-module ([[def-group-ring]]). Grouping the sum by
the cardinality of $T$, the subsets of cardinality $a$ form a single $S_n$-orbit
with stabilizer the ordered block subgroup
$S_{\{0,\dots,a-1\}}\times S_{\{a,\dots,n-1\}}\cong S_a\times S_{n-a}$, so the
orbit summand is identified with an induced module
([[def-induced-r-linear-g-module-by-h-covariant-functions]]):

$$M(W)_n\cong\bigoplus_{a=0}^{n}\operatorname{Ind}_{S_a\times S_{n-a}}^{S_n}\bigl(W_a\boxtimes k\bigr),$$

where $W_a:=W(\{0,\dots,a-1\})$ is the value of the FB-module on an $a$-element
set, the first factor acts on $W_a$ through $W$ and the second factor acts
trivially, and $\boxtimes$ is the external tensor product of modules for the
two direct factors ([[def-outer-induction-product-for-symmetric-group-characters]],
[[lem-character-ring-of-a-direct-product-is-the-tensor-product]],
[[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]]).

**Adjunction.** Let $\pi$ be the functor from FI-modules to FB-modules that
forgets the maps between distinct cardinalities. The inclusion of the $T=S$
summand is a natural map $\eta_W\colon W\to\pi M(W)$, and evaluating a map
$F\colon M(W)\to V$ of FI-modules on that summand yields a map of FB-modules
$\pi F\circ\eta_W\colon W\to\pi V$. Conversely, a map of FB-modules
$\varphi\colon W\to\pi V$ extends uniquely to a map of FI-modules
$\widetilde\varphi\colon M(W)\to V$ whose value on the summand $W(T)\subseteq
M(W)_S$ is $V(\iota_{T,S})\circ\varphi_T$, with $\iota_{T,S}\colon T\to S$ the
inclusion; the components are compatible with injections and the two
constructions are inverse, so
$\operatorname{Hom}_{FI\text{-}Mod}(M(W),V)\cong
\operatorname{Hom}_{FB\text{-}Mod}(W,\pi V)$ naturally in $V$ and $W$: $M$ is
left adjoint to $\pi$, with unit $\eta$.

For $m\ge0$ write $k[S_m]$ for the FB-module with $k[S_m](T)$ the free $k$-module
on the bijections $[m]\to T$, and zero when $|T|\ne m$; its value on an
$m$-element set is the regular representation of $S_m$. Put
$M(m):=M(k[S_m])$. Then $M(m)_S$ has as $k$-basis the injections
$[m]\hookrightarrow S$ — equivalently, the ordered sequences of $m$ distinct
elements of $S$ — and for a partition $\lambda$ with $|\lambda|=m$ and a field
$k$ of characteristic $0$, put $M(\lambda):=M(S^\lambda_k)$, where the FB-module
$S^\lambda_k$ is supported on $m$-element sets and $S^\lambda_k(T):=
k[\operatorname{Iso}([m],T)]\otimes_{kS_m}S^\lambda_k$. By the adjunction, a map
$M(m)\to V$ of FI-modules corresponds naturally to the choice of an element of
$V_m$: the module $M(m)$ represents the functor $V\mapsto V_m$. All
constructions are given by finitely many canonical bijections of finite sets;
no choice principle is used.

Let $V$ be an FI-module over $k$, with surjectivity degree and stability degree
as in [[def-injectivity-surjectivity-and-stability-degree-of-an-fi-module]] and
weight as in [[def-weight-of-a-characteristic-zero-fi-module]].

(a) Every quotient $V\twoheadrightarrow W$ of FI-modules satisfies
$\operatorname{surj-deg}(W)\le\operatorname{surj-deg}(V)$.

(b) If $V$ is generated in degree $\le d$
([[def-free-fi-module-generated-by-an-sm-module]] is the source of the
notation), then $\operatorname{surj-deg}(V)\le d$.

(c) If moreover $k$ is a field of characteristic $0$ and $V$ is generated in
degree $\le d$, then $\operatorname{weight}(V)\le d$.

No choice principle is used.

Let $W$ be an FB-module over $k$ and let $M(W)$ be the free FI-module of
[[def-free-fi-module-generated-by-an-sm-module]]. Then
$\operatorname{inj-deg}(M(W))=0$, and if $W_i=0$ for all $i>m$ then
$\operatorname{surj-deg}(M(W))\le m$; in particular
$M(m)=M(k[S_m])$ satisfies $\operatorname{inj-deg}(M(m))=0$ and
$\operatorname{stab-deg}(M(m))=m$
([[def-injectivity-surjectivity-and-stability-degree-of-an-fi-module]]).
If moreover $k$ is a field of characteristic $0$ and $\lambda$ is a partition,
then $\operatorname{weight}(M(\lambda))=|\lambda|$
([[def-weight-of-a-characteristic-zero-fi-module]]) and
$\operatorname{stab-deg}(M(\lambda))=\lambda_1$. No choice principle is used.

Let $k$ be a commutative Noetherian ring containing $\mathbb Q$
([[def-noetherian-ring]], [[def-restriction-and-extension-of-scalars]]), and
let $V$ be a finitely generated FI-module over $k$
([[def-finite-generation-and-generation-degree-of-an-fi-module]],
[[def-fi-category-and-fi-module]]). Then every sub-FI-module
$W\subseteq V$ is again finitely generated: the category of FI-modules over
$k$ is Noetherian, in the sense that every subobject of a finitely generated
object is finitely generated. The hypothesis that $k$ contains $\mathbb Q$ is
used only through the exactness of the functors $\Phi_a$ and through
restriction of scalars to $\mathbb Q$
([[def-fi-coinvariant-functors-and-transition-maps]]). No choice principle is
used.

A **graded $k[T]$-module** consists of $k$-modules $U_n$, $n\ge0$, together
with $k$-linear maps $T=T_n\colon U_n\to U_{n+1}$ for all $n\ge0$. A
**morphism** $U\to U'$ of graded $k[T]$-modules is a family of $k$-linear maps
$u_n\colon U_n\to U'_n$ with $u_{n+1}\circ T_n=T'_n\circ u_n$ for all $n$.

Fix $a\ge0$, a set $\mathbf a$ of cardinality $a$, and a functorial disjoint
union of finite sets. Let $V$ be an FI-module over $k$
([[def-fi-category-and-fi-module]]) and let $n\ge0$. Put

$$\Phi_a(V)_n:=(V_{\mathbf a\sqcup n})_{S_n},$$

the coinvariants of the $kS_n$-module $V_{\mathbf a\sqcup n}$: the quotient by
the span of the elements $\sigma\cdot v-v$, $\sigma\in S_n$, $v\in
V_{\mathbf a\sqcup n}$ ([[def-coinvariants-functor-of-a-group-module]],
[[def-quotient-module]]). Equivalently $\Phi_a(V)_n=k\otimes_{kS_n}
V_{\mathbf a\sqcup n}$, the two descriptions being identified by the balancing
argument of [[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]] and
the corresponding identification for $\mathbb Z$ in
[[def-coinvariants-functor-of-a-group-module]]; the group ring $kS_n$ is a
unital $k$-algebra with basis the group elements
([[def-group-ring]], [[thm-group-ring-is-a-unital-algebra-with-basis-g]]).

To define the transition map $T\colon\Phi_a(V)_n\to\Phi_a(V)_{n+1}$, choose an
injection $f\colon n\to n+1$. It induces the injection
$\mathrm{id}_{\mathbf a}\sqcup f\colon\mathbf a\sqcup n\to\mathbf a\sqcup n+1$
and hence a $k$-linear map $(V_{\mathbf a\sqcup n}\to
V_{\mathbf a\sqcup n+1})$. This map is $S_n$-equivariant, where $S_n$ acts on
the target through the injection $\mathrm{id}_{\mathbf a}\sqcup f$, so it
descends to the quotient map $T=T_f$ on coinvariants. The map $T_f$ is
independent of $f$: for two injections $f,g\colon n\to n+1$ the composite
$g\circ f^{-1}$ is a bijection $f(n)\to g(n)$, which extends along the
complement to a permutation $\tau\in S_{n+1}$ with $g=\tau\circ f$; then
$\mathrm{id}_{\mathbf a}\sqcup g=(\mathrm{id}_{\mathbf a}\sqcup
\tau)\circ(\mathrm{id}_{\mathbf a}\sqcup f)$, and the map induced by
$\mathrm{id}_{\mathbf a}\sqcup\tau$ on
$(V_{\mathbf a\sqcup n+1})_{S_{n+1}}$ is the identity because it comes from
the action of the group element $\tau$. Thus $T$ is well defined and
$(\Phi_a(V),T)$ is a graded $k[T]$-module.

A map of FI-modules $\alpha\colon V\to W$ gives $k$-linear maps
$\alpha_{\mathbf a\sqcup n}\colon V_{\mathbf a\sqcup n}\to W_{\mathbf
a\sqcup n}$ commuting with the $S_n$-actions and with the maps induced by
$\mathrm{id}_{\mathbf a}\sqcup f$, hence maps $(\Phi_a\alpha)_n$ of coinvariants
commuting with $T$; so $\Phi_a$ is a functor from FI-modules over $k$ to graded
$k[T]$-modules.

**Exactness.** Coinvariants of a group module are right exact
([[prop-the-coinvariants-functor-is-right-exact]]), so the functor
$M\mapsto M_{S_n}\cong k\otimes_{kS_n}M$ is right exact and each $\Phi_a$ is
right exact in every degree. If $k$ contains $\mathbb Q$, then $1/n!$ exists in $k$
and the averaging map
$s\colon\Phi_a(V)_n\to V_{\mathbf a\sqcup n}$,
$s([v])=\frac1{n!}\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\sigma\cdot v$, is a well-defined
$k$-linear section of the quotient map that is natural in $V$; it identifies
$\Phi_a(V)_n$ with the invariants $V_{\mathbf a\sqcup n}^{S_n}$. Under this
natural identification $\Phi_a$ becomes the invariants functor, which is left
exact (kernels of equivariant maps are computed pointwise), and therefore
$\Phi_a$ is exact; in that case the induced map $\Phi_a(W)\to\Phi_a(V)$ is
injective for every sub-FI-module $W\subseteq V$
([[def-submodule]], [[def-module-homomorphism-kernel-image-and-cokernel]]), so
$\Phi_a(W)$ is identified with a submodule of $\Phi_a(V)$. Finite averaging
uses only the finite groups $S_n$; no choice principle is used.

Let $V$ be an FI-module over $k$ and let $\Phi_a$ and $T$ be the coinvariant
functors and transition maps of
[[def-fi-coinvariant-functors-and-transition-maps]]. The **injectivity degree**
$\operatorname{inj-deg}(V)$ is the least $s\ge0$ such that for every $a\ge0$
the transition map $T\colon\Phi_a(V)_n\to\Phi_a(V)_{n+1}$ is injective for all
$n\ge s$; the **surjectivity degree** $\operatorname{surj-deg}(V)$ is the least
$s\ge0$ such that for every $a\ge0$ the map $T$ is surjective for all $n\ge s$.
The **stability degree** is

$$\operatorname{stab-deg}(V):=\max\bigl(\operatorname{inj-deg}(V),\operatorname{surj-deg}(V)\bigr).$$

Each of the three is $+\infty$ when no such $s$ exists; here the bounds are
read as elements of the extended nonnegative integers
$\mathbb N\cup\{+\infty\}$ with the evident order, in which every nonempty
subset of $\mathbb N$ has a least element
([[def-natural-numbers]]), so "the least $s$" is well defined. Equivalently,
$T\colon\Phi_a(V)_n\to\Phi_a(V)_{n+1}$ is an isomorphism for all $a\ge0$ and
all $n\ge\operatorname{stab-deg}(V)$: the map is an isomorphism exactly when it
is both injective and surjective, and for finite bounds a threshold that
controls all $a$ simultaneously is the larger of the two thresholds, while
each of the two stated bounds remains the least threshold controlling its own
property.

The three bounds are kept distinct: $\operatorname{stab-deg}(V)$ is the maximum
of the other two, and nothing in the definition requires
$\operatorname{inj-deg}(V)=\operatorname{surj-deg}(V)$. No finiteness is
asserted: each bound is allowed to be $+\infty$. No choice principle is used.

Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $0$ and let $V$ be an FI-module over $k$
with finite-dimensional values, weight $d:=\operatorname{weight}(V)<\infty$ and
stability degree $s:=\operatorname{stab-deg}(V)<\infty$
([[def-weight-of-a-characteristic-zero-fi-module]],
[[def-injectivity-surjectivity-and-stability-degree-of-an-fi-module]]). Let
$(V_n,\varphi_n)$ be the consistent sequence determined by $V$
([[def-uniform-representation-stability-for-consistent-sn-sequences]]). Then
$(V_n,\varphi_n)$ is uniformly representation stable with stable range
$n\ge d+s$: the maps $\varphi_n$ are injective for all $n\ge d+s$, the
$S_{n+1}$-span of $\varphi_n(V_n)$ is all of $V_{n+1}$ for all $n\ge d+s$, and
for every partition $\lambda$ the multiplicity $c_{\lambda,n}$ of $V(\lambda)_n$
in $V_n$ is independent of $n$ for all $n\ge d+s$. No choice principle is
used.

Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $0$ and let $V$ be an FI-module over $k$
([[def-fi-category-and-fi-module]]). For a partition $\lambda$ and
$n\ge|\lambda|+\lambda_1$ put $\lambda[n]:=(n-|\lambda|,\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\dots)$,
the first-row padding ([[def-first-row-padding-of-a-partition]]), and let

$$V(\lambda)_n:=k\otimes_{\mathbb Q}S^{\lambda[n]}_{\mathbb Q}$$

be the scalar extension of the rational Specht model of $\lambda[n]$
([[thm-complex-specht-modules-are-irreducible]],
[[lem-specht-modules-classify-irreducibles-over-characteristic-zero-fields]]).
By the classification lemma, $V(\lambda)_n$ is the irreducible $kS_n$-module
with label $\lambda[n]$, and every irreducible $kS_n$-module is isomorphic to
exactly one $V(\lambda)_n$: indeed, every partition $\mu=(\mu_1,\mu_2,\dots)$
of $n$ is uniquely $\lambda[n]$ for the partition
$\lambda=(\mu_2,\mu_3,\dots)$ obtained by deleting the first row, and
$n\ge|\lambda|+\lambda_1$ holds precisely because $\mu_1\ge\mu_2$;
consequently the labels $\lambda[n]$ run over the partitions of $n$ without
repetition.

Say that $V(\lambda)_n$ **occurs as a constituent** of $V_n$ when there are
$kS_n$-submodules $U\subseteq W\subseteq V_n$ with
$W/U\cong V(\lambda)_n$ ([[def-submodule]], [[def-quotient-module]]); this is a
condition on subquotients and requires no decomposition or finite-dimensionality
of $V_n$. The **weight** of $V$ is

$$\operatorname{weight}(V):=\sup\bigl\{|\lambda|:V(\lambda)_n\text{ occurs as a constituent of }V_n\text{ for some }n\ge|\lambda|+\lambda_1\bigr\},$$

the supremum over all pairs $(\lambda,n)$ as displayed. The set of integers
displayed is a set of nonnegative integers, so the supremum is well defined in
$\mathbb N\cup\{\infty\}$; it is $0$ for $V=0$, and $\operatorname{weight}(V)=\infty$
exactly when the displayed set is unbounded. No finiteness of
$\operatorname{weight}(V)$ is asserted.

If $W$ is a **subquotient** of $V$, meaning that $W\cong U'/U$ for sub-FI-modules
$U\subseteq U'\subseteq V$ computed pointwise, then
$\operatorname{weight}(W)\le\operatorname{weight}(V)$: a constituent of $W_n$ is
a subquotient of the subquotient $U'_n/U_n$ of $V_n$, hence a subquotient of
$V_n$, so it contributes the same label $|\lambda|$ to the supremum for $V$. No
choice principle is used: the labels $\lambda[n]$, constituents and the
supremum are set-theoretic data, and no bases or decompositions are chosen.

Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $0$, let $V$ be an FI-module over $k$
([[def-fi-category-and-fi-module]]), and put
$s:=\operatorname{stab-deg}(V)<\infty$
([[def-injectivity-surjectivity-and-stability-degree-of-an-fi-module]]). Then
for every $n\ge0$, every irreducible constituent $V(\lambda)_n$ of the
$kS_n$-module $V_n$ satisfies

$$\lambda_1\le s.$$

Equivalently, since the padded partition is
$\lambda[n]=(n-|\lambda|,\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\dots)$, the second row of the
Specht diagram $\lambda[n]$ has length at most $s$; the first row of the
padding tail is the second row of the full diagram
([[def-first-row-padding-of-a-partition]],
[[def-weight-of-a-characteristic-zero-fi-module]]). No choice principle is
used.

For every partition $\lambda$ with $|\lambda|=m$ there is a character polynomial
$P_\lambda\in\mathbb Q[X_1,X_2,\dots]$ of weighted degree at most $m$
([[def-character-polynomial-in-cycle-counts]]) such that for every
$n\ge m+\lambda_1$ and every $\sigma\in S_n$

$$\chi^{\lambda[n]}(\sigma)=P_\lambda\bigl(X_1(\sigma),X_2(\sigma),\dots\bigr),$$

where $\lambda[n]=(n-m,\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\dots)$ is the first-row padding
([[def-first-row-padding-of-a-partition]]) and $\chi^{\lambda[n]}$ is the
character of the irreducible Specht module $S^{\lambda[n]}$
([[thm-complex-specht-modules-are-irreducible]]). No choice principle is used.

Let $\alpha=(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_k)$ be a partition with $|\alpha|=\alpha_1+\cdots+\alpha_k$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]), and let $n\ge0$ be
an integer. Whenever

$$n\;\ge\;|\alpha|+\alpha_1,$$

define the **first-row padding** of $\alpha$ to size $n$ to be
$$\alpha[n]:=\bigl(n-|\alpha|,\ \alpha_1,\ \alpha_2,\ \dots,\ \alpha_k\bigr).$$

The threshold is exact.

**Above the threshold.** Suppose $n\ge|\alpha|+\alpha_1$. Then
$n-|\alpha|\ge\alpha_1\ge0$, so every entry of the displayed sequence is a
nonnegative integer, the entries sum to $(n-|\alpha|)+|\alpha|=n$, and the
sequence is weakly decreasing because $n-|\alpha|\ge\alpha_1$ and $\alpha$ is
weakly decreasing ([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]).
If $\alpha$ is nonempty then $\alpha_1\ge1$, hence $n-|\alpha|\ge1$ and the
displayed sequence is a partition of $n$ with positive parts. If
$\alpha=\varnothing$ then the displayed sequence is $(n)$; this is a partition
of $n$ for every $n\ge1$, while for $n=0$ one takes $\varnothing[0]:=\varnothing$,
the unique partition of $0$. Thus the padding is defined and is a partition of
$n$ on the whole displayed range.

**Below the threshold.** If $\alpha$ is nonempty and $n<|\alpha|+\alpha_1$,
then $n-|\alpha|<\alpha_1$; if also $n\ge|\alpha|$ the leading entry is
nonnegative but smaller than the second entry $\alpha_1$, and if $n<|\alpha|$
it is negative. In both cases the displayed sequence is not a partition, so
$\alpha[n]$ is left undefined. The threshold $|\alpha|+\alpha_1$ is therefore
the exact size at which the padded family begins: at
$n=|\alpha|+\alpha_1$ the padding equals $(\alpha_1,\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\dots)$,
which is a partition with a repeated first part when $\alpha$ is nonempty.

**Neutrality of the notation.** This definition records a family of partitions;
it asserts no constancy of any quantity along the family and no stability
property. The same notation is used by the FI-module and
representation-stability developments, where the padding threshold reappears as
the generation degree of the family under consideration.

Throughout, $R$ is a commutative ring, $n\ge0$, and $\lambda\vdash n$ with
Young diagram $[\lambda]$. Tabloids, the left action
$\sigma\cdot\{t\}:=\{\sigma\cdot t\}$ of $S_n$ on the finite set
$\Omega_\lambda$ of $\lambda$-tabloids, and the complex tabloid module
$M^\lambda=\mathbb C^{(\Omega_\lambda)}$ are as in
[[def-young-subgroup-tabloid-and-permutation-module]]: rows are labelled and
the order of entries inside a row is forgotten.

**The tabloid module over $R$.** Put
$$M^\lambda_R:=R^{(\Omega_\lambda)},$$
the free left $R$-module with the tabloids as $R$-basis, and let $S_n$ act on
$M^\lambda_R$ by $R$-linear extension of
$\sigma\cdot\{t\}:=\{\sigma\cdot t\}$ on basis elements. The row-set
computation of [[def-young-subgroup-tabloid-and-permutation-module]] shows
that this rule is well defined on tabloids, and because the action on tableaux
is a left action, $\mathrm{id}\cdot\{t\}=\{t\}$ and
$\sigma\cdot(\tau\cdot\{t\})=(\sigma\tau)\cdot\{t\}$; hence $M^\lambda_R$ is a
left module over $S_n$ and over the group ring $R[S_n]$.

**Antisymmetrizers, polytabloids, and Specht modules.** Let $t$ be a
$\lambda$-tableau with column stabilizer $C_t$
([[def-row-and-column-stabilizers-of-a-tableau]]), and let
$\operatorname{sgn}:S_n\to\{+1,-1\}$ be the sign homomorphism
([[thm-sign-is-a-homomorphism]]); its values are read in $R$ through the
unique unital ring homomorphism $\mathbb Z\to R$. Define
$$\kappa_t:=\sum_{\gamma\in C_t}\operatorname{sgn}(\gamma)\,\gamma\ \in R[S_n],\qquad e_t:=\kappa_t\cdot\{t\}=\sum_{\gamma\in C_t}\operatorname{sgn}(\gamma)\,\{\gamma\cdot t\}\ \in M^\lambda_R,$$
and let
$$S^\lambda_R:=\operatorname{span}_R\{\,e_t:\ t\text{ is a }\lambda\text{-tableau}\,\}\ \subseteq M^\lambda_R.$$
All sums here are finite sums over the finite group $C_t$, so $\kappa_t$,
$e_t$ and $S^\lambda_R$ are well defined for every commutative ring $R$. For
the empty partition the empty tableau is the unique one and has
